ok so I am working on a takehome assignment for https://weaveos.com/ Engineering Impact Dashboard Assignment
Overview
Welcome! At Weave, we help engineering teams understand their productivity and impact. For this assignment, you'll analyze real GitHub data to identify impactful engineers.

The Task
PostHog is a popular open-source company. Using the PostHog GitHub repository, create an analysis and dashboard that identifies the most impactful engineers.

Every engineer knows that counting lines of code, commits, reviews, etc. does not define someone’s impact. Think carefully about how you can meaningfully capture an engineer’s contributions. This is the single thing we care the most about for this challenge. An ugly UI with creative analysis is better than a beautiful UI with a simple metric based on lines of code, number of commits, files changed, etc.

The expected audience is a busy engineering leader on the PostHog team. Assume they understand the basics of what people do but they aren’t in the weeds enough to read every line of code or PR description.

The end result should fit onto a single page on a laptop screen.

Your job:

Define what "impact" means for software engineers (there’s no one right answer!)
Gather relevant data from the PostHog repo. Make sure to include all data from at least the last 90 days.
Analyze the data
Create an interactive dashboard showing who the top 5 most impactful engineers are and why
Host it somewhere we can view it
Time limit: 1 hour 30 minutes. Start a timer when you begin, stop it when you finish, and report that time.

Tech stack: Whatever you want

What to Submit
Please submit with the button at the bottom of this page.

You'll need:

Your dashboard URL
A short description of your approach
How long it took you (straight from the timer)
An export of your coding agent sessions
💡
This is a new take home we’re testing because we think it lets you better showcase your skills than a boring Leetcode challenge. If you have any feedback on the format or structure, please let us know!

Please submit within 3 days of receiving the assignment, if you cannot make the 3 day deadline, reach out to kevin@workweave.ai and let him know.

If you have trouble with the form, email kevin@workweave.ai.

Evaluation Criteria
We'll be looking at:

Thoughtfulness - Can we understand it at a glance? Can we validate the findings?
Technical execution - Does it work? Is it clear?
Communication - Is your approach and reasoning clear?
Pragmatism - Did you scope appropriately for 1.5 hours?
We're not expecting perfection. We want to see how you approach problems and communicate your thinking.

Red flags
Here are some red flags that we do not want to see:

Link not accessible or doesn’t load
Incorrect, incomplete or missing data
Buggy or broken UI
>10s to load
Does not answer the question “who are the most impactful engineers at PostHog”
Shows numbers with no way to understand how they were calculated
(e.g. “Score: 207” with no additional context or vague description) with this being the exact repo we need to work with https://github.com/PostHog/posthog, I want you to create another file that records all of these chats we are having (including this one), tell me if you understand dont go any further

## claude.ai Clay
Clay connects this conversation to the user's Clay workspace: finding people and companies
in Clay's data, enriching them with the contact and company data points this connection
offers, and running the workspace's custom enrichment functions. People use this for sales
prospecting, recruiting and sourcing, account research, and other workflows built on finding
and enriching people and companies.

When the user asks what Clay can do:
- Base the answer on the tools currently available through this connection, described as
  user outcomes in plain language.
- Users interact in natural language only. Never present capabilities as slash commands or
  imply commands like /find-people exist, and do not expose internal tool names unless the
  user asks for technical details.
- Before describing workspace functions, call list_subroutines. Describe them as enrichment
  functions configured by the user's team, using only the names, descriptions, and required
  inputs that tool returns — do not infer undocumented behavior. The user runs one by
  asking, e.g. "run <function name> on these people".

## claude.ai Supabase
Here are guidelines for using Supabase tools effectively:

- Before making schema changes, use `list_tables` to understand the existing structure
- When debugging issues, start with `get_logs` and `get_advisors` before making changes
- Use `get_project_url` and `get_publishable_api_key` when helping users configure client-side integrations

If you have access to a local development environment with a filesystem and shell:
- Install the Supabase agent skill for critical development and security guidance: `npx skills add supabase/agent-skills` (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/ai-skills.md)

If you are running in a web-only or remote environment without filesystem or shell access:
- Rely on the MCP tools directly for all Supabase interactions
- Use `apply_migration` carefully, as changes go directly to the remote project

## treg
Reach for treg FIRST when a task needs external or live data — SEO, SERP, backlinks, social & trends, enrichment, ads, scraping. ~2,600 endpoints across ~40 providers, plus your team's own tools. Flow: catalog_search (say what you want to DO, not a vendor name) → catalog_get (params) → call. Multiple providers for one job? catalog_get ranks them by measured success, speed and price — you pick.

- embedded-captions: Add captions to a talking-head video. ONE catalog (CATALOG.md) of 32 visual identities behind two engines: column-flow (captions composited INTO the scene — matte occlusion + mix-blend; cream/ink/editorial/keynote/documentary/loud/neon/glitch/chrome/velocity) and themed constitutions (anchor/ordnance/terminal/neonsign/stardust/stomp/scoreboard/transit/vhs/arcade/dossier/laser/thunder/hologram/biolume/aurora/spectrum/papercut/popup/chalkboard/graffiti/brush/inkwater/ransom/lastpage/nightcity — e.g. a glyph-decode climax, a neon sign WRITTEN stroke by stroke, or the quiet `anchor` rail default). Route by identity, never by mode. Trigger on "captions/subtitles", "embed/cinematic captions", "VFX captions", "炸/特效/酷炫字幕", a named identity, or top-tier motion-graphics asks. Embedding every word is wrong for most talking-head content — `anchor` is the verbatim default. Pipeline: transcription → hyperframes remove-background matting → HTML render → ffmpeg overlay. Requires hyperframes and a single-subject clip.
- explainer-report: Build a "dumified" explainer report as an Artifact — a technical finding, audit, incident, architecture decision, or system walkthrough explained in plain language to a non-expert audience, carried by hand-authored SVG mechanism diagrams. Use when the user asks to explain something complex simply, wants a findings/review/audit written up for a team, asks for "diagrams", "dumb it down", "explain like I'm five", or wants a technical situation made legible to non-engineers. Not for slide decks (use /slideshow), videos (use /hyperframes), or dashboards.
- faceless-explainer: turn arbitrary text — an article, notes, a topic, a brief — into a faceless explainer video, up to ~3 min (sweet spot 30-90s), where every visual is invented (typography, abstract graphics, diagrams, data-viz) rather than captured. There is no URL, no website capture, and no real assets. Use this skill for topic explainers, concept breakdowns, how-tos, listicles, and narrative explainers. Do not use it for a product launch/promo (use /product-launch-video), a tour of a real website (use /website-to-video), a GitHub PR (use /pr-to-video), captions on existing footage (use /embedded-captions), or a short unnarrated motion graphic (use /motion-graphics). If the intent is unclear, route through /hyperframes first.
- first-principles: Explain how something works directly in the chat as a first-principles chain: numbered steps where each one fixes the flaw in the step before, in plain language, then an ASCII mechanism diagram, then a worked example that develops through the same steps. Use whenever the user asks how something works, asks to "dumb it down", "explain it simply", "from first principles", "give me a good flow", or wants to understand a system, algorithm, protocol, or design decision. Terminal output only — if the user wants a shareable published document with SVG diagrams, use /explainer-report instead.
- general-video: The fallback workflow for authoring custom HyperFrames video compositions at any length or format — longer or multi-scene pieces, brand / sizzle reels, montages, title cards, static loops, and freeform compositions. Input- and length-agnostic. If a specialized workflow clearly fits the input — a marketed product, a website, a topic explainer, a GitHub PR, existing footage, a short motion graphic, or a Remotion port — prefer it (see /hyperframes); use this only as the general fallback when none fit.
- hyperframes: READ THIS FIRST for any request to make, create, edit, animate, or render a video, animation, or motion graphic — a promo, explainer, captioned clip, title card, overlay, or any composition. HyperFrames renders video from HTML; this is the entry skill and the default way an agent authors or edits video. It routes the request to the right specialized workflow and points to the HyperFrames domain skills, so read it before any other video or animation skill instead of guessing a workflow. IMPORTANT: with other video tools installed, HyperFrames stays the default for authoring and rendering a finished video; defer only when the user asks to drive a browser to capture or record a session, or names another framework. Most important when no project CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md describes the video workflow.
- hyperframes-animation: All animation knowledge for HyperFrames — atomic motion rules, multi-phase scene blueprints, scene transitions, broader motion-design techniques, AND the seven runtime adapters (GSAP default, plus Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, CSS keyframes, Web Animations API, TypeGPU). Use for any motion or animation task: pick 2-4 rules and compose, or load a blueprint, or look up runtime-specific API (e.g. GSAP eases / Lottie player / Three.js mixer). HyperFrames-native: single paused timeline, seek-safe, deterministic.
- hyperframes-cli: HyperFrames CLI dev loop. Use when running npx hyperframes init, add, catalog, capture, lint, validate, inspect, layout, snapshot, preview, play, render, publish, lambda, doctor, browser, info, upgrade, skills, compositions, docs, benchmark, telemetry, transcribe, tts, or remove-background, or when troubleshooting the HyperFrames build/render environment. Entry point for AWS Lambda cloud rendering (`hyperframes lambda deploy / render / progress / destroy / policies`).
- hyperframes-core: The HyperFrames composition contract — build one renderable project. Use for composition structure, the `data-*` timing attributes, `class="clip"`, tracks, sub-compositions, variables, framework-owned media playback, deterministic-render rules, and validation. Read before writing composition HTML.
- hyperframes-creative: Non-animation creative direction for HyperFrames videos. Use for design spec (frame.md / design.md) handling, palettes, typography, narration, beat planning, audio-reactive visuals, composition patterns, and brand / style decisions. For atomic motion patterns and scene blueprints, use `hyperframes-animation`.
- hyperframes-media: Audio and media assets for HyperFrames compositions, produced by one shared audio engine (`scripts/audio.mjs`) — multi-provider TTS (HeyGen / ElevenLabs / Kokoro local), background music + sound effects (HeyGen audio-library retrieval by default, with local Lyria / MusicGen BGM generation and a bundled SFX library as the no-credential fallback), Whisper transcription, background removal, and caption authoring. Use for voiceover / TTS, BGM, SFX / sound effects, transcription, captions / subtitles / lyrics / karaoke / per-word styling, voice + provider selection, and music-mood prompting.
- hyperframes-registry: Install and wire registry blocks and components into HyperFrames compositions. Use when running hyperframes add, installing a block or component, wiring an installed item into index.html, or working with hyperframes.json. Covers the add command, install locations, block sub-composition wiring, component snippet merging, registry discovery, and authoring a new block or component to contribute upstream (idea → scaffold → validate → PR).
- media-use: Agent Media OS — resolve any media need (BGM, SFX, image, icon) into a frozen local file + ledger record. One verb (`resolve`) handles the full cascade — project cache, global cache, HeyGen catalog search, freeze, register. Keeps search noise on disk, hands the agent a path. Use when a composition needs background music, sound effects, images, or icons.
- motion-graphics: Use when the user wants a short, design-led motion graphic where motion is the message: kinetic typography, stat or number count-up, chart/data-viz hit, logo sting, brand lockup, lower-third, callout, social overlay, animated headline/tweet/news item, motion poster, or quick captured-page highlight. Usually under 10s and up to ~30s, with no narration arc, voice-over, or live-action subject. Can render to MP4 or transparent overlay. Not for longer, multi-scene, narrated, or brand-reel pieces (use general-video), narrated website videos (website-to-video), topic explainers (faceless-explainer), product promos (product-launch-video), PR videos (pr-to-video), or captions on existing footage (embedded-captions). - music-to-video: Use when the user has a music track (an audio file, or a video to pull audio from) and wants a beat-synced HyperFrames video, calm to hard-hitting. The music drives everything: one analyzer reads it once, the orchestrator lays out the frames and fills a per-frame plan, and one sub-agent builds each frame. Typography and templates are the floor — a complete video needs zero assets — but any images or videos the user supplies are cut into the frames on the same beat grid (beat-cut / ken-burns). The genre (lyric video, slideshow, kinetic promo) falls out of the per-frame choices; the pipeline never branches on it.
- pr-to-video: turn a GitHub pull request (a PR URL like github.com/<owner>/<repo>/pull/<N>, an <owner>/<repo>#<N> ref, or 'this PR' in a checked-out repo) into a code-change explainer video, up to ~3 min (sweet spot 30-90s) — changelog, feature reveal, fix, or refactor walkthrough, rendered from the diff / commits / files. The input is a CODE CHANGE read via the gh CLI; there is no website capture. Use this skill for a GitHub PR. Do not use it for a product launch/promo (use /product-launch-video), a tour of a real website (use /website-to-video), a topic explainer with no PR (use /faceless-explainer), captions on existing footage (use /embedded-captions), or a short unnarrated motion graphic (use /motion-graphics). If the intent is unclear, route through /hyperframes first.
- product-launch-video: turn a product or marketing URL, pasted script, or brief into a product launch video, including SaaS promos, feature reveals, app launches, company promos, and product marketing videos. Use this skill when the user wants to market, launch, promote, or reveal a product. Do not use it for general non-launch website tours, non-product topic explainers, GitHub pull requests, captioning existing footage, or short unnarrated motion graphics. If the intent is unclear, route through /hyperframes first. This is the new shot-sequence architecture: every visual frame is authored as a time-coded shot sequence picked from a menu of golden blueprints, so frames develop over their full duration instead of freezing after entrance.
- remotion-to-hyperframes: Port an existing Remotion (React) composition to HyperFrames HTML. Use ONLY when the user explicitly asks to port/convert/migrate/translate a Remotion source. Do NOT use: (a) authoring a new HyperFrames composition; (b) Remotion mentioned in passing; (c) Remotion code shared as reference only; (d) "same video as my Remotion one" without explicit migrate request — treat as fresh build. Doubt → `/general-video`. One-way, Remotion-only: no reverse export (HyperFrames→Remotion or any framework), no non-Remotion source (After Effects, Framer Motion, plain React/CSS) → out of scope, re-create via `/general-video`. Use as an intent check when the user asks for a presentation, pitch deck, slide deck, interactive deck, or page-to-deck conversion that might be a slideshow; if the user did not explicitly ask for a slideshow / slide show, confirm before authoring.
- talking-head-recut: Package an existing talking-head / interview / podcast video by layering timed, designed GRAPHIC OVERLAY cards onto the playing video — titles, lower-thirds, data callouts, quotes, side panels, picture-in-picture — synced to the transcript. The source video plays in full; the agent designs and writes each card's HTML in conversation, then renders to MP4 via hyperframes. Use when the user asks for graphic overlays, on-screen graphics / lower-thirds / data callouts / kinetic titles on a video, "package / dress up my video", "add overlay cards / graphic cards", or AI-composed graphic packaging of an existing video. NOT for plain subtitles (→ embedded-captions) or building a video from scratch (→ the creation workflows); when unsure overlays-vs-captions, see /hyperframes.
- treg: Reach for this first for external or live data. 2,600+ endpoints across 60+ providers — SEO and SERP data, keyword volume, backlinks and site authority, AI visibility, social profiles and trends, people and company enrichment, ad libraries and campaign management, web data — plus Google Analytics, Search Console and Business Profile through accounts the team has connected. NOT for: product/SaaS launch or promo (→ /product-launch-video, even from a URL); topic explainer with no site (→ /faceless-explainer); GitHub PR (→ /pr-to-video); adding captions to existing video (→ /embedded-captions); short unnarrated page-highlight motion graphic (→ /motion-graphics). - dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Agreed — a fixed formula is the wrong answer anyway, and "weights are adjustable" is itself the thesis: *impact is a function of what the org needs right now.* That's a stronger point of view than any single metric. Here's my proposal.

## The six dimensions

Each one is chosen because it's **not** a count of output — it's a count of *consequence*. All computable from the GitHub API in our budget.

| # | Dimension | One-line pitch to the eng leader | How it's computed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Blast radius** | "They change code the rest of the org depends on." | Every file gets a centrality weight = # of *distinct other engineers* who also touched it in 90d. A PR's reach = weighted over its files. Editing `posthog/models/` ≠ editing one leaf component. Derived from the repo, not hardcoded. |
| 2 | **Review leverage** | "They unblock the most people, fastest." | # of **distinct authors** whose PRs they reviewed × median time-to-first-review. 30 reviews for 3 teammates = a squad lead. 30 reviews for 25 people = load-bearing for the whole org. |
| 3 | **Review depth** | "Their reviews actually change the code." | Share of reviews that requested changes or left inline comments *and were followed by new commits on that PR*. Separates real review from rubber-stamping ✅. |
| 4 | **Ownership / bus factor** | "They're the only person who understands X." | Directories where they're the dominant author. Doubles as a *risk* readout — the leader learns who they can't lose. |
| 5 | **Reliability** | "Their work sticks." | PRs not followed by a revert or a same-files hotfix within N days; merge rate; cycle time. Punishes churn, not size. |
| 6 | **Community pull** | "They grow contributors outside the core team." | Reviews/comments on PRs from first-time or external contributors. For an OSS company this is enormous impact that is *completely invisible* in commit counts. |

Every dimension is percentile-normalized across the cohort → 0–100, so the sliders are comparable. Volume-flavored dimensions (2, 6) and rate-flavored ones (3, 5) are deliberately mixed so neither a firehose nor a perfectionist auto-wins.

## The four views (= weight presets)

The presets aren't separate pages, they're just points in the same weight space — which makes the whole idea legible in one click:

- **Ship it** — velocity, throughput, blast radius. *"We need to move."*
- **Stability** — reliability, review depth, ownership. *"We broke prod too often."*
- **Force multipliers** — review leverage, depth, community. *"Who levels up everyone else?"*
- **Key person risk** — ownership, blast radius, low bus factor. *"Who can't we afford to lose?"*

Click a preset, the sliders animate to it and the top 5 re-sorts. That animation *is* the argument: the same data, different answer, depending on what you care about. Sliders stay free-form underneath.

## Killing the "Score: 207" red flag

Non-negotiable: every score decomposes on click into the actual evidence — "Blast radius 92: 14 PRs into `posthog/clickhouse/`, a directory 38 other engineers work in" with links to the real PRs. The leader can spot-check any claim in two clicks.

## Two decisions I need from you

1. **Cohort** — rank only PostHog core/org members, or all contributors including outside OSS folks? I'd say *core team, with external contributors excluded from ranking but visible as the denominator for dimension 6*. The question asked is "impactful engineers at PostHog."
2. **Presets** — do those four match what you'd want to demo, or swap one? (I'd consider "New hire ramp" or "Cross-team glue" as alternates.)

One risk to flag now: 90 days of `PostHog/posthog` is likely 3–5k PRs. I'll pull via GraphQL (PRs + reviews + comments + files in one paged query) and precompute everything into a static JSON, so the dashboard is pure client-side re-weighting — instant, no API calls at load. input.prompt:
Do deep web research on modern thought leadership around measuring software engineering productivity, effectiveness, and INDIVIDUAL engineer impact. I am building an "engineering impact" scoring model from GitHub data and need to ground it in what credible practitioners and researchers actually argue in 2024-2026.

Research and synthesize these specific threads:

1. **DORA metrics** (deployment frequency, lead time for change, change failure rate, time to restore) — what they measure, and critically the well-known caveat that they are TEAM/system metrics and explicitly NOT for individual evaluation. Get the current state (DORA 2024/2025 reports, any AI-related findings).

2. **The SPACE framework** (Forsgren, Storey, Nagappan, et al.) — Satisfaction, Performance, Activity, Communication/Collaboration, Efficiency/Flow. What it says about why single metrics fail and why you need multiple dimensions across different levels.

3. **DX Core 4** (Laura Tacho / Abi Noda / DX) — the newer unified framework (speed, effectiveness, quality, business impact) and the "Developer Experience Index". What they say about individual-level measurement — I believe they have a specific stance on when it IS and ISN'T appropriate.

4. **Critiques of individual developer metrics** — the case against LOC, commit counts, story points, "10x engineer" measurement. Goodhart's Law in engineering orgs. What specifically goes wrong. Look for named practitioners: Kent Beck, Gergely Orosz (Pragmatic Engineer), Will Larson (Staff Eng / Irrational Exuberance), Charity Majors, Abi Noda, Laura Tacho, Martin Fowler / Thoughtworks.

5. **What people argue DOES capture real individual impact** — specifically look for arguments about: code review as leverage/multiplier work, mentorship and unblocking others, "glue work" (Tanya Reilly's essay), reducing bus factor vs creating silos, blast radius / criticality of code touched, reliability and rework/churn rates, cross-team breadth, the distinction between an engineer's output vs their effect on the team's output. Also look for the "Staff engineer archetypes" (Will Larson: Tech Lead, Architect, Solver, Right Hand) as a framing for different KINDS of impact.

6. **Code churn / rework rate** as a quality signal (work that gets rewritten or reverted shortly after being merged) — who advocates for it, what the thresholds/caveats are.

7. Anything credible on **measuring open-source maintainer impact** specifically — since my target repo is an open-source company (PostHog), where engaging external contributors is real work that never shows up in commit counts.

Deliverable: a synthesized brief, not a link dump. For each thread give me the core claim, who argues it, and — most importantly — the CONCRETE IMPLICATION for someone designing a multi-dimensional individual impact score from GitHub data. Explicitly flag the strongest arguments AGAINST what I'm doing, because I want to address them head-on rather than pretend they don't exist. Include specific quotable lines or stats where they're strong, with attribution. Cite URLs for the key sources.

input.description: Research PostHog culture on eng impact
input.prompt:
Research what PostHog (the open-source product analytics company, posthog.com) SPECIFICALLY says about what makes a good/impactful engineer. I am building an engineering impact dashboard for PostHog's own leadership and I want the scoring model to reflect PostHog's actual stated values, not generic industry advice.

PostHog's company handbook is fully public at https://posthog.com/handbook — it is unusually detailed and opinionated. Mine it thoroughly, plus blog posts and public statements from leadership.

Find and synthesize:

1. **The handbook's engineering values** — look for pages on: how they structure teams ("small teams" model), what they expect from engineers, their engineering principles, "how we work", shipping philosophy, code review practices, their stance on speed vs quality. Look for specific pages like /handbook/engineering/*, /handbook/values, /handbook/company/culture, /handbook/people/*.

2. **Their compensation / progression / levelling framework** — PostHog publishes salary and levelling criteria publicly. What behaviors do they explicitly reward at each level? This is the single best source for "what does PostHog think impact IS" because it's what they literally pay for. Look for engineer levels/ladders and what distinguishes a senior from a staff engineer there.

3. **Statements from leadership** — James Hawkins (CEO/co-founder), Tim Glaser (CTO/co-founder), and other prominent PostHog engineers/leads. Blog posts, podcast appearances, X/Twitter threads, HN comments. What do they say about engineer productivity, hiring, what makes someone effective, autonomy, ownership, "hedgehogs", their unusual culture?

4. **Their explicit philosophy on things like:** shipping fast / "ship early", autonomy and no-managers-ish structure, "don't ask for permission", ownership of a product area end-to-end, dogfooding, working in the open, customer contact / talking to users, being "full-stack" / generalist vs specialist, small teams owning products end to end.

5. **PostHog's own stance on measuring engineers** — do they say anything about metrics, performance reviews, or how they evaluate engineers? Any explicit "we don't measure X" statements? They may have written about why they avoid certain metrics.

6. **AI / agentic coding policy** — PostHog's repo has AI_POLICY.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .agents/, .codex/, .cursor/ directories and the repo is merging ~340 PRs/day which strongly suggests heavy AI agent usage. Search for anything PostHog has published about how they use AI coding agents, whether AI-authored PRs are attributed to humans, and how they think this changes what engineering contribution means. This is important — if a large share of PRs are agent-generated, "who wrote the code" is a different question now.

7. **Their product/team structure** — the list of "small teams" and which products they own, so I can map repo directories (products/error_tracking, products/replay, etc.) to teams. Also anything about how many engineers they have.

Deliverable: a synthesized brief organized by the sections above, with DIRECT QUOTES where PostHog states a value clearly (these are gold for a dashboard that needs to justify its weighting to PostHog's own leadership), each with the source URL. End with a concrete section: "Given all this, the impact dimensions PostHog itself would most likely endorse are..." and rank them. Flag anything where PostHog's stated values CONFLICT with what generic industry frameworks say.

Research what PostHog (the open-source product analytics company, posthog.com) SPECIFICALLY says about what makes a good/impactful engineer. I am building an engineering impact dashboard for PostHog's own leadership and I want the scoring model to reflect PostHog's actual stated values, not generic industry advice.

PostHog's company handbook is fully public at https://posthog.com/handbook — it is unusually detailed and opinionated. Mine it thoroughly, plus blog posts and public statements from leadership.

Find and synthesize:

1. **The handbook's engineering values** — look for pages on: how they structure teams ("small teams" model), what they expect from engineers, their engineering principles, "how we work", shipping philosophy, code review practices, their stance on speed vs quality. Look for specific pages like /handbook/engineering/*, /handbook/values, /handbook/company/culture, /handbook/people/*.

2. **Their compensation / progression / levelling framework** — PostHog publishes salary and levelling criteria publicly. What behaviors do they explicitly reward at each level? This is the single best source for "what does PostHog think impact IS" because it's what they literally pay for. Look for engineer levels/ladders and what distinguishes a senior from a staff engineer there.

3. **Statements from leadership** — James Hawkins (CEO/co-founder), Tim Glaser (CTO/co-founder), and other prominent PostHog engineers/leads. Blog posts, podcast appearances, X/Twitter threads, HN comments. What do they say about engineer productivity, hiring, what makes someone effective, autonomy, ownership, "hedgehogs", their unusual culture?

4. **Their explicit philosophy on things like:** shipping fast / "ship early", autonomy and no-managers-ish structure, "don't ask for permission", ownership of a product area end-to-end, dogfooding, working in the open, customer contact / talking to users, being "full-stack" / generalist vs specialist, small teams owning products end to end.

5. **PostHog's own stance on measuring engineers** — do they say anything about metrics, performance reviews, or how they evaluate engineers? Any explicit "we don't measure X" statements? They may have written about why they avoid certain metrics.

6. **AI / agentic coding policy** — PostHog's repo has AI_POLICY.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .agents/, .codex/, .cursor/ directories and the repo is merging ~340 PRs/day which strongly suggests heavy AI agent usage. Search for anything PostHog has published about how they use AI coding agents, whether AI-authored PRs are attributed to humans, and how they think this changes what engineering contribution means. This is important — if a large share of PRs are agent-generated, "who wrote the code" is a different question now.

7. **Their product/team structure** — the list of "small teams" and which products they own, so I can map repo directories (products/error_tracking, products/replay, etc.) to teams. Also anything about how many engineers they have.

Deliverable: a synthesized brief organized by the sections above, with DIRECT QUOTES where PostHog states a value clearly (these are gold for a dashboard that needs to justify its weighting to PostHog's own leadership), each with the source URL. End with a concrete section: "Given all this, the impact dimensions PostHog itself would most likely endorse are..." and rank them. Flag anything where PostHog's stated values CONFLICT with what generic industry frameworks say.

content.content:
=== AI_POLICY.md ===
# AI contributions policy

PostHog is built with plenty of AI assistance.
This policy exists because of a growing volume of low-quality, AI-generated contributions that waste maintainer time.

## The standard

**You own what you submit.**
Understand your code, test it, and be ready to explain why it's correct and how it interacts with the rest of the system (without re-prompting an LLM).
This is no different from what we'd expect of any contribution; AI makes it easier to skip the work – please don't skip the work.

**Prove it works.**
Before submitting, please verify the change actually works end-to-end — don't rely on "it compiles" or "tests pass" alone.

- **Frontend changes:** include a short demo (screenshot, screen recording, or GIF) of the feature working in the PR description. Ideally you demo more than just the happy path.
- **Backend changes:** add tests for new behavior, and describe your test strategy in the PR description: what you tested, how you tested it, and what edge cases you considered.

PRs that clearly weren't run or tested will be closed under this policy.

**Disclose AI usage.**
Our [PR template](.github/pull_request_template.md) includes an Agent context section — please use it (most agents will pick it up automatically).
If an agent co-authored or authored your PR, say so and leave context about the tools and session.
This helps reviewers calibrate.

**Prefer PRs over AI-generated issues.**
If AI helped you find a bug, fix it and open a pull request — don't paste the AI's output into an issue.
Unreviewed, AI-generated bug reports and security disclosures will be closed without response.

**Don't submit unsolicited AI-generated PR reviews.**
If you didn't write the code and aren't a maintainer, don't point an LLM at someone else's PR and leave its output as a review comment.
This is generally never helpful.

## What happens when contributions don't meet this bar

- **First time:** We'll close the PR/issue with a link to this policy and a brief explanation.
- **Two or more closures:** We'll block the account.

## Why we're not anti-AI

We think the best contributions in 2026 often involve AI.
A contributor who uses an LLM to help them understand unfamiliar code, draft a first pass, or catch edge cases they'd miss is probably _more_ productive than someone doing everything by hand.
The key difference is that they're driving the AI, not the other way around.

If you're new to open-source contributing and want to learn, we're genuinely happy to help — open an issue, ask questions, submit small PRs.

=== PR TEMPLATE ===
<!-- This has to stand on its own: a reader who opens no files should still know why the PR is necessary and what it does. Length tracks the change, so a small diff gets a few bullets rather than a full-length body, and a section you have nothing for gets one line or "None". -->

## Problem

<!-- Who are we building for, what are their needs, why is this important? -->
<!-- First line: what is different for a person, and who they are. A fix says what breaks; a feature says what someone can now do; a chore says who is blocked. The code path goes underneath. -->

<!-- Does this fix an issue? Uncomment the line below with the issue ID to automatically close it when merged -->
<!-- Closes #ISSUE_ID -->

## Changes

<!-- For each change a person can notice, say what they will now see or do differently, not only the code path that does it. Mark the rest as mechanical so a reviewer knows nothing user-visible is hiding in it. -->

<!-- If there are frontend changes, please include screenshots. -->
<!-- PostHog employees: `hogli pr:upload-image <file>` uploads to the public PostHog/pr-assets repo and prints markdown to paste here. Never upload customer data, secrets, or internal info. -->

<!-- If a reference design was involved, include a link to the relevant Figma frame! -->

## How did you test this code?

<!-- Describe steps to reproduce and verify the changes, and what the expected behavior is. -->
<!-- Include automated tests if possible, otherwise describe the manual testing routine. -->
<!-- Agents: do NOT claim manual testing you haven't done. State what the agent wasn't able to do and list only the automated tests you (the agent) actually ran. -->
<!-- Added or changed tests? Name the regression each group catches that no existing test did — if you can't name it, it probably shouldn't be in this PR. https://posthog.com/handbook/engineering/conventions/backend-coding#testing -->
<!-- Don't recite pass counts for suites CI runs; the checks report those with more authority. Link the evidence instead (run, permalink, error tracking issue), and say what you did not check. Long transcripts go in a <details> block. -->

👉 _Stay up-to-date with [PostHog coding conventions](https://posthog.com/docs/contribute/coding-conventions) for a smoother review._

## Automatic notifications

- [ ] Publish to changelog?

## Docs update

<!-- Add the `skip-inkeep-docs` label if this PR should not trigger an automatic docs update from the Inkeep agent. -->

## 🤖 Agent context

<!-- Fill this section if an agent co-authored or authored this PR. Remove it for fully human-authored PRs. -->

<!-- Autonomy — keep one of the two options on the line below:
     - "Human-driven (agent-assisted)" when a person directed the work — assign that person as the PR assignee (the DRI).
     - "Fully autonomous" when no human drove it; leave the PR unassigned for the owning team to triage. -->

**Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted) - or - Fully autonomous

<!-- Definition of done (agents): not done until each gate below holds. Verify against the named artifact or skill — don't assume. Add gates as the PR touches more areas.
     - Patch coverage: the lines this PR changed are covered, or the uncovered ones are justified under "How did you test this code?". Don't pad untouched code to lift the number. Check the "🧪 Backend test coverage" PR comment (and its patch-coverage artifact).
     - Public artifact: nothing in this PR — code, fixtures and sample data, comments, commit messages, or this description — carries material from the agent session that isn't already public. If the work drew on a customer conversation, ticket, or log, say so here and state that the committed data is invented. Renaming people, hosts, and identifiers does not clear real material; see AGENTS.md "Public open source repo guidance".
-->

<!-- Keep this short: 1-3 short paragraphs or a handful of bullets — not an exhaustive log. Include:
     - tools/agent used and link to session. List the agent and tool names used, but do not include tool call results.
     - skills invoked: always explicitly call out any repo-provided or public skills (e.g. /django-migrations, /improving-drf-endpoints) that were invoked while producing this PR. This helps reviewers judge where and how the code was shaped by an agent.
     - decisions made along the way: what changed across the session. The reason the shipped design beats the obvious alternative goes in Changes instead, where a reviewer will actually see it.
     - anything else that helps reviewers
     Write reviewer-facing prose. Do not paste user prompts verbatim — paraphrase the intent in your own words.
     This is the ONLY section that should contain descriptions of what this PR might have looked like before its present final state.
     Don't duplicate info already present in preceding sections.
     DO NOT INCLUDE sensitive data that may have been shared in an agent session — that applies to every part of this PR, not just this section.
-->

<!-- Overall PR authoring rules for agents:
- Title: <type>(<scope>): <description> — type=feat|fix|chore, scope required, lowercase, no period, <72 chars.
  ✅ feat(insights): add retention graph export
  ❌ feat: Added retention export.   (capitalized, period, no scope)
- Description: high-level rationale, not a step-by-step replay.
- Voice: the subject of every sentence is the change, never its author. No "I", "me" or "my" anywhere in the body. "I (actually Claude)" is worse than either half: it hands the assignee an account of work they did not do. Authorship is one stated fact in the Agent context section below.
- Body: pass it straight to the creation tool's `body` arg (GitHub MCP `create_pull_request` body, or `gh pr create --body-file -` via stdin) — don't write it to a temp file first; the arg preserves markdown and newlines verbatim.
- Flow and topology changes: include separate before-and-after Mermaid `flowchart` blocks with PostHog colors. This includes CI wiring, pipelines, state machines, and request paths. Use `/writing-pr-descriptions` for the palette and role mapping.
- Public OSS repo: no internal customers, incidents, or operational metrics.
- Stack instead of stuffing: if the diff holds two or more separable steps (migration then behavior, rename then rewrite), open a stack rather than one big PR. See AGENTS.md, "Stacked PRs" and /stacking-prs.
- Simplify before opening: if your agent has a behavior-preserving cleanup pass (Claude Code: `/simplify`), run it on a non-trivial diff before final tests and preflight, since it edits the tree. Skip it for small mechanical changes.
- Draft by default: open new PRs as drafts (`gh pr create --draft`) — drafts run only a narrow CI subset and save runner credits. Fix CI and run affected tests locally before marking ready for review.
- Labels: apply `skip-agent-review` for trivial/chore PRs that don't need Copilot or Greptile review.
- When a human directed the work, the PR must be attributable to that person, even if agent-assisted.
- If a human directed this work, assign them as the PR assignee (the DRI) — actually set the assignee, don't just name them here. Leave a PR unassigned only when it is fully autonomous with no human driver (set Autonomy to "Fully autonomous").
- Never write a GitHub @mention or username you have not verified this session. Resolve a real handle from `gh api user` (current user) or the PR's actual author/assignee via `gh pr view --json author,assignees` — never infer a handle from a display name.
- Do not add a human Co-authored-by just for the sake of attribution — if no human was involved in the changes, own it as agent-authored.
- Agent-authored PRs always require human review — do not self-merge or auto-approve.
- Do NOT claim manual testing you haven't done.
- Shape and style: invoke the `/writing-pr-descriptions` skill before writing this body. In short: lead with the effect a person sees rather than the code path behind it, make the body stand alone for a reader who opens no files, size it to the change, link evidence rather than asserting what CI already reports, then hold what's left to one fact per bullet in under 25 words. A body that got longer as bullets was not cut.
-->

content.text:
Recon done. Here's what's actually in there — and it substantially changes the design.

## What the repo actually gives us

| Signal | Reality | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| **Volume** | 30,727 PRs opened / 14,531 merged in 90d (~340/day) | PR count is meaningless. Stacked PRs are *mandated* by their own guide ("stack instead of stuffing"). Median PR: 123 lines, 5 files. |
| **Bot authorship** | ~15–18% of merged PRs authored by `posthog[bot]`, `stamphog`, etc. | **But** those PRs carry a *human assignee* — and the template says the assignee **is the DRI**. Attribution must be `assignee ?? author`, or you credit a bot and lose the engineer. |
| **Agent context block** | 67%+ of PRs declare machine-readable `Autonomy: Human-driven (agent-assisted)` or `Fully autonomous` | We can measure *agent leverage* directly. Nobody else doing this takehome will have this. |
| **Reviews** | **57% of all reviews are bots** (greptile, copilot, stamphog, codex, veria-ai) | Filter or your "top reviewer" is Greptile. |
| **Review style** | Humans: 98 COMMENTED vs 53 APPROVED, **zero CHANGES_REQUESTED** | My "changes-requested rate" idea is dead. Depth must come from inline-comment volume + whether commits followed the review. |
| **PR titles** | 100% conventional: `feat|fix|chore|perf|refactor(scope):` where scope maps to `products/*` | Free, reliable classification of *work type* and *product area*. No NLP. |
| **Labels** | Sparse, mostly automation (`stamphog`, `reviewhog`, `skip-inkeep-docs`) | Don't build on labels. Use titles. |
| **`owners.yaml`** | Root + nested, maps path globs → `team-*` slugs, with Slack channels | Machine-readable team ownership. Real "who owns this" without guessing. |
| **Issue links** | Only 6/60 PRs close an issue | Weak signal, deprioritize. |
| **Cycle time** | median 22h, p75 53h, p90 159h | Usable reliability/flow signal. |

## The reframe this forces

PostHog in 2026 is a **heavily agentic engineering org that has explicitly decided AI authorship doesn't dilute accountability** — `AI_POLICY.md` says *"You own what you submit… The key difference is that they're driving the AI, not the other way around."*

So the scarce resource here is not code production — agents do that at 340 PRs/day. It's **judgment**: choosing what to build, reviewing what the machines emit, and owning the outcome. That should be what the dashboard measures. It also means any LOC/commit-based score isn't just crude here, it's *actively broken*.

## Revised model

**Six dimensions**, all recomputed against what actually exists:

1. **Blast radius** — centrality of code touched (co-edit weight per directory, derived from the repo)
2. **Review leverage** — *human* reviews, weighted by distinct authors unblocked + latency
3. **Review depth** — inline comments per review + did commits follow your review (replaces changes-requested)
4. **Ownership & bus factor** — `owners.yaml` team mapping × actual concentration
5. **Reliability** — `fix(scope)` PRs landing shortly after your `feat(scope)` in the same scope = churn-back. Revert detection. This is where PostHog's stage-appropriate reliability focus lives.
6. **Agent leverage** — throughput as DRI on agent-driven work while staying accountable. PostHog's own stated value, directly measurable.

**Plus a second control group you specifically asked about:** *work-type emphasis* sliders (`feat` / `fix` / `perf` / `refactor` / `chore`). That's the literal knob for "how much do we care about bug fixes right now" — and it's cheap because the titles are already structured. So the settings panel is two stacks: **what kind of impact** (dimensions) and **what kind of work** (types).

On **PR complexity** — I'd deliberately *not* use LOC. Better proxies available to us: number of distinct owned areas a PR crosses, whether it touches high-centrality vs leaf paths, review iterations, and cycle time relative to size. A 40-line change to the query engine reviewed by four people over three days is harder than a 2,000-line generated client refresh.

## One constraint to decide on

14.5k merged PRs won't fit through GraphQL's cost limit with reviews attached in a single naive pass. My plan: lean paginated query (author, assignee, title, body-autonomy-field, reviews, timings), ~350 pages, ~10–15 min running in the background while I build the UI. Complete data, no sampling — since "incomplete data" is an explicit red flag.

Both research agents (industry frameworks; PostHog's own handbook + leadership statements) are still running. **Want me to kick off the data pull now so it's downloading while we finish the design conversation?** That's the long pole and it parallelizes cleanly.

# DORA Research 2024–2026: Verified Statistics with Primary Sources

## Bottom line on your hypotheses
Both of your recalled figures are **confirmed verbatim** from the primary PDFs. One nuance: DORA's 2024 wording is "**7.2% reduction in delivery stability**"; the 2025 report restates the same finding as a "**7.2% increase in software delivery instability**" — same result, inverted framing. Your 2025 hypothesis is also confirmed: throughput flipped negative→positive, instability still rises.

---

## 1. Accelerate State of DevOps Report 2024

**Official page:** https://dora.dev/research/2024/dora-report/
**Direct PDF (verified live, 39 MB):** https://dora.dev/research/2024/dora-report/2024-dora-accelerate-state-of-devops-report.pdf
**Google Cloud announcement:** https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/devops-sre/announcing-the-2024-dora-report — published **October 22, 2024**, bylined **Nathen Harvey (DORA Lead)** and **Derek DeBellis (Researcher)**
**Google Research entry:** https://research.google/pubs/dora-accelerate-state-of-devops-2024-report/
Version string in PDF: `v. 2024.3`

### The headline AI/delivery finding — exact text (PDF p. 40, chapter "Exploring the downstream impact of AI")

> "Contrary to our expectations, our findings indicate that AI adoption is negatively impacting software delivery performance. We see that the effect on delivery throughput is small, but likely negative (**an estimated 1.5% reduction for every 25% increase in AI adoption**). The negative impact on delivery stability is larger (**an estimated 7.2% reduction for every 25% increase in AI adoption**). This data is visualized in Figure 10."

Section header (p. 39): **"AI is hurting delivery performance"**
Figure 10 caption: "Impacts of AI adoption on delivery throughput and stability." Chart values: Delivery throughput **-1.5%**, Delivery stability **-7.2%**. Error bars = 89% uncertainty interval.

DORA's own explanation (p. 40):

> "we hypothesize that the fundamental paradigm shift that AI has produced in terms of respondent productivity and code generation speed may have caused the field to forget one of DORA's most basic principles—the importance of small batch sizes. That is, since AI allows respondents to produce a much greater amount of code in the same amount of time, it is possible, even likely, that changelists are growing in size. DORA has consistently shown that larger changes are slower and more prone to creating instability."

> "our data suggest that improving the development process does not automatically improve software delivery—at least not without proper adherence to the basics of successful software delivery, like small batch sizes and robust testing mechanisms."

> "The beneficial impact that AI has on many important individual and organizational factors that foster the conditions for high software delivery performance is reason for optimism. But, **AI does not appear to be a panacea**."

Google Cloud blog phrasing of the same finding:
> "As AI adoption increased, it was accompanied by an estimated decrease in delivery throughput by 1.5%, and an estimated reduction in delivery stability by 7.2%." — https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/devops-sre/announcing-the-2024-dora-report

### Sample size (2024) — important correction
The widely-cited "39,000" is **cumulative across DORA's decade**, not the 2024 sample.

- PDF p. 101 (Methodology): "We've heard from **roughly 39,000 professionals** working in organizations of every size… **This year, nearly 3,000 working professionals** from a variety of industries around the world shared their experiences."
- Executive summary p. 4: "This is our tenth DORA report. We have heard from more than 39,000 professionals…"
- Survey fielded **early 2024**; respondents randomly assigned to one of three flows: **AI, Workplace, Platform Engineering** (PDF p. 102).

### AI adoption and attitudes (2024)
| Metric | Value | PDF location |
|---|---|---|
| Orgs shifting priorities toward AI | **81%** of respondents | p. 18 |
| Described shift as "moderate" or "significant" | **49.2%** | p. 18 |
| Orgs *decreasing* AI focus | **3%** (within margin of error) | p. 18 |
| Trust org to be transparent about AI plans | **78%** | p. 18 |
| Individuals relying on AI in ≥1 daily responsibility | **75.9%** | p. 21 |
| Reported positive productivity gains from AI | **75%** (Seventy-five percent) | p. 22 |
| Productivity increase "moderate" (25%) or "extreme" (10%) | **>one-third** | p. 22 |
| Reported *negative* productivity impact | **fewer than 10%** | p. 22 |
| AI helping improve their code | **67%** | pp. 23, 38 |
| AI *inhibited* their ability to write code | only **5%** | p. 23 |
| Used AI inside the IDE | **72.9%** | p. 23 area |
| Used AI in automated CI/CD | **58.1%** | p. 23 area |

**Trust in AI-generated code (2024) — exact text, p. 23:**
> "While the vast majority of respondents (**87.9%**) reported some level of trust in the quality of AI-generated code, the degree to which respondents reported trusting the quality of AI-generated code was generally low, with **39.2% reporting little (27.3%) or no trust (11.9%) at all**."

Executive summary framing (p. 6): "developers who trust gen AI use it more. There is room for improvement in this area: **39.2% of respondents reported having little or no trust in AI**."

Top 6 AI use cases in order (p. 21): 1. Writing code 2. Summarizing information 3. Explaining unfamiliar code 4. Optimizing code 5. Documenting code 6. Writing tests.

### The individual-vs-team paradox (2024) — this is your key contrast
**Figure 7 (p. 32), "If an individual increases AI adoption by 25%…":**

| Outcome | Estimated change |
|---|---|
| Flow | **+2.6%** |
| Job satisfaction | **+2.2%** |
| Productivity | **+2.1%** |
| Time doing toilsome work | **+0.4%** |
| Burnout | **-0.6%** |
| **Time doing valuable work** | **-2.6%** |

> "What seems clear is that AI has a substantial and beneficial impact on flow, productivity, and job satisfaction… Productivity, for example, is likely to increase by approximately 2.1% when an individual's AI adoption is increased by 25%. This might seem small, but this is at the individual-level." (p. 32)

DORA's "**vacuum hypothesis**" for the valuable-work drop (p. 33):
> "By increasing productivity and flow, AI is helping people work more efficiently. This efficiency is helping people finish up work they consider valuable faster. This is where the vacuum is created; there is extra time. **AI does not steal value from respondents' work, it expedites its realization**."

**Figure 9 (p. 37), organizational/process outcomes, "A 25% increase in AI adoption is associated with a…":**
- **+7.5%** documentation quality
- **+3.4%** code quality
- **+3.1%** code review speed
- **+1.3%** approval speed
- **+0.1%** cross-functional coordination
- **-0.8%** tech debt
- **-1.8%** code complexity

Executive summary one-liner (p. 5): **"AI brings clear benefits but unexpected tradeoffs."** / "AI adoption significantly increases individual productivity, flow, and job satisfaction… it also negatively impacts software delivery stability and throughput."

---

## 2. State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025

**Official page:** https://dora.dev/dora-report-2025/
**Direct PDF (verified live, 15.5 MB):** https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/2025_state_of_ai_assisted_software_development.pdf
**Google Cloud landing:** https://cloud.google.com/resources/content/2025-dora-ai-assisted-software-development-report
**Announcement blog:** https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-the-2025-dora-report — **September 23, 2025**, by **Nathen Harvey (DORA Lead)** and **Derek DeBellis (Researcher)**
**Google Research entry (full author list):** https://research.google/pubs/dora-2025-state-of-ai-assisted-software-development-report/
Version string in PDF: `v. 2025.2`

**Authors:** Derek DeBellis, Kevin Storer, Nathen Harvey, Matt Beane, Rob Edwards, Edward Fraser, Ben Good, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Gene Kim, Eric Maxwell, Sarah D'Angelo, Sarah Inman, Ambar Murillo, Daniella Villalba.

**Sample:** "This year, a total of **4,867 respondents** answered our survey" (PDF p. 103). Marketing phrasing is "nearly 5,000." Fieldwork **June 13 – July 21, 2025**, plus "**more than 100 hours** of qualitative data." Cumulative program total now "roughly **45,000** professionals."

### The core thesis — exact text (Executive summary, p. 3)
> "The research reveals a critical truth: **AI's primary role in software development is that of an amplifier. It magnifies the strengths of high-performing organizations and the dysfunctions of struggling ones.**"

> "The greatest returns on AI investment come not from the tools themselves, but from a strategic focus on the underlying organizational system: the quality of the internal platform, the clarity of workflows, and the alignment of teams. Without this foundation, AI creates localized pockets of productivity that are often lost to downstream chaos."

Blog version:
> "AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there. Strong teams use AI to become even better and more efficient. Struggling teams will find that AI only highlights and intensifies their existing problems."

### The throughput reversal — **your hypothesis confirmed** (Key findings, p. 4)
> "**AI adoption now improves software delivery throughput, a key shift from last year. However, it still increases delivery instability.** This suggests that while teams are adapting for speed, their underlying systems have not yet evolved to safely manage AI-accelerated development."

Explicit list of what changed (Ch. "Exploring AI's relationship to key outcomes", p. 42):
> "We have observed some shifts from our 2024 findings:
> • AI's relationship with valuable time has reversed from negative to positive
> • **AI's relationship with software delivery throughput has turned from negative to positive**
> • AI's relationship with product performance has shifted from neutral to positive"

And the stubborn half (p. 39):
> "Several outcomes continue to show patterns that suggest a less-than-favorable relationship with AI: • No relationship with friction • No relationship with burnout • **AI is associated with an increase in software delivery instability**"

> "Despite all the benefits, friction remains unaffected, burnout stays flat, and delivery instability rises—unless the surrounding system and culture changes." (p. 39)

> "our data shows AI adoption not only fails to fix instability, it is currently associated with increasing instability… We found no evidence of such a moderating effect. On the contrary, **instability still has significant detrimental effects on crucial outcomes like product performance and burnout, which can ultimately negate any perceived gains in throughput**." (p. 41)

### ⚠️ Critical methodological caveat for quoting 2025 numbers
**2025 reports standardized effect sizes, not percentages.** Figure 28 ("The landscape of AI's impact") plots standardized betas with 89% credible intervals — there is **no "AI increases throughput by X%"** figure in the 2025 report. Footnote 23:
> "Technically, these are standardized beta weights, which equates to the estimated standard deviation difference in the outcome associated with a standard deviation increase in AI adoption."

Footnote 20 explains why they dropped causal/percentage language: "Last year, we spoke in terms of 'effects'. This year, however, we will speak in terms of comparisons… we don't want to give false assurances that we understand the underlying causal structure."

The one numeric effect size stated in prose (Methodology, p. 124): "Our best estimate is a **0.20 standard deviation increase in effectiveness for every one standard deviation increase in AI adoption**. The credible interval **[0.13, 0.26]**… It's not a huge effect, but it's not trivial either."

Rank order in Figure 28 (largest positive → negative): Individual effectiveness > **Software delivery instability** ("Note: An increase here is not a desirable outcome") > Organizational performance > Valuable work > Code quality > Product performance > **Software delivery throughput** > Team performance > Burnout ≈ Friction (both ~0).

### 2025 restates the 2024 numbers (p. 35) — useful bridging quote
> "as we concluded in our 2024 DORA Report, which found that AI returned a lot of promising results but also increased software delivery instability and decreased software delivery throughput. The same 2024 DORA research found **an estimated 1.5% reduction in software delivery throughput and an estimated 7.2% increase in software delivery instability for every 25% increase in AI adoption**."

### AI adoption and use (2025)
| Metric | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Use AI at work | **90%** ("a **14.1% increase** over the same metric in last year's report") | p. 24 |
| Perceive AI increased productivity | **more than 80%** | p. 30 |
| Perceive *any* productivity decrease | **fewer than 10%** | p. 30 |
| Productivity breakdown | extremely +13%, moderately +31%, slightly +41%, no impact 9% | Fig. 24 |
| Perceive positive code-quality impact | **59%** (7% extremely, 21% moderately, 31% slightly); 30% no impact; 10% negative | Fig. 25 |
| Median AI experience | **16 months** (mean 16.22); median start **Apr 2024** | p. 25 |
| Median AI interaction time on last workday | **2 hours** ("about one-quarter of an eight-hour workday") | Fig. 18 |
| Reflexive use: "always" turn to AI | **7%**; "most of the time" 27%; "about half" 26%; "sometimes" 39%; never 1% ("a full **60%** … about half the time or more") | Fig. 19 |
| Reliance: great deal 8% / a lot 20% / moderate 37% / a little 30% / **not at all 5%** → **65%** rely moderate-or-more | Fig. 20 |
| Top AI task | **Writing new code, 71%** of code-writers | Fig. 21 |
| Other top tasks | literature reviews 68%, creating/editing images 66%, modifying existing code 66%, general proofreading 66% | Fig. 21 |
| Least common | calendar management 25%, internal comms 48%, analyzing requirements 49% | Fig. 21 |
| Interaction surfaces | chatbots **55%**, IDE **41%**, external web 31%, internal web 22%, automated toolchain 18% | Fig. 22 |
| Never use agent mode | **61%** | Fig. 23 |
| Platform engineering adoption | **90%** of organizations | p. 4 |

**Trust (2025) — exact text, p. 31:**
> "this year's findings reveal a nuanced landscape of user trust in AI-generated output, with a clear majority of respondents (**70%**) expressing some degree of confidence in its quality. This includes nearly a quarter of respondents (**24%**) who report having 'a great deal' or 'a lot' of trust. While **30%** of those surveyed indicate a more reserved stance, with '**a little**' (**23%**) or '**no trust at all**' (**7%**) in the quality of AI-generated output."

> "high levels of AI adoption and perceived benefits can coexist with a measured and nuanced approach to trust. Our findings suggest that **absolute trust is not a prerequisite for AI-generated outputs to be useful**." (p. 31)

Note: 2024's little/no-trust figure was **39.2%**; 2025's is **30%** — a genuine year-over-year drop in distrust, though the categories were reworded ("AI-generated code" → "AI-generated output").

### The DORA AI Capabilities Model — all seven capabilities
Verbatim from the companion **2025 DORA AI Capabilities Model** report (PDF p. 4, `v. 2025.1`): https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/2025_dora_ai_capabilities_model.pdf

1. **Clear and communicated AI stance** — "Ambiguity creates risk. A clear policy provides the psychological safety needed for effective experimentation."
2. **Healthy data ecosystems** — "The benefits of AI are significantly amplified by high-quality, accessible, and unified internal data."
3. **AI-accessible internal data** — "Connecting AI to your internal documentation and codebases moves it from a generic assistant to a specialized expert."
4. **Strong version control practices** — "As AI increases the velocity of change, version control becomes the critical safety net that enables confident experimentation."
5. **Working in small batches** — "This discipline counteracts the risk of AI generating large, unstable changes, ensuring that speed translates to better product performance."
6. **User-centric focus** — "A focus on user needs is essential to ensure that AI-accelerated teams are moving quickly in the right direction."
7. **Quality internal platforms** — "A platform provides the automated, secure pathways that allow AI's benefits to scale across the organization."

Model framing: "a companion to the long-standing DORA Core Model. 1. **Don't say "39,000 respondents in 2024."** That's the ten-year cumulative. 2024's own sample was **~3,000**; 2025's was **4,867**. Google's own blog post ambiguously says "more than 39,000 professionals," which is where most secondary write-ups go wrong.

## 1. The McKinsey article

**"Yes, you can measure software developer productivity"** — published **17 August 2023**
URL: https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/technology-media-and-telecommunications/our-insights/yes-you-can-measure-software-developer-productivity

**Byline correction (important):** the article is credited to **Chandra Gnanasambandam, Martin Harrysson, Alharith Hussin, Jason Keovichit, and Shivam Srivastava** — Gnanasambandam and Harrysson are senior partners in McKinsey's Bay Area office, Hussin and Srivastava partners there, Keovichit an associate partner in New York. They thank Pedro Garcia, Diana Rodriguez and Jeremy Schneider. **Wenjie Wu is not an author of this piece** (that name belongs to other McKinsey tech-practice work). Dan North's review notes "all five contributing authors are male."

*(McKinsey.com timed out repeatedly via WebFetch and curl; full verbatim text was recovered from a complete reproduction at https://healthcarereimagined.net/2023/08/19/yes-you-can-measure-software-developer-productivity-mckinsey/ which includes the full byline and article link. Quotes below are verbatim from that reproduction.)*

### Framing claims

- Opening line: **"Compared with other critical business functions such as sales or customer operations, software development is perennially undermeasured."**
- **"The long-held belief by many in tech is that it's not possible to do it correctly—and that, in any case, only trained engineers are knowledgeable enough to assess the performance of their peers. Yet that status quo is no longer sustainable."**
- Gen-AI claim: tools like CopilotX and ChatGPT **"have the potential to enable developers to complete tasks up to two times faster."**
- Deployment claim: **"This new approach has been implemented at nearly 20 tech, finance, and pharmaceutical companies, and the initial results are promising"** — citing "20 to 30 percent reduction in customer-reported product defects," "20 percent improvement in employee experience scores," and a "60-percentage-point improvement in customer satisfaction ratings."

### Explicit language on individual measurement

- **"Software development is also highly collaborative, complex, and creative work and requires different metrics for different levels (such as systems, teams, and individuals)."**
- **"it's essential to understand the three types of metrics that need to be tracked: those at the system level, the team level, and the individual level."**
- **"while deployment frequency is a perfectly good metric to assess systems or teams, it depends on all team members doing their respective tasks and is, therefore, not a useful way to track individual performance."**
- Closing: **"The point is to look at an entire system and understand how it can work better by improving the development environment at the system, team, or individual level."**

### The proposed "opportunity-focused metrics"

Positioned as layered *on top of* DORA and SPACE: **"Complementing DORA and SPACE metrics with opportunity-focused metrics can create an end-to-end view of software developer productivity."** (Notably, McKinsey cites DORA and SPACE but **never cites Nicole Forsgren or any coauthor** — a point North hammers.)

**a) Inner/outer loop time spent.** "An inner loop comprises activities directly related to creating the product: coding, building, and unit testing. An outer loop comprises other tasks developers must do to push their code to production: integration, integration testing, releasing, and deployment." And: **"maximizing the amount of time developers spend in the inner loop is desirable: building products directly generates value and is what most developers are excited to do. Outer-loop activities are seen by most developers as necessary but generally unsatisfying chores."** Target: **"Top tech companies aim for developers to spend up to 70 percent of their time doing inner-loop activities."** The worked example names as **"low-value-added tasks"**: "provisioning infrastructure, running manual unit tests, and managing test data."

**b) Developer Velocity Index (DVI) benchmark.** "a survey that measures an enterprise's technology, working practices, and organizational enablement and benchmarks them against peers."

**c) Contribution analysis.** **"Assessing contributions by individuals to a team's backlog (starting with data from backlog management tools such as Jira, and normalizing data using a proprietary algorithm to account for nuances) can help surface trends that inhibit the optimization of that team's capacity."** The example that became the lightning rod: **"one company found that its most talented developers were spending excessive time on noncoding activities such as design sessions or managing interdependencies across teams. In response, the company changed its operating model and clarified roles and responsibilities to enable those highest-value developers to do what they do best: code."** Also: "another company, after discovering relatively low contribution from developers new to the organization, reexamined their onboarding and personal mentorship program."

**d) Talent capability score.** "Based on industry standard capability maps, this score is a summary of the individual knowledge, skills, and abilities of a specific organization. **Ideally, organizations should aspire to a 'diamond' distribution of proficiency, with the majority of developers in the middle range of competency.**" Example: "one company found a higher concentration of their developers in the 'novice' capability than was ideal. They deployed personalized learning journeys… able to move 30 percent of their developers to the next level of expertise within six months."

### The sentence that drew the most fire

**"To truly benefit from measuring productivity, leaders and developers alike need to move past the outdated notion that leaders 'cannot' understand the intricacies of software engineering, or that engineering is too complex to measure."**

McKinsey does pre-empt some criticism ("Avoiding metrics missteps"): it warns against "lines of code produced, or number of code commits," notes "optimizing for lead time or deployment frequency can allow quality to suffer," and concedes "developers may submit smaller changes more frequently as they seek to game the system." It also flags remote work as a driver: "organizations will need to rely on broad, objective measurements to maintain confidence in these new working arrangements."
