## 2. Kent Beck + Gergely Orosz — the joint response

**It is a TWO-part series, not 3–4** — but it exists as **four published artifacts**, because each part was cross-published simultaneously on both newsletters, and Part 2's final section **diverges into two separate answers**. That's likely the source of the "3–4 parts" impression. There is also a January 2024 sequel (below).

| # | Title | Date | URL |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 (PE) | Measuring developer productivity? A response to McKinsey | 29 Aug 2023 | https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity |
| P1 (KB) | Measuring developer productivity? A response to McKinsey | 29 Aug 2023 | https://newsletter.kentbeck.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity |
| P2 (PE) | Measuring developer productivity? A response to McKinsey, Part 2 | 31 Aug 2023 | https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity-part-2 |
| P2 (KB) | Measuring developer productivity? A response to McKinsey 2 | 31 Aug 2023 | https://newsletter.kentbeck.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity-440 |
| Sequel | Measuring Developer Productivity: Real-World Examples (Gergely + Abi Noda, 17 companies) | 16 Jan 2024 | https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity-bae |

Orosz on the origin: *"A few hours after publishing this article, I was already on a call with Kent, as we tried to pinpoint exactly why both of us felt frustrated with this report."* Parts 1 and the bulk of Part 2 are written **"with one, shared voice."**

### Kent Beck — before the series (LinkedIn, ~20–24 Aug 2023)

The precursor post (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kentbeck_mckinsey-claims-its-possible-to-measure-activity-7099764438496407552-v8P2):

> **"McKinsey claims it's possible to measure developer productivity. The report is so absurd & naive that it makes no sense to critique it in detail."** — Kent Beck

> **"McKinsey folks are smart. They know that their intended market wants this report to be good advice, wants to act this way, wants McKinsey's help/permission to do so."** — Kent Beck

> **"What they published damages people I care about. I'm here to help geeks feel safe in the world. This kind of surveillance makes geeks feel less safe."** — Kent Beck (quoted in ShiftMag)

The surgeon analogy (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kentbeck_mckinseys-you-can-measure-developer-productivity-activity-7101918867161051136-b8F4):

> **"McKinsey's 'you can measure developer productivity' is like if we measured surgeon productivity on what percentage of their time they were cutting with a scalpel or stitching with a needle and we ignored whether the patient got better."** — Kent Beck

He extends it: an expert surgeon on a complex case needs time to "observe & assess," not rush to avoid the "bottom 10%"; and the perverse incentive is that a surgeon might **"turn down a difficult case because it would lower their"** score. He also asks: measuring **"with what units? How do those units correlate with profit? What profit dysfunctions are created by measuring & assessing those units?"**

### Part 1 — key quotable lines

**Kent Beck, on the Facebook survey death-spiral (verbatim, his first-person block):**
> "At Facebook we instituted the sorts of surveys McKinsey recommends. That was good for about a year. The surveys provided valuable feedback about the current state of developer sentiment. Then folks decided that they wanted to make the survey results more legible so they could track trends over time. They computed an overall score from the survey. Very reasonable thing to do. That was good for another year. A 4.5 became a 4. What happened? Then those scores started cropping up in performance reviews… Then those scores started getting rolled up. A manager's score was the average of their reports' scores. A director's score would be the average of their reporting managers' scores. **Now things started getting unhinged.** Directors put pressure on managers for better scores. Managers started negotiating with individual contributors for better survey scores. **'Give me a 5 & I'll make sure you get an "exceeds expectations".'** Directors started cutting managers & teams with poor scores, whether those cuts made organizational sense or not."

> **"Things went from, 'we'd like to know how things are going,' to, 'we know even less about how things are going. But they are definitely going worse because people are now gaming the system.'"** — Beck & Orosz

**On refusing a line-by-line rebuttal:**
> **"As tempting as it is, we won't go into a detailed critique of the McKinsey article and the measurement methodology. The thinking that's evident in the article is absurdly naive and ignores the dynamics of high-performing software engineering teams."**

**On why the article exists — the political read:**
> **"CEOs and CFOs are increasingly frustrated by CTOs throwing up their hands and saying software engineering is too nuanced to measure, when sales teams have individual measurements and quotas to hit… The executive reasoning goes: if other groups can measure individual performance, it's absurd that engineering cannot."**

> **"If they try to [avoid the question], they risk the CEO or CFO turning instead to McKinsey, who will bring their custom framework, deploy it – even as the CTO protests – and start reporting on custom McKinsey metrics like 'Developer Velocity Benchmark Index,' 'Contribution Analysis,' and 'Talent Capability.'"**

> **"We believe that introducing such a framework is wrong-headed and certain to backfire. The McKinsey framework will most likely do far more harm than good to organizations – and to the engineering culture at companies. Such damage could take years to undo."**

**On the intended audience (a barb):**
> **"When reading articles like McKinsey's, keep in mind they're written for a very different, and specific, audience: untechnical CEOs and CFOs with little to zero experience with software development. Engineering is just another department."**

**The core analytical move — the effort → output → outcome → impact model.** Effort (planning, coding); output (the feature, code, design docs); outcome (customers behave differently); impact (feedback, revenue, referrals). All four DORA metrics map to outcome/impact. Then the central charge:

> **"One critique of McKinsey's system we have is that nearly every one of its custom metrics which differ from DORA and SPACE metrics, measure effort or output."** (Their exhibit: "4 out of the 5 new metrics suggested by McKinsey's measure effort or output.")

> **"First, the only folks who care about these metrics are the people collecting them. Customers don't care. Executives don't care. Investors don't care. Second, and most crucially, collecting & evaluating these metrics hinders the measures downstream folks actually do care about, like profitability."**

> **"Why is McKinsey adding ways to measure effort? One reason is that it's the easiest thing to measure! But the McKinsey approach ignores an important truth: the act of measurement changes how developers work, as they try to 'game' the system."**

> **"The earlier in the cycle you measure, the easier it is to measure. And also the more likely that you introduce unintended consequences."**

**Kent Beck's sales-vs-engineering meeting anecdote** (verbatim, his voice) — sales leader: *"'My team's target for the quarter was $600K, and we delivered $520K. I take accountability for the miss…'"* vs. engineering: *"'So, this quarter we shipped Feature A, and we are slightly behind on some tech debt migration…'"* — **"My goodness, the contrast was stark."** And: **"The level of accountability which sales and customer support work with is on a completely different scale from what a CEO observes from engineering. But when the CEO examines overall departmental costs, engineering probably costs more than sales!"**

**Their positive proposal:**
> **"We urge engineering leaders to look to outcome and impact measurements, to identify what to measure."**
> **"Producing at least one customer-facing thing per team, per week. This output might not sound so impressive, but in practice is very hard to achieve."**

**Uber footnote (Orosz's reporting):** after Uber shipped an Eng Metrics dashboard, *"the lines of code did not change drastically, but the CI systems saw a visible increase in utilization. Basically, people started to create far, far more diffs, which put a much larger load on the continuous integration (CI) systems, and increased CI costs."*

### Part 2 — key quotable lines

> **"We believe that introducing a kind of framework that McKinsey is proposing is wrong-headed and certain to backfire. Such a framework will most likely do far more harm than good to organizations – and to the engineering culture at companies and the damage could take years to undo."**

**Kent Beck on outcome-only measurement (sales quota gaming, his voice):**
> "Individual goals discourages people from working together, as everyone is chasing their own quota… I saw firsthand how a 'star' salesperson operated. They always hit their quota, and collected a hefty bonus. How did they do it? Well, they knew that sales could fall through any time, so they always had several prospects 'in the pocket'… **In order to maximize personal gains, they did not maximize the company's gain.**"

**Gergely Orosz on the "rockstar" recruiter with a 100% close rate** who had made verbal bonus promises that were "outrageously untrue": *"It took us managers months to sort out the mess, and left engineers feeling tricked and with declining faith in the company."*

> **"Measuring outcomes and impact is important, but there must be checks and balances which ensure outcomes are reached the right way."**

**The sports argument (Greece Euro 2004; Real Madrid's Galácticos; the NHL plus-minus stat):**
> **"Individual performance does not directly predict team performance. And if it's not possible to deduct team performance from individual performance in a domain that's as easy to measure as sports, then we can expect even less success in software engineering."**
> **"Team performance is easier to measure than individual performance."**

**Gergely Orosz's own answer (his half of the divergence):**
> **"Know that people optimize for what is being measured."** — invoking Goodhart's Law, *"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."*
> **"Know that measurement interferes with the system. Every new thing you start measuring will lead to engineers optimizing to make that measure look better. The more you measure, the more you shape the culture and how people work."**
> **"Be skeptical when consultants claim it is possible to measure without impacting how people work. It never is."**
> His four-way gaming taxonomy: **"Measure effort: create high-effort busywork of dubious value / Measure output: increase the quantity of the output by what's easiest to do / Measure outcomes: aim to beat targets, even if this means taking shortcuts / Measure impact: get creative in reaching this with less effort and output."**
> On PR-count metrics: *"it might not be desirable if people now start to split pull requests to separate the code changes and the test changes: just to increase their PR count."*
> On slack time: *"A problem with measurements focused on effort and output is that they transform the engineering culture to one where 'slack time'… is frowned upon."*
> **"Running a high-performing team is a hands-on approach. Looking to metrics to get numbers that show that a team is high-performing is wishful thinking."**
> **"Take two teams. Team A: communicates their impact clearly, and has a hands-on leader on the team. Team B: has fancy metrics and a hands-off leader. I will take Team A over Team B, anytime."**
> **"Yes, you can measure developer productivity, but at what cost? McKinsey is not wrong to state developer productivity can be measured. However, they avoid the question of what is the cost of the measurements."**
> **"Attributing this impact to individual engineers is also possible, but the more granular you make the attribution, the more this interferes with incentives, and the more likely you are to create an organization which incentivizes busywork."**
> **"My suggestion is that if you measure, then start with impact. Not individual impact: but team impact."**

**Kent Beck's own answer (his half — "Kent here."), from newsletter.kentbeck.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity-440.** Beck's version carries a sharper subtitle than Gergely's: **"They only measure activity, not productivity from a business perspective. And measuring activity comes with costs & risks they do not address."** His closing bullets are the most quotable material in the whole series:

> **"Be clear about why you are asking & what your power relationship is with the person or people being measured. When the person with power is measuring the person without, you're going to get distortions."**
> **"Avoid perverse incentives by analyzing data at the same level as you collect the data. I can analyze my own data. My team can analyze its own aggregated data."**
> **"If you choose to create incentives (broadly defined—money, status, promotion, autonomy) around measures, know that you will never again receive accurate data."**
> **"Red Team any incentives. What would a clever (you hired them, of course they are clever), motivated person do to make the numbers look better. How much damage could they cause in the process."**
> **"Get comfortable with your own judgement. Executives relying unnecessarily on 'data' seem to be running from responsibility. Grasp that nettle."**
> **"Measure developer productivity? Not possible. There are too many confounding factors, network effects, variance, observation effects, and feedback loops to get sensible answers to questions like, 'How many times more profit did Joan create than Harry?' or, 'How much better (or worse) is Harry doing this quarter than last?' You can measure activity, but not without directing that activity away from the ends you care about."**
> **"Be suspicious of anyone claiming to measure developer productivity. Ask who is asking & why. Ask them what unit they are measuring & how those units are connected to profit."**
> **"I am 100% pro-accountability. Weekly delivery of customer-appreciated value is the best accountability, the most aligned, the least distorting."**

## 3. Dan North (Daniel Terhorst-North)

**"McKinsey Developer Productivity Review"** — **4 October 2023**, ~17 min read.
URL: **https://dannorth.net/blog/mckinsey-review/** (the older `https://dannorth.net/mckinsey-review/` 301-redirects there). Also announced on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/danielterhorstnorth_mckinsey-developer-productivity-review-activity-7115397513485922305-gnT8

Note: **there is no Dan North post titled "Do you really want to know…?"** on this topic — that title doesn't exist in his catalogue as far as I can find. The two relevant pieces are the review above and **"The Worst Programmer I Know"** (2 Sept 2023, https://dannorth.net/blog/the-worst-programmer/).

He writes it as **an open letter / peer review**: *"I am writing this as though the authors have approached me for a technical review of their article… Dear Chandra and team,"* — and notes at the outset that **"I have not seen anyone engage with the content of the article itself, so I thought this would be useful."**

**The two "erroneous planks" — his central thesis:**
> **"To cut to the chase, I see two main planks to your thesis, which I will return to as we go through the content, and which are both erroneous: 1. Software development is a reducible activity, and can be measured with reductionist tools. 2. Software development is primarily about coding, and anything other than typing code into a computer terminal is waste which we should seek to eliminate."**

**On "undermeasured":**
> **"Software development is one of the most ruthlessly scrutinized and measured of all business activities."**
> **"The one thing you cannot call this era is under-measured. Mis-measured, for sure… but never under-measured!"**
> **"This assumption that software development has the same reducible complexity as assembling a car lies at the heart of the developer productivity challenge."**

**On the 2x Gen-AI claim:**
> **"most of programming is not typing code."**
> **"Most of programming is learning the business domain; understanding the problem; assessing possible solutions; validating assumptions through feedback and experimentation; identifying, assessing and meeting cross-functional needs such as compliance, security, availability, resilience, accessibility, usability…"**
> **"the typing-the-code part is only a modest part of all of this, so using Gen-AI to speed that up, while useful, is hardly 'making developers twice as fast'."**

**On the "nearly 20 companies" evidence base:** he invokes Kahneman's Law of Small Numbers, notes there is **"no control basis,"** that they **"fail to consider the Hawthorne Effect,"** and asks **"Is this approach causal, just correlated, or coincidental?"** — concluding: **"presenting a newly minted methodology as showing 'promising results' with what is effectively anecdotal evidence could be misleading."**

**On the missing Forsgren citation:**
> **"you fail to cite Dr. Nicole Forsgren, the lead researcher on both initiatives, or any of her coauthors… our industry has a history of erasing female contributors to software engineering, so I presume you will rectify this in the next revision."**

**On Contribution Analysis specifically:**
> **"This whole segment, which appears to be a cornerstone of the paper, is unfortunately simply misguided. It falls into the fallacy that software development is reducible, like building a wall, where you can measure who lays the most bricks, or whose work is the neatest or needs the fewest corrections."**
> **"those who contribute less code to solve the same problem, or even who remove unnecessary or redundant code, are often your highest-value developers."**
> On "enable those highest-value developers to code": **"And this is the nub of the whole article. Your highest-value developers are 10x by enabling other developers! Often the least useful thing they can be doing is producing code themselves."**
> **"You appear to be adopting a simplistic model where senior people just do what junior people do but more so, which means the goal is to keep their hands to the keyboard. The whole push of the article is that the best developers should be doing rather than thinking or supporting."**
> **"Next you make the assumption that the backlog is the product… but it makes no sense to use it for individual policing."**

**On inner loop / outer loop:**
> **"I am finding your model of inner and outer loops confusing. They certainly do not reflect my experience of enterprise software development, which I presume is your target audience."**
> **"The idea that security or compliance audits and requirements are a separate review activity in some outer loop is in direct conflict with the principle of shifting left that McKinsey promotes. Security and compliance should be an intrinsic part of software development."**
> **"Meetings, too, are not an outer loop activity. Any collaboration is a meeting! Pair-programming is a continual meeting…"**
> **"Again, 'code-test-build' is the easy part; what about solve?"**
> He counters with David Marquet's *Turn the Ship Around* "inviting inspection": high-performing teams **"welcome experts in security, compliance, accessibility, resilience… as consultants into their development activities rather than as gatekeepers at the end."**

**On the "low-value" tasks (test data, infrastructure):**
> He recounts a major ISP that **"accidentally emailed 16,000 active subscribers to tell them that their broadband was being terminated by using real addresses in a test run."**
> **"Your categorization of 'low-value' work again seems subject to the idea that any non-coding activities are of low value, which is demonstrably wrong."**

**On Talent Capability Score:**
> **"Your example where a client has 'more developers in "novice" capability than was ideal' unfortunately makes no sense. Each developer will have a unique skills profile…"**
> **"This is the same error that we find in stack-ranking of teams. In a high-performing team, all the players are on one end of the curve! There is no normal distribution and there is no 'weakest link'."**
> **"In terms of resourcing teams, a lack of capability in an area is irrelevant if the team's ability to deliver is not constrained by this lack."**

**The most-quoted line of the whole piece:**
> **"However, attempting to measure the individual contribution of a person is like trying to measure the individual contribution of a piston in an engine. The question itself makes no sense."**
> And on method: **"Applying reductionist thinking and tooling is a category error. 'Better' reductionist tooling is just doubling down on doing the wrong thing with the illusion of rigour."**

**On the conclusion's self-contradiction:**
> **"Then you conclude that measuring productivity is contextual, while the entire article is promoting your context-free assessment tooling."**
> Also: **"code coverage is a well-documented red herring, since it is neither necessary nor sufficient to demonstrate quality."**

**His alternative:**
> **"if someone is identified as a 'weak' performer, I take that as signal that we are letting that person down."**
> **"If the mindset is 'weeding out poor performers' then this suggests an abdication of responsibility; the idea that the flower is at fault for failing to grow rather than the soil or climate."**
> He proposes flow metrics (lead time, throughput), Theory of Constraints, Goldratt and Reinertsen, plus peer feedback questions like *"Who do you most want to be in this team, and why?"*

## Bottom-line framing of the debate

Everyone attacked the same seam from a different angle:
- **Beck/Orosz:** McKinsey measures the **wrong stage of the value chain** — 4 of its 5 novel metrics sit at *effort/output*, the cheapest place to measure and the most expensive place to distort. Cost of measurement is the unasked question.
- **North:** McKinsey commits a **category error** — reductionist tools on an irreducible activity, plus the coding-is-the-work fallacy that makes mentoring, security, infra and test data look like "waste."
- **Booch/Farley:** it's **not science** — astrology dressed in DORA's clothes.
- **Majors/Vaughn/North:** the **team is the unit**, and individual attribution is the specific thing that poisons the well.
- All of them converge on **Goodhart's Law** and the observer effect: the moment Contribution Analysis touches a performance review, the data is gone.</result>

## 1. The McKinsey article

**"Yes, you can measure software developer productivity"** — published **17 August 2023**
URL: https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/technology-media-and-telecommunications/our-insights/yes-you-can-measure-software-developer-productivity

**Byline correction (important):** the article is credited to **Chandra Gnanasambandam, Martin Harrysson, Alharith Hussin, Jason Keovichit, and Shivam Srivastava** — Gnanasambandam and Harrysson are senior partners in McKinsey's Bay Area office, Hussin and Srivastava partners there, Keovichit an associate partner in New York. They thank Pedro Garcia, Diana Rodriguez and Jeremy Schneider. **Wenjie Wu is not an author of this piece** (that name belongs to other McKinsey tech-practice work). Dan North's review notes "all five contributing authors are male."

*(McKinsey.com timed out repeatedly via WebFetch and curl; full verbatim text was recovered from a complete reproduction at https://healthcarereimagined.net/2023/08/19/yes-you-can-measure-software-developer-productivity-mckinsey/ which includes the full byline and article link. Quotes below are verbatim from that reproduction.)*

### Framing claims

- Opening line: **"Compared with other critical business functions such as sales or customer operations, software development is perennially undermeasured."**
- **"The long-held belief by many in tech is that it's not possible to do it correctly—and that, in any case, only trained engineers are knowledgeable enough to assess the performance of their peers. Yet that status quo is no longer sustainable."**
- Gen-AI claim: tools like CopilotX and ChatGPT **"have the potential to enable developers to complete tasks up to two times faster."**
- Deployment claim: **"This new approach has been implemented at nearly 20 tech, finance, and pharmaceutical companies, and the initial results are promising"** — citing "20 to 30 percent reduction in customer-reported product defects," "20 percent improvement in employee experience scores," and a "60-percentage-point improvement in customer satisfaction ratings."

### Explicit language on individual measurement

- **"Software development is also highly collaborative, complex, and creative work and requires different metrics for different levels (such as systems, teams, and individuals)."**
- **"it's essential to understand the three types of metrics that need to be tracked: those at the system level, the team level, and the individual level."**
- **"while deployment frequency is a perfectly good metric to assess systems or teams, it depends on all team members doing their respective tasks and is, therefore, not a useful way to track individual performance."**
- Closing: **"The point is to look at an entire system and understand how it can work better by improving the development environment at the system, team, or individual level."**

### The proposed "opportunity-focused metrics"

Positioned as layered *on top of* DORA and SPACE: **"Complementing DORA and SPACE metrics with opportunity-focused metrics can create an end-to-end view of software developer productivity."** (Notably, McKinsey cites DORA and SPACE but **never cites Nicole Forsgren or any coauthor** — a point North hammers.)

**a) Inner/outer loop time spent.** "An inner loop comprises activities directly related to creating the product: coding, building, and unit testing. An outer loop comprises other tasks developers must do to push their code to production: integration, integration testing, releasing, and deployment." And: **"maximizing the amount of time developers spend in the inner loop is desirable: building products directly generates value and is what most developers are excited to do. Outer-loop activities are seen by most developers as necessary but generally unsatisfying chores."** Target: **"Top tech companies aim for developers to spend up to 70 percent of their time doing inner-loop activities."** The worked example names as **"low-value-added tasks"**: "provisioning infrastructure, running manual unit tests, and managing test data."

**b) Developer Velocity Index (DVI) benchmark.** "a survey that measures an enterprise's technology, working practices, and organizational enablement and benchmarks them against peers."

**c) Contribution analysis.** **"Assessing contributions by individuals to a team's backlog (starting with data from backlog management tools such as Jira, and normalizing data using a proprietary algorithm to account for nuances) can help surface trends that inhibit the optimization of that team's capacity."** The example that became the lightning rod: **"one company found that its most talented developers were spending excessive time on noncoding activities such as design sessions or managing interdependencies across teams. In response, the company changed its operating model and clarified roles and responsibilities to enable those highest-value developers to do what they do best: code."** Also: "another company, after discovering relatively low contribution from developers new to the organization, reexamined their onboarding and personal mentorship program."

**d) Talent capability score.** "Based on industry standard capability maps, this score is a summary of the individual knowledge, skills, and abilities of a specific organization. **Ideally, organizations should aspire to a 'diamond' distribution of proficiency, with the majority of developers in the middle range of competency.**" Example: "one company found a higher concentration of their developers in the 'novice' capability than was ideal. They deployed personalized learning journeys… able to move 30 percent of their developers to the next level of expertise within six months."

### The sentence that drew the most fire

**"To truly benefit from measuring productivity, leaders and developers alike need to move past the outdated notion that leaders 'cannot' understand the intricacies of software engineering, or that engineering is too complex to measure."**

McKinsey does pre-empt some criticism ("Avoiding metrics missteps"): it warns against "lines of code produced, or number of code commits," notes "optimizing for lead time or deployment frequency can allow quality to suffer," and concedes "developers may submit smaller changes more frequently as they seek to game the system." It also flags remote work as a driver: "organizations will need to rely on broad, objective measurements to maintain confidence in these new working arrangements."

## 2. Kent Beck + Gergely Orosz — the joint response

**It is a TWO-part series, not 3–4** — but it exists as **four published artifacts**, because each part was cross-published simultaneously on both newsletters, and Part 2's final section **diverges into two separate answers**. That's likely the source of the "3–4 parts" impression. There is also a January 2024 sequel (below).

| # | Title | Date | URL |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 (PE) | Measuring developer productivity? A response to McKinsey | 29 Aug 2023 | https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity |
| P1 (KB) | Measuring developer productivity? A response to McKinsey | 29 Aug 2023 | https://newsletter.kentbeck.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity |
| P2 (PE) | Measuring developer productivity? A response to McKinsey, Part 2 | 31 Aug 2023 | https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity-part-2 |
| P2 (KB) | Measuring developer productivity? A response to McKinsey 2 | 31 Aug 2023 | https://newsletter.kentbeck.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity-440 |
| Sequel | Measuring Developer Productivity: Real-World Examples (Gergely + Abi Noda, 17 companies) | 16 Jan 2024 | https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity-bae |

Orosz on the origin: *"A few hours after publishing this article, I was already on a call with Kent, as we tried to pinpoint exactly why both of us felt frustrated with this report."* Parts 1 and the bulk of Part 2 are written **"with one, shared voice."**

### Kent Beck — before the series (LinkedIn, ~20–24 Aug 2023)

The precursor post (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kentbeck_mckinsey-claims-its-possible-to-measure-activity-7099764438496407552-v8P2):

> **"McKinsey claims it's possible to measure developer productivity. The report is so absurd & naive that it makes no sense to critique it in detail."** — Kent Beck

> **"McKinsey folks are smart. They know that their intended market wants this report to be good advice, wants to act this way, wants McKinsey's help/permission to do so."** — Kent Beck

> **"What they published damages people I care about. I'm here to help geeks feel safe in the world. This kind of surveillance makes geeks feel less safe."** — Kent Beck (quoted in ShiftMag)

The surgeon analogy (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kentbeck_mckinseys-you-can-measure-developer-productivity-activity-7101918867161051136-b8F4):

> **"McKinsey's 'you can measure developer productivity' is like if we measured surgeon productivity on what percentage of their time they were cutting with a scalpel or stitching with a needle and we ignored whether the patient got better."** — Kent Beck

He extends it: an expert surgeon on a complex case needs time to "observe & assess," not rush to avoid the "bottom 10%"; and the perverse incentive is that a surgeon might **"turn down a difficult case because it would lower their"** score. He also asks: measuring **"with what units? How do those units correlate with profit? What profit dysfunctions are created by measuring & assessing those units?"**

### Part 1 — key quotable lines

**Kent Beck, on the Facebook survey death-spiral (verbatim, his first-person block):**
> "At Facebook we instituted the sorts of surveys McKinsey recommends. That was good for about a year. The surveys provided valuable feedback about the current state of developer sentiment. Then folks decided that they wanted to make the survey results more legible so they could track trends over time. They computed an overall score from the survey. Very reasonable thing to do. That was good for another year. A 4.5 became a 4. What happened? Then those scores started cropping up in performance reviews… Then those scores started getting rolled up. A manager's score was the average of their reports' scores. A director's score would be the average of their reporting managers' scores. **Now things started getting unhinged.** Directors put pressure on managers for better scores. Managers started negotiating with individual contributors for better survey scores. **'Give me a 5 & I'll make sure you get an "exceeds expectations".'** Directors started cutting managers & teams with poor scores, whether those cuts made organizational sense or not."

> **"Things went from, 'we'd like to know how things are going,' to, 'we know even less about how things are going. But they are definitely going worse because people are now gaming the system.'"** — Beck & Orosz

**On refusing a line-by-line rebuttal:**
> **"As tempting as it is, we won't go into a detailed critique of the McKinsey article and the measurement methodology. The thinking that's evident in the article is absurdly naive and ignores the dynamics of high-performing software engineering teams."**

**On why the article exists — the political read:**
> **"CEOs and CFOs are increasingly frustrated by CTOs throwing up their hands and saying software engineering is too nuanced to measure, when sales teams have individual measurements and quotas to hit… The executive reasoning goes: if other groups can measure individual performance, it's absurd that engineering cannot."**

> **"If they try to [avoid the question], they risk the CEO or CFO turning instead to McKinsey, who will bring their custom framework, deploy it – even as the CTO protests – and start reporting on custom McKinsey metrics like 'Developer Velocity Benchmark Index,' 'Contribution Analysis,' and 'Talent Capability.'"**

> **"We believe that introducing such a framework is wrong-headed and certain to backfire. The McKinsey framework will most likely do far more harm than good to organizations – and to the engineering culture at companies. Such damage could take years to undo."**

**On the intended audience (a barb):**
> **"When reading articles like McKinsey's, keep in mind they're written for a very different, and specific, audience: untechnical CEOs and CFOs with little to zero experience with software development. Engineering is just another department."**

**The core analytical move — the effort → output → outcome → impact model.** Effort (planning, coding); output (the feature, code, design docs); outcome (customers behave differently); impact (feedback, revenue, referrals). All four DORA metrics map to outcome/impact. Then the central charge:

> **"One critique of McKinsey's system we have is that nearly every one of its custom metrics which differ from DORA and SPACE metrics, measure effort or output."** (Their exhibit: "4 out of the 5 new metrics suggested by McKinsey's measure effort or output.")

> **"First, the only folks who care about these metrics are the people collecting them. Customers don't care. Executives don't care. Investors don't care. Second, and most crucially, collecting & evaluating these metrics hinders the measures downstream folks actually do care about, like profitability."**

> **"Why is McKinsey adding ways to measure effort? One reason is that it's the easiest thing to measure! But the McKinsey approach ignores an important truth: the act of measurement changes how developers work, as they try to 'game' the system."**

> **"The earlier in the cycle you measure, the easier it is to measure. And also the more likely that you introduce unintended consequences."**

**Kent Beck's sales-vs-engineering meeting anecdote** (verbatim, his voice) — sales leader: *"'My team's target for the quarter was $600K, and we delivered $520K. I take accountability for the miss…'"* vs. engineering: *"'So, this quarter we shipped Feature A, and we are slightly behind on some tech debt migration…'"* — **"My goodness, the contrast was stark."** And: **"The level of accountability which sales and customer support work with is on a completely different scale from what a CEO observes from engineering. But when the CEO examines overall departmental costs, engineering probably costs more than sales!"**

**Their positive proposal:**
> **"We urge engineering leaders to look to outcome and impact measurements, to identify what to measure."**
> **"Producing at least one customer-facing thing per team, per week. This output might not sound so impressive, but in practice is very hard to achieve."**

**Uber footnote (Orosz's reporting):** after Uber shipped an Eng Metrics dashboard, *"the lines of code did not change drastically, but the CI systems saw a visible increase in utilization. Basically, people started to create far, far more diffs, which put a much larger load on the continuous integration (CI) systems, and increased CI costs."*

### Part 2 — key quotable lines

> **"We believe that introducing a kind of framework that McKinsey is proposing is wrong-headed and certain to backfire. Such a framework will most likely do far more harm than good to organizations – and to the engineering culture at companies and the damage could take years to undo."**

**Kent Beck on outcome-only measurement (sales quota gaming, his voice):**
> "Individual goals discourages people from working together, as everyone is chasing their own quota… I saw firsthand how a 'star' salesperson operated. They always hit their quota, and collected a hefty bonus. How did they do it? Well, they knew that sales could fall through any time, so they always had several prospects 'in the pocket'… **In order to maximize personal gains, they did not maximize the company's gain.**"

**Gergely Orosz on the "rockstar" recruiter with a 100% close rate** who had made verbal bonus promises that were "outrageously untrue": *"It took us managers months to sort out the mess, and left engineers feeling tricked and with declining faith in the company."*

> **"Measuring outcomes and impact is important, but there must be checks and balances which ensure outcomes are reached the right way."**

**The sports argument (Greece Euro 2004; Real Madrid's Galácticos; the NHL plus-minus stat):**
> **"Individual performance does not directly predict team performance. And if it's not possible to deduct team performance from individual performance in a domain that's as easy to measure as sports, then we can expect even less success in software engineering."**
> **"Team performance is easier to measure than individual performance."**

**Gergely Orosz's own answer (his half of the divergence):**
> **"Know that people optimize for what is being measured."** — invoking Goodhart's Law, *"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."*
> **"Know that measurement interferes with the system. Every new thing you start measuring will lead to engineers optimizing to make that measure look better. The more you measure, the more you shape the culture and how people work."**
> **"Be skeptical when consultants claim it is possible to measure without impacting how people work. It never is."**
> His four-way gaming taxonomy: **"Measure effort: create high-effort busywork of dubious value / Measure output: increase the quantity of the output by what's easiest to do / Measure outcomes: aim to beat targets, even if this means taking shortcuts / Measure impact: get creative in reaching this with less effort and output."**
> On PR-count metrics: *"it might not be desirable if people now start to split pull requests to separate the code changes and the test changes: just to increase their PR count."*
> On slack time: *"A problem with measurements focused on effort and output is that they transform the engineering culture to one where 'slack time'… is frowned upon."*
> **"Running a high-performing team is a hands-on approach. Looking to metrics to get numbers that show that a team is high-performing is wishful thinking."**
> **"Take two teams. Team A: communicates their impact clearly, and has a hands-on leader on the team. Team B: has fancy metrics and a hands-off leader. I will take Team A over Team B, anytime."**
> **"Yes, you can measure developer productivity, but at what cost? McKinsey is not wrong to state developer productivity can be measured. However, they avoid the question of what is the cost of the measurements."**
> **"Attributing this impact to individual engineers is also possible, but the more granular you make the attribution, the more this interferes with incentives, and the more likely you are to create an organization which incentivizes busywork."**
> **"My suggestion is that if you measure, then start with impact. Not individual impact: but team impact."**

**Kent Beck's own answer (his half — "Kent here."), from newsletter.kentbeck.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity-440.** Beck's version carries a sharper subtitle than Gergely's: **"They only measure activity, not productivity from a business perspective. And measuring activity comes with costs & risks they do not address."** His closing bullets are the most quotable material in the whole series:

> **"Be clear about why you are asking & what your power relationship is with the person or people being measured. When the person with power is measuring the person without, you're going to get distortions."**
> **"Avoid perverse incentives by analyzing data at the same level as you collect the data. I can analyze my own data. My team can analyze its own aggregated data."**
> **"If you choose to create incentives (broadly defined—money, status, promotion, autonomy) around measures, know that you will never again receive accurate data."**
> **"Red Team any incentives. What would a clever (you hired them, of course they are clever), motivated person do to make the numbers look better. How much damage could they cause in the process."**
> **"Get comfortable with your own judgement. Executives relying unnecessarily on 'data' seem to be running from responsibility. Grasp that nettle."**
> **"Measure developer productivity? Not possible. There are too many confounding factors, network effects, variance, observation effects, and feedback loops to get sensible answers to questions like, 'How many times more profit did Joan create than Harry?' or, 'How much better (or worse) is Harry doing this quarter than last?' You can measure activity, but not without directing that activity away from the ends you care about."**
> **"Be suspicious of anyone claiming to measure developer productivity. Ask who is asking & why. Ask them what unit they are measuring & how those units are connected to profit."**
> **"I am 100% pro-accountability. Weekly delivery of customer-appreciated value is the best accountability, the most aligned, the least distorting."**

---

## 3. Dan North (Daniel Terhorst-North)

**"McKinsey Developer Productivity Review"** — **4 October 2023**, ~17 min read.
URL: **https://dannorth.net/blog/mckinsey-review/** (the older `https://dannorth.net/mckinsey-review/` 301-redirects there). Also announced on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/danielterhorstnorth_mckinsey-developer-productivity-review-activity-7115397513485922305-gnT8

Note: **there is no Dan North post titled "Do you really want to know…?"** on this topic — that title doesn't exist in his catalogue as far as I can find. The two relevant pieces are the review above and **"The Worst Programmer I Know"** (2 Sept 2023, https://dannorth.net/blog/the-worst-programmer/).

He writes it as **an open letter / peer review**: *"I am writing this as though the authors have approached me for a technical review of their article… Dear Chandra and team,"* — and notes at the outset that **"I have not seen anyone engage with the content of the article itself, so I thought this would be useful."**

**The two "erroneous planks" — his central thesis:**
> **"To cut to the chase, I see two main planks to your thesis, which I will return to as we go through the content, and which are both erroneous: 1. Software development is a reducible activity, and can be measured with reductionist tools. 2. Software development is primarily about coding, and anything other than typing code into a computer terminal is waste which we should seek to eliminate."**

**On "undermeasured":**
> **"Software development is one of the most ruthlessly scrutinized and measured of all business activities."**
> **"The one thing you cannot call this era is under-measured. Mis-measured, for sure… but never under-measured!"**
> **"This assumption that software development has the same reducible complexity as assembling a car lies at the heart of the developer productivity challenge."**

**On the 2x Gen-AI claim:**
> **"most of programming is not typing code."**
> **"Most of programming is learning the business domain; understanding the problem; assessing possible solutions; validating assumptions through feedback and experimentation; identifying, assessing and meeting cross-functional needs such as compliance, security, availability, resilience, accessibility, usability…"**
> **"the typing-the-code part is only a modest part of all of this, so using Gen-AI to speed that up, while useful, is hardly 'making developers twice as fast'."**

**On the "nearly 20 companies" evidence base:** he invokes Kahneman's Law of Small Numbers, notes there is **"no control basis,"** that they **"fail to consider the Hawthorne Effect,"** and asks **"Is this approach causal, just correlated, or coincidental?"** — concluding: **"presenting a newly minted methodology as showing 'promising results' with what is effectively anecdotal evidence could be misleading."**

**On the missing Forsgren citation:**
> **"you fail to cite Dr. Nicole Forsgren, the lead researcher on both initiatives, or any of her coauthors… our industry has a history of erasing female contributors to software engineering, so I presume you will rectify this in the next revision."**

**On Contribution Analysis specifically:**
> **"This whole segment, which appears to be a cornerstone of the paper, is unfortunately simply misguided. It falls into the fallacy that software development is reducible, like building a wall, where you can measure who lays the most bricks, or whose work is the neatest or needs the fewest corrections."**
> **"those who contribute less code to solve the same problem, or even who remove unnecessary or redundant code, are often your highest-value developers."**
> On "enable those highest-value developers to code": **"And this is the nub of the whole article. Your highest-value developers are 10x by enabling other developers! Often the least useful thing they can be doing is producing code themselves."**
> **"You appear to be adopting a simplistic model where senior people just do what junior people do but more so, which means the goal is to keep their hands to the keyboard. The whole push of the article is that the best developers should be doing rather than thinking or supporting."**
> **"Next you make the assumption that the backlog is the product… but it makes no sense to use it for individual policing."**

**On inner loop / outer loop:**
> **"I am finding your model of inner and outer loops confusing. They certainly do not reflect my experience of enterprise software development, which I presume is your target audience."**
> **"The idea that security or compliance audits and requirements are a separate review activity in some outer loop is in direct conflict with the principle of shifting left that McKinsey promotes. Security and compliance should be an intrinsic part of software development."**
> **"Meetings, too, are not an outer loop activity. Any collaboration is a meeting! Pair-programming is a continual meeting…"**
> **"Again, 'code-test-build' is the easy part; what about solve?"**
> He counters with David Marquet's *Turn the Ship Around* "inviting inspection": high-performing teams **"welcome experts in security, compliance, accessibility, resilience… as consultants into their development activities rather than as gatekeepers at the end."**

**On the "low-value" tasks (test data, infrastructure):**
> He recounts a major ISP that **"accidentally emailed 16,000 active subscribers to tell them that their broadband was being terminated by using real addresses in a test run."**
> **"Your categorization of 'low-value' work again seems subject to the idea that any non-coding activities are of low value, which is demonstrably wrong."**

**On Talent Capability Score:**
> **"Your example where a client has 'more developers in "novice" capability than was ideal' unfortunately makes no sense. Each developer will have a unique skills profile…"**
> **"This is the same error that we find in stack-ranking of teams. In a high-performing team, all the players are on one end of the curve! There is no normal distribution and there is no 'weakest link'."**
> **"In terms of resourcing teams, a lack of capability in an area is irrelevant if the team's ability to deliver is not constrained by this lack."**

**The most-quoted line of the whole piece:**
> **"However, attempting to measure the individual contribution of a person is like trying to measure the individual contribution of a piston in an engine. The question itself makes no sense."**
> And on method: **"Applying reductionist thinking and tooling is a category error. 'Better' reductionist tooling is just doubling down on doing the wrong thing with the illusion of rigour."**

**On the conclusion's self-contradiction:**
> **"Then you conclude that measuring productivity is contextual, while the entire article is promoting your context-free assessment tooling."**
> Also: **"code coverage is a well-documented red herring, since it is neither necessary nor sufficient to demonstrate quality."**

**His alternative:**
> **"if someone is identified as a 'weak' performer, I take that as signal that we are letting that person down."**
> **"If the mindset is 'weeding out poor performers' then this suggests an abdication of responsibility; the idea that the flower is at fault for failing to grow rather than the soil or climate."**
> He proposes flow metrics (lead time, throughput), Theory of Constraints, Goldratt and Reinertsen, plus peer feedback questions like *"Who do you most want to be in this team, and why?"*

**Footnote/correction** (worth flagging for accuracy): North appended — *"Correction: I misread the section Avoiding metrics missteps, which in fact says to 'move past the outdated notion that […] engineering is too complex to measure.' However, my point stands…"*

### Dan North — "The Worst Programmer I Know" (2 Sept 2023)
https://dannorth.net/blog/the-worst-programmer/ — the companion parable about **Tim Mackinnon**, scored on story points delivered at a Big Bank consultancy:
> **"Tim's score was consistently zero. Zero! Not just low, or trending downwards, but literally zero."** (he never signed up for stories; *"Instead he would spend his day pairing with different teammates."*)
> **"Tim wasn't delivering software; Tim was delivering a team that was delivering software."**
> **"The entire team became more effective, more productive, more aligned, more idiomatic, more fun, because Tim was in the team."**
> **"Don't try to measure the individual contribution of a unit in a complex adaptive system, because the premise of the question is flawed."**

---

## 4. Other credible critiques

**Grady Booch** — the shortest and most-circulated reaction. Quote-tweeting the McKinsey article, 20 Aug 2023: **"Ah. This from McKinsey. It's rubbish."** (@Grady_Booch; archived in ShiftMag.)

**Dave Farley** — quoted in LeadDev: **"Apart from the use of DORA metrics in this model, the rest is pretty much astrology"** and **"Measuring software development in terms of individual developer productivity is a terrible idea."**

**Charity Majors** — not a direct response (predates it, July 2020) but the canonical text the backlash leaned on: https://charity.wtf/2020/07/07/questionable-advice-can-engineering-productivity-be-measured/
> **"The right way to look at performance is at the team level. Individual engineers don't own or maintain code; teams do. The team is the irreducible unit of ownership."**
> **"Some of the hardest and most impactful engineering work will be all but invisible on any set of individual metrics."**
> **"The more challenging and novel a problem, the less reliable these metrics will be. In fact, to the extent you can reduce a job to a set of metrics, that job can be automated away."**

**Kelly Vaughn (Dir. of Engineering, Spot AI) & Ori Keren (CEO, LinearB)** — Dev Interrupted episode #147, "The McKinsey Developer Productivity Debate," Sept 2023: https://linearb.io/dev-interrupted/podcast/the-mckinsey-developer-productivity-debate (also https://devinterrupted.substack.com/p/the-mckinsey-developer-productivity, video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=61deMA-8Yc4)
> **Ori Keren:** "I think the best engineers that I've worked with, they're the best readers of code… The best developers can read code. They have patience to read code… if you just let them code, you miss some of their greatest qualities." — a direct hit on Contribution Analysis's "let them do what they do best: code."
> **Kelly Vaughn:** "Completely agree. I would be terrible. I would actually be absolutely awful if I were the developer on the receiving end of this and all I was told to do was just code."
> On individual metrics: **"I feel strongly that you cannot use a system to measure individual metrics. It's almost like creating an autoimmune system that attacks its own culture."**

**Abi Noda (DX; coauthor of the DevEx paper with the DORA/SPACE creators)** — quoted in both Orosz's Part 2 and LeadDev; notes McKinsey's methods contradict what Google and Microsoft actually do. His reframe, quoted verbatim by Orosz: *"What the CEO wants is to know you're being a good steward of their investment in engineering. You can demonstrate strong stewardship by providing a full picture of engineering, including: Business impact / System performance / And developer effectiveness."* He later supplied the empirical counter-evidence in the Jan 2024 Pragmatic Engineer piece surveying what DevProd teams at 17 companies (Google, LinkedIn, Peloton, etc.) actually measure.

**Jennifer Riggins, LeadDev, 23 Oct 2023** — "What McKinsey got wrong about developer productivity": https://leaddev.com/career-development/what-mckinsey-got-wrong-about-developer-productivity — the best journalistic roundup; also quotes **Peter Gillard-Moss** (Thoughtworks) on the framework missing culture.

**Antonija Bilic Arar, ShiftMag, 24 Aug 2023** — "McKinsey: We can measure developer productivity. Kent Beck: You can't.": https://shiftmag.dev/mckinsey-measure-developer-productivity-1166/ — earliest aggregation, source of the Booch and "geeks feel less safe" quotes.

**Jason Yip (Medium, Aug 2023)** — "Yes, you can measure software developer productivity… but are you sure that's what you're measuring or want to measure?": https://jchyip.medium.com/yes-you-can-measure-software-developer-productivity-but-are-you-sure-thats-what-you-re-measuring-d6b081897840 (Medium returned 403 to automated fetch; title itself is the argument — a measurement-validity critique).

**Bob Marshall, "Think Different," 1 Sept 2023** — "The Fallacy of Measuring Developer Productivity: McKinsey's Misguided Metrics": https://flowchainsensei.wordpress.com/2023/09/01/the-fallacy-of-measuring-developer-productivity-mckinseys-misguided-metrics/

**Jason Gorman (Codemanship), 25 Sept 2023** — "The Illusion Of Developer 'Productivity' Opens The Door To Snake Oil": https://codemanship.wordpress.com/2023/09/25/the-illusion-of-developer-productivity-opens-the-door-to-snake-oil/

**Hacker News thread** (the article hit #1): https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=37203108 — plus a second thread on North's review where he participated: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=37800249

**Mozaic Works roundup + video**: https://mozaicworks.com/blog/reactions-to-mckinseys-dev-productivity-metrics-kent-beck-gergely-orosz-and-dan-north and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uGtM1gRcMgE

### Negative findings (do not attribute these)
- **Marc Andreessen: nothing found.** No public response to the McKinsey piece. The 2023 Andreessen results are all his "Techno-Optimist Manifesto" (Oct 2023), unrelated.
- **Titus Winters: nothing found.** No public critique of this article surfaced, despite his relevance (Google, *Software Engineering at Google*).
- **Nicole Forsgren: no direct public rebuttal found.** Her role in the story is as the **uncited author** McKinsey leaned on — North's charge — not as a responder. The closest thing is her later Pragmatic Engineer appearance (19 Feb 2025, https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/developer-productivity-with-dr-nicole). Don't quote her as a critic of McKinsey without a source.

---

## Bottom-line framing of the debate

Everyone attacked the same seam from a different angle:
- **Beck/Orosz:** McKinsey measures the **wrong stage of the value chain** — 4 of its 5 novel metrics sit at *effort/output*, the cheapest place to measure and the most expensive place to distort. Cost of measurement is the unasked question.
- **North:** McKinsey commits a **category error** — reductionist tools on an irreducible activity, plus the coding-is-the-work fallacy that makes mentoring, security, infra and test data look like "waste."
- **Booch/Farley:** it's **not science** — astrology dressed in DORA's clothes.
- **Majors/Vaughn/North:** the **team is the unit**, and individual attribution is the specific thing that poisons the well.
- All of them converge on **Goodhart's Law** and the observer effect: the moment Contribution Analysis touches a performance review, the data is gone.</result>

#!/bin/bash
# Full 90-day PR pull for PostHog/posthog. Lean GraphQL, no sampling.
# Window: merged 2026-06-04..2026-09-02. Paginates by CREATED_AT desc with a
# 21-day buffer (p90 cycle time is 6.6d) so late-merging PRs are still captured.
set -uo pipefail
D="/Users/mihaiposea/Weave Takehome/data"
OUT="$D/prs.ndjson"; LOG="$D/pull.log"
STOP_EPOCH=$(date -j -f "%Y-%m-%d" "2026-05-14" +%s)
: > "$OUT"; : > "$LOG"
CURSOR=""; PAGE=0; TOTAL=0

while true; do
  PAGE=$((PAGE+1))
  if [ -z "$CURSOR" ]; then AFTER="null"; else AFTER="\"$CURSOR\""; fi
  cat > "$D/q.graphql" <<EOF
query {
  rateLimit { remaining resetAt }
  repository(owner:"PostHog", name:"posthog") {
    pullRequests(first:100, after:$AFTER, orderBy:{field:CREATED_AT, direction:DESC}) {
      pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor }
      nodes {
        number title createdAt mergedAt closedAt state isDraft
        additions deletions changedFiles
        author { login __typename }
        assignees(first:2) { nodes { login } }
        body
        commits(last:1) { nodes { commit { committedAt } } }
        reviews(first:10) { nodes { author { login __typename } state submittedAt comments { totalCount } } }
      }
    }
  }
}
EOF
  RESP=""
  for attempt in 1 2 3 4 5; do
    RESP=$(gh api graphql -F query=@"$D/q.graphql" 2>>"$LOG")
    if [ -n "$RESP" ] && echo "$RESP" | jq -e '.data.repository.pullRequests' >/dev/null 2>&1; then break; fi
    echo "page $PAGE attempt $attempt failed, backing off" >> "$LOG"; sleep $((attempt*10)); RESP=""
  done
  if [ -z "$RESP" ]; then echo "FATAL: page $PAGE gave up" >> "$LOG"; break; fi

  echo "$RESP" | jq -c '.data.repository.pullRequests.nodes[] | {
    n:.number, t:.title, ca:.createdAt, ma:.mergedAt, st:.state, dr:.isDraft,
    add:.additions, del:.deletions, cf:.changedFiles,
    au:(.author.login // "ghost"), aut:(.author.__typename // "User"),
    asg:[.assignees.nodes[].login],
    lc:(.commits.nodes[0].commit.committedAt // null),
    auto:((.body // "") | if test("Autonomy[^\n]*Fully autonomous") and (test("Autonomy[^\n]*Human-driven")|not) then "autonomous"
                          elif test("Autonomy[^\n]*Human-driven") and (test("Autonomy[^\n]*Fully autonomous")|not) then "assisted"
                          elif test("Agent context") then "agent_unspecified" else "none" end),
    rv:[.reviews.nodes[] | {a:(.author.login // "ghost"), ty:(.author.__typename // "User"), s:.state, at:.submittedAt, ic:.comments.totalCount}]
  }' >> "$OUT"

  N=$(echo "$RESP" | jq '.data.repository.pullRequests.nodes | length')
  TOTAL=$((TOTAL+N))
  OLDEST=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.data.repository.pullRequests.nodes[-1].createdAt // empty')
  HASNEXT=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.data.repository.pullRequests.pageInfo.hasNextPage')
  CURSOR=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.data.repository.pullRequests.pageInfo.endCursor')
  REM=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.rateLimit.remaining')
  echo "page=$PAGE got=$N total=$TOTAL oldest=$OLDEST ratelimit=$REM" >> "$LOG"

  [ "$HASNEXT" != "true" ] && { echo "DONE: no more pages" >> "$LOG"; break; }
  if [ -n "$OLDEST" ]; then
    OE=$(date -j -f "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ" "$OLDEST" +%s 2>/dev/null || echo 9999999999)
    [ "$OE" -lt "$STOP_EPOCH" ] && { echo "DONE: reached buffer boundary $OLDEST" >> "$LOG"; break; }
  fi
  if [ "$REM" != "null" ] && [ "$REM" -lt 150 ]; then echo "throttling, remaining=$REM" >> "$LOG"; sleep 300; fi
done
echo "PULL COMPLETE total=$TOTAL pages=$PAGE" >> "$LOG"
SCRIPT

HN username for James Hawkins is **james_impliu** (not jamesefhawkins, which does not exist); Tim Glaser is **timgl**.

## 1. What makes a good/impactful engineer; the "product engineer" concept

> "A product engineer decides what to build. As opposed to someone who follows a product requirements doc."
— **James Hawkins**, *No Babysitters, No Bottlenecks: Inside PostHog's Unstoppable Product Machine* (Untrapping Product Teams podcast, host-published pull quote), https://dpereira.substack.com/p/no-babysitters-no-bottlenecks-inside — 10 July 2025

> "Instead of providing a product manager who tells the engineers what to build, we're trying to help our engineers be good product managers."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "So we like hiring like slightly frontend-oriented engineers because we think they're slightly stronger at product. And we give them principles to operate."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "The role of a product manager at PostHog is to provide context to teams. It is not to decide what to build or set deadlines."
— **James Hawkins**, https://dpereira.substack.com/p/no-babysitters-no-bottlenecks-inside — 10 July 2025

> "Cracked engineers apply themselves to the craft of building products with a quasi-religious fervor, and love what they do." … "Joy comes from the craft itself, not creating shareholder value."
— **Charles Cook**, "Hiring (and managing) cracked engineers", https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/hiring-and-managing-cracked-engineers — 23 May 2024

> "Good product engineers: Ship quickly so they have a fast feedback loop … Have users that they're friendly with … Manage to build things without lots of internal meetings"
> "Bad product engineers: Consider research something that takes two weeks rather than two hours … Don't know the names of any of their users … Spend 6 months on a huge feature before a user can try it"
— **PostHog handbook** (company-authored, not individually attributed), https://posthog.com/handbook/engineering/product-engineering — source: `contents/handbook/engineering/product-engineering.md`, PostHog/posthog.com master

## 2. Measuring/evaluating engineers; metrics they reject

> "We understand that all the work an engineer does can't be properly represented in a tool that just looks at PR output. Data in Weave is _not_ the decision-maker for whether someone is succeeding in their role at PostHog. It can be, however, a part of the conversation."
— **PostHog handbook**, https://posthog.com/handbook/company/management

> "We don't use Weave to: … Monitor your PRs - our management layer is stretched way too thin to micromanage this … Creep on your use of AI - we don't care how or if you use AI to get a job done, as long as it gets done … Make a call on how valuable someone is - some people with low PR output are very valuable to the company, and we're 100% aware that things like heavy support load can impact output"
— **PostHog handbook**, https://posthog.com/handbook/company/management

> "Setting deadlines, creating arbitrary reporting obligations, or saying 'if you ship X, you will get to Y title' are examples of trying to use extrinsic motivation. This is un-cracked."
— **Charles Cook**, https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/hiring-and-managing-cracked-engineers — 23 May 2024

> "If you need to introduce deadlines to get work done, you've already failed."
— **James Hawkins**, https://dpereira.substack.com/p/no-babysitters-no-bottlenecks-inside — 10 July 2025

> "The 20% of your team who are underperforming will take up 80% of your effort. … It's the 9/10 quality output that will delight your users, so you should focus on that, even if the absolute increase in performance is less."
— **Charles Cook**, https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/hiring-and-managing-cracked-engineers — 23 May 2024

> "one of the most interesting learnings so far from the data we've seen (~400 developers using it for the last month to log issues in their code/processes, >1,000 survey responses) is that the average developer encountering an issue loses more than twice as much time in Planning and Deployment than in Writing Code."
— **James Hawkins** (HN: james_impliu), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=21750586 — 10 December 2019 (thread: "Ask HN: How to improve code quality while maintaining decent velocity?")

---

## 3. Shipping fast; speed vs. quality

> "And we concluded, like, we're not going to win on design polish here. We're going to win on engineering velocity. So The entire company is designed to ship quickly."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "our preferred method of communication from an engineer is not to spend ages like super validating your product, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. Just build something real, ship it."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "I think if you read a lot of like product management stuff online, it's all kind of thou shalt Validate your ideas … But I don't think this is really, I think that's like a cultural thing from really risk-averse, extremely large companies that might spend like $20 billion on some new thing and they need to be ultra risk-averse. Whereas with a startup, like you're screwed by default, like you're going to fail."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "I feel like a weird industry has popped up that makes you feel like you can validate everything in advance. I think this comes from Product Managers in large, risk-averse companies that excessively try to minimize mistakes. However, if you want to start a startup, you aren't optimizing for mistake minimization! You are figuring out if anyone cares as quickly as possible."
— **James Hawkins** (HN: james_impliu), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=36584166 — 4 July 2023

> "We win on our ability to ship quickly. Who ships fast with more than 3 people? Almost no one."
— **James Hawkins**, https://dpereira.substack.com/p/no-babysitters-no-bottlenecks-inside — 10 July 2025

> "Now we just continuously ship new stuff. It creates a brand where every week, there's something cool."
— **James Hawkins**, https://dpereira.substack.com/p/no-babysitters-no-bottlenecks-inside — 10 July 2025

> "Duplicate effort is one of the downside risks. But I think it's kind of like saying, oh, if I buy a Porsche, there's no point because a bird might poo on it … Okay, cool. Let's take 10 steps forward and then one to the side and one backwards by accident. But net, we're probably up 9 steps compared to where we would've been had we still been doing the pre-meeting for the pre-meeting for the meeting to plan the thing."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

---

## 4. Autonomy, no managers, permissionless building, ownership

> "we'd rather have some risk-taking over what gets built in an extremely low consensus environment is our preferred way of building stuff."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "our preferred method of communication is a pull request, as in like, here is the code." … "But we prefer that an engineer is just like, I've built this thing. Um, let's test. Um, as opposed to like, okay, I'm going to spend a month thinking about it. It's like, no, I've just spent a week building it in practice. Let's find out."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "The biggest challenge is, it's not everyone fighting to be the manager, it's people fighting to not be the manager."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "I'm 100% certain our company would not be as successful had I been able to control everything anyway. Because our, some, like I would say our most impactful ever idea was going from one product to 2 products. And that came from an individual developer having the freedom to just build what he wanted."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "there's just this effect in engineering where it's like the first few people working on an idea, could go so much further. Like, it's so ridiculously disproportionately far compared to like the 50th, the 51st person, the 100th person you add to a team that, because of accountability, basically, and freedom and not having to get committees and stuff."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "If you find yourself approving stuff for your team because of your position as their manager, remove yourself from the process." … "Long approval processes that exist for the sake of having someone senior sign off on something in order to kick accountability up the chain? Very un-cracked."
— **Charles Cook**, https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/hiring-and-managing-cracked-engineers — 23 May 2024

> "A manager at PostHog is _not_ responsible for: … 'Approving,' whether that's projects, expenses, days off, or accounts - people should have admin access by default to most things"
> "Management is intentionally spread thin at PostHog. This is a forcing function for making sure that teams and ICs continue to have high levels of autonomy. Bored managers are micromanagers."
— **PostHog handbook**, https://posthog.com/handbook/company/management

> "we are growing through more autonomy and transparency not through process."
— **Tim Glaser** (HN: timgl), recurring line in PostHog's Ask HN: Who Is Hiring posts, e.g. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47980397 — 1 May 2026 (same wording used monthly since at least 2023)

## 5. Hiring engineers / the "cracked" (10x) engineer

> "One of the ways to not get hired at PostHog is to say, I want to manage loads of people, for example. We'll hire people that are just very passionate about building stuff in general."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "the thing we're prioritizing for an engineer in the Superday is how much useful stuff can you build basically in a day?" … "There's remarkable difference between what candidates say and what they do."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "we have lots of ex-YC founders or generally ex-founders or like, I'm a disgruntled CTO of a struggling European startup that just wants to write code, but I have to deal with all these idiots all day long. Like these are the kind of people that will be really successful in A higher autonomy environment."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "the kind of person that would be very happy working at Google is probably going to be really unhappy working at PostHog because they won't have any, they'll just like, there's no boundaries or spoonfeeding or resources available to them"
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "There is no number of years of experience that correlates with crackedness, in either direction." … "You don't need to have worked at a FAANG/MAMAA/shit-hot SV-based company. We welcome cracked engineers who held together failing companies – we like their paranoia."
— **Charles Cook**, https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/hiring-and-managing-cracked-engineers — 23 May 2024

> "The number one thing you can do to motivate cracked people? Find them more cracked people to work with! … Conversely, the number one thing you can do to demotivate them is to make them work with un-cracked people."
— **Charles Cook**, https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/hiring-and-managing-cracked-engineers — 23 May 2024

> "The best applicants are ones who are existing users and who really are interested in the product, versus those who are doing a pull request to stand out. The latter is still a positive, but the former (depending on the quality of PRs!) is the home run!"
— **James Hawkins** (HN: james_impliu), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32863754 — 16 September 2022

> "You mean Product Engineers? We've hired ~80 people in that role in the last year!"
— **Tim Glaser** (HN: timgl), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48225663 — 21 May 2026

## 6. Dogfooding, talking to customers, working in the open

> "in the early days, it was about trust. We, when we were just 2 idiots building something from scratch with nothing. We're like, well, how can we get people on the internet to kind of trust who we are before we were remotely kind of legit? And I thought, well, transparency is kind of the foundation of trust."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "If your internal wiki or Notion or whatever isn't exposed to the world, it's going to be kind of badly written and not that well thought out most of the time … But if you know that you'll get like angry mobs on the internet talking about your like policies around hiring or firing people or whatever it might be, it just means you have to be a bit more rigorous in how you think through stuff."
— **James Hawkins**, https://truthliesandwork.com/189/ — 17 April 2025

> "My advice would be - you have to _both_ talk to people and _at the same time_ create whatever your MVP is to launch as fast as possible. It might be a spreadsheet. It might be you doing stuff manually for them before building the software. Get something into their hands as quickly as possible."
— **James Hawkins** (HN: james_impliu), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=36584166 — 4 July 2023

> "Do the stuff that arrogant senior people would find 'boring'. Write tests. Respond to customer support queries. Go weirdly deep into some piece of analysis. Do something badly that's not your job, so you at least understand it better."
— **Charles Cook**, https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/hiring-and-managing-cracked-engineers — 23 May 2024

> "the magic of working in an open source company is that we can post stuff like this. We're hiring!"
— **Tim Glaser** (HN: timgl), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=26306949 — 1 March 2021

## 7. AI coding agents changing engineering

> "I rewrote PostHog's SQL parser using multiple long-running Claude Code sessions in parallel. The result was 16K lines of \"hand\"-rolled parser code, 5K lines of tooling, a few more K of tests, and a ~70x speed up."
— **Robbie Coomber** (PostHog engineer), "I wrote a 70x faster SQL parser while barely looking at the code", https://posthog.com/blog/sql-parser — 24 June 2026

> "We didn't write this parser by hand because, at least pre-AI-coding, parsers were extremely difficult to maintain. Writing one without AI would have taken months and likely not been worth it, even if it had dramatically improved our p95 response time."
— **Robbie Coomber**, https://posthog.com/blog/sql-parser — 24 June 2026

> "Sadly, it's not as easy as telling Claude to \"write a new parser in Rust, make no mistakes.\" It did, in fact, make a lot of mistakes, kept doubting whether such a rewrite was even possible, and wanted to call it a day after each round of coding. To be honest, I didn't really know if it was possible either."
— **Robbie Coomber**, https://posthog.com/blog/sql-parser — 24 June 2026

> "It's interesting to think about what this means for tools like ANTLR. I suspect an AI-based approach like mine will become the new normal."
— **Robbie Coomber**, https://posthog.com/blog/sql-parser — 24 June 2026

> "one of the interesting parts to me while working on this is that the breakpoint for when it's worth writing your own parser vs accepting ANTLR's slowness has shifted massively. Previously it would have been someone's full-time job to maintain. Now with this approach you can get the best of both worlds."
— **Robbie Coomber** (HN: robbie-c), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48666381 — 24 June 2026

> "It took about 2 days to get a proof of concept, and about a week to get something I could ship to production."
— **Robbie Coomber** (HN: robbie-c), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48664983 — 24 June 2026

> "we don't care how or if you use AI to get a job done, as long as it gets done"
— **PostHog handbook**, https://posthog.com/handbook/company/management

> "we now have a kind of a platform AI team and they have much deeper expertise on how to build things with AI … one of the AI people will move to the, will go to like live in the product analytics team for a sprint, 3 sprints, whatever. And they will pair with one of that team so that the other team is owning the functionality still"
