# TOPIC 2 — Maintainer burnout, workload, invisible labor (2024–2026)

## A. Tidelift — 2024 State of the Open Source Maintainer Report (Nov 2024)

**PDF:** https://www.sonarsource.com/open-source-maintainer-survey-2024.pdf (also mirrored at https://assets-eu-01.kc-usercontent.com/ef593040-b591-0198-9506-ed88b30bc023/d325a56f-05be-4379-bfd1-ee4776fcad41/2024-tidelift-state-of-the-open-source-maintainer-report-.pdf) · landing: https://www.tidelift.com/open-source-maintainer-survey-2024

**Methodology, verbatim:** *"We contacted maintainers through a social campaign in July and August 2024. After screening for quality and completeness, we analyzed the answers from **437 respondents** who maintain at least one open source project."* Third maintainer-specific survey; sixth year of Tidelift open source surveys.

**Pay (n=437):** 60% unpaid — **16%** "unpaid hobbyist and do not want to get paid" (14% in 2023), **44%** "unpaid hobbyist, but would appreciate getting paid" (46% in 2023), **24%** semi-professional (23% in 2023), **12%** professional earning most/all income (13% in 2023), 4% other.
> "Sixty percent of maintainers report they are unpaid hobbyists, and only 12% of maintainers consider themselves professionals who earn most or all of their income from their maintenance work."
> "Full disclosure: it would have been awesome if this headline was different... But the fact is that things haven't changed, and especially in the year of the xz utils hack ... this is a newsworthy—and disappointing—finding to report."

**Solo maintainership:** Paid maintainers — 26% solo, 22% one other, **53% two or more**. Unpaid hobbyists — **61% solo**, 19% one other, 20% two or more. (Professional n=42; semi-pro n=91; unpaid hobbyist n=227.)

**Hours/week:** **82%** of professional maintainers work >20 hrs/wk (81% in 2023). **78%** of unpaid hobbyists work ≤10 hrs/wk (81% in 2023). Semi-professionals: 20% >20 hrs, 51% 11–20 hrs, 29% ≤10 hrs. (n=45 / 96 / 253.)

**Time allocation — the non-code split (n=378 in 2024, n=327 in 2021):**

| Area | 2021 | 2024 |
|---|---|---|
| Day-to-day maintenance work | 53% | **50%** |
| Building new features | 25% | 35% |
| Security work | 4% | **11%** (≈3×) |
| Seeking financial support/sponsors | 2% | 2% |
| Other | 16% | 2% |

Tidelift defines "day-to-day maintenance work" explicitly as *"including writing documentation, reviewing PRs from contributors, general dependency management, reviewing and responding to issues, and removing technical debt"* — i.e. **half of maintainer time is non-feature, largely non-code work.** Paid vs unpaid split: paid spend 13% security / 53% maintenance / 29% features; unpaid 10% / 48% / 39%.

**Quitting (n=350 in 2024, n=265 in 2023):**
> "This year the percentage of maintainers who have either quit or considered quitting their work was **60%**, which is consistent with the 58% in 2023 and 59% in 2021."
Breakdown: **22% "Yes, I have quit"**, **38% "Yes, I have considered quitting"**, 40% no.

**Dislikes (n=338 in 2024; 253 in 2023; 253 in 2021):** not financially compensated enough/at all **50%** (52% in 2023, 49% in 2021); feel underappreciated / work is thankless **48%** (40% in 2021, not asked 2023); adds to my personal stress **43%** (54% in 2023, 45% in 2021); asked to comply with requirements I don't have time for **36%** (38% in 2023); users too demanding **31%** (29%/33%); reviewing code with narrow self-interest; can be lonely **32%** (42% in 2023, 36% in 2021); "what used to be fun now feels like work" **32%**; takes too much of my time **17%** (21% in 2023, 31% in 2021).

**Quotable maintainer voices (verbatim from the report):**
> "You end up doing a lot of stuff simply because it needed to be done, and nobody else was doing it. You feel you're responsible for it, the work just keeps piling up, and in the end, you're so busy you don't even have time to try to find co-maintainers."

> "Users can be so entitled. 'Why haven't you merged/fixed this? This project is dead.' No, I have debts, a full-time job, a young family, my parent just died, and my wife has a serious medical issue. I have already sunk thousands of hours into this project, I don't have time to deal with this right now."

> "The entitlement of the open source community is off the charts."

> "Open source has powered a massive trillion-dollar injection of value into the world, the financial value of which has been reaped by large corporations, which on the whole give very little back to the ecosystem, not even appreciation, respect, or gratitude."

**AI / review burden (Headline #10, n=344):**
- **45%** expect AI coding tools to have a negative impact on their work (23% extremely negative + 22% somewhat negative); 22% somewhat positive; 9% extremely positive; 24% neutral.
- **64%** would be **less willing** to review and accept contributions they knew were AI-produced (37% much less willing + 27% somewhat less willing). Only 9% more willing. 27% unsure.
- On automated vulnerability-remediation PRs: **36%** "not very useful", 10% "not at all useful", 25% "very useful", 8% "extremely useful", 21% not sure.
Maintainer quotes:
> "The increase of spam PRs, comments, and false positives from AI tools and users has been enormous and very frustrating."
> "I don't want to become the gate for reviewing tons of automatically generated pull requests. Sounds like it would further wear me and my co-maintainers down."
> "AI-based coding tools exponentially increase the chance that someone without context of the codebase or the project will build a PR that looks correct but contains breakages that can bring the entire language ecosystem down until a patch fix is released."

**Aging (Headline #12, n=344/259/322):** maintainers under 26 fell from **25% (2021) → 12% (2023) → 10% (2024)**. Maintainers 46–65 roughly doubled since 2021. Report's own reading: *"almost half of maintainers feel underappreciated and like the work is thankless... Almost two-thirds of maintainers have quit or considered quitting their maintenance work."*

**Also:** only **1%** of maintainers report direct income from governments/public entities; **5%** receive income directly from companies; **81%** prefer predictable monthly income over a lump payment; **70%** of respondents are not Tidelift maintainer partners.

## B. Tidelift — 2023 State of the Open Source Maintainer Report (April 2023)

**PDF:** https://www.sonarsource.com/open-source-maintainer-survey-2023.pdf · fielded late 2022, n=326.

- **60% unpaid hobbyists**; 14% don't want pay, 46% would appreciate pay; 23% semi-professional; 13% professional.
- *"our survey found that **77%** of the maintainers who are not paid would prefer to get paid. Only 23% would like to keep open source as an unpaid hobby."* (n=194)
- Hours: 81% of professional maintainers >20 hrs/wk, 93% >10 hrs/wk; **44% of unpaid hobbyists are solo maintainers** — actually: *"The most common answer (by more than 2:1 over the next choice at 44%) was 'I am a solo maintainer'"* across all respondents (n=326); 20% have one co-maintainer, 22% have 3–5, 3% have 6–10, 11% have >10.
- Stress: *"An increasing percentage of respondents (**54%** this year vs. 45% previously) responded that open source maintenance adds to their personal stress."* Loneliness up from 36% → **42%**. "Asked to comply with requirements I don't have time for" — new option, **38%**, 4th place.
- Headline #8 verbatim: *"**Maintainer burnout is real. Almost 60% of maintainers have quit or considered quitting.** Fifty-eight percent of maintainers have either quit (**22%**) or considered quitting (**36%**) their maintenance work on a project."* (n=265)
- **Reasons for quitting/considering:** other priorities **54%**; lost interest **51%**; **burnout 44%**; not paid enough to make it worthwhile **38%** (up from 32%); took too much time 36%; didn't enjoy maintenance work 34%; project completed 29%; overwhelmed by demands from users 27%; conflicts with contributors 16%; compliance requirements 14% (new); employer redeployment 9%.
- **57%** of maintainers who quit or considered quitting said something would have kept them working on the project.

## C. Linux Foundation Research

**Census III of Free and Open Source Software – Application Libraries** (Dec 4, 2024; LF + Harvard Laboratory for Innovation Science). Press release: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/open-source-usage-trends-and-security-challenges-revealed-in-new-study-302321765.html · report: https://www.linuxfoundation.org/research/census-iii
Authors: Frank Nagle (HBS), Kate Powell (LISH), Richie Zitomer (HBS), David A. Wheeler (OpenSSF).
> "Derived from over **12 million observations** of FOSS libraries in production applications at **more than ten thousand companies**"
Key findings include, verbatim: *"**Much of the most widely used FOSS is developed by only a handful of contributors.**"* · *"Individual developer account security is increasingly important."* · *"Legacy software persists in the open source space."* · *"Use of components from Rust package repositories have increased considerably since Census II."*
Tim Mackey (Black Duck), quoted in the release: *"If there are only a handful of contributors to a critical component or if the supplier is effectively one anonymous GitHub user account, the cybersecurity and software hygiene decisions of those individuals could introduce unexpected business risks."*
(Census II, March 2022, was based on ~500,000 observations of FOSS usage in 2020 — https://www.linuxfoundation.org/research/census-ii-of-free-and-open-source-software-application-libraries)

**Maintainer Perspectives on Open Source Software Security** — Stephen Hendrick and Ashwin Ramaswami, The Linux Foundation, foreword by Stephen Augustus (Cisco), December 2023 / published Jan 17, 2024. DOI 10.70828/PVSN3075.
PDF: https://www.linuxfoundation.org/hubfs/LF%20Research/MaintainerSecurityBPs_011724.pdf · page: https://www.linuxfoundation.org/research/maintainer-perspectives-on-security
Sample: 2022 OpenSSF supply chain security survey data, n≈271–283 valid cases.
- Maintainers and core contributors are **36%** of OSS contributors (maintainers 20%, core contributors 16%); occasional 49%, one-time 12%, non-development 3%.
- **69%** of OSS contributors want defined best practices for secure software development; **49%** want employer incentives for OSS contributions.
- **27%** of maintainers are responsible for *defining* OSS security policy; **30%** for *implementing* it.
- *"Reducing developer fatigue through automation is the #2 approach to improve security across the OSS supply chain."* (#1 is "making security tools more intelligent.")
- *"The #1 reason for maintaining OSS projects is the enjoyment of learning."* — 72% "I enjoy learning" (76% for maintainers/core contributors); 59% "since I use OSS I feel I should contribute something back"; 52% creative/challenging work; 46% helping others; **45% of maintainers/core contributors** say their employer allows some paid work hours for OSS (vs 24% for other contributors); only **7–8%** are paid independently of an employer to develop OSS.
- Report page framing: *"There is room for greater automation, better documentation, employer incentives, and defined best practices to better support maintainers and avoid burnout."*

## D. GitHub Octoverse

**Octoverse 2025** (published Oct 28, 2025; updated Feb 28, 2026) — https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/octoverse-a-new-developer-joins-github-every-second-as-ai-leads-typescript-to-1/
- *"Every second, more than one new developer on average joined GitHub—over **36 million** in the past year"*; **180M+** developers total; 630M total repositories, +121M new in 2025.
- Open source: *"**1.12 billion** contributions across public repositories (+13% YoY). **March 2025 marked the largest single month of new open source contributors in GitHub history: 255,000 first-timers.**"* · **518.7M** merged PRs (+29% YoY) · 395M public repos (+19% YoY).
- Monthly averages 2024→2025: issues closed ≈3.4M→**4.25M**; PRs merged 35M→**43.2M**; code pushes 65M→**82.19M**. PRs created +20.4% (39.5M→47.5M); issues created +11.3%. **"Comments on issues/PRs: essentially flat (+0.35%)"** — i.e. contribution volume rose ~20–29% while human discussion did not.
- **Governance gap, verbatim:** *"Governance is not keeping pace with velocity."* — README on ~63% of public repos; **contributor guides on just 5.5%**; **codes of conduct at 2% penetration**. *"At 5.5%, contributor guides remain an ecosystem-wide opportunity as the number of first-time contributors increases."*
- AI: **1.1M+** public repos now use an LLM SDK (+178% YoY); 80% of new developers use Copilot in their first week; *"**Half (50%) of open source projects have at least one maintainer using GitHub Copilot.**"*; *"Nearly 20% of the most popular open source projects among first-time contributors in 2025 were AI-focused."*; six of the top ten projects by contributors are AI-centric, averaging **+150% contributor growth YoY — "triple the OSS median."**
- **Caveat worth flagging:** the widely-quoted lines about "AI slop" pull requests and *"a denial of service attack on human attention"* do **not** appear in GitHub's own Octoverse 2025 post — they come from third-party commentary (e.g. Forbes' Janakiram MSV summary). Don't attribute them to GitHub.

**Octoverse 2024** — https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/octoverse-2024/
- *"In 2024, developers around the world made more than **5.2 billion contributions** to more than **518 million** open source, public, and private projects."* Nearly 1 billion contributions to open source and public repos specifically.
- *"There's a continued increase in first-time contributors to open source projects. **1.4 million new developers globally joined open source** with a majority contributing to commercially backed and generative AI projects. **Notably, we did not see a rise in rejected pull requests.** This could indicate that quality remains high despite the influx of new contributors."*
- *"But we aren't seeing signs that AI has hurt open source with low-quality contributions."* — GitHub's 2024 position, useful as a contrast with maintainer testimony and with 2025–26 developments.
- **59%** surge in contributions to generative AI projects, **98%** increase in number of such projects; 70,000+ new public/OSS genAI projects created in 2024.
- *"More than one million open source maintainers, and verified students and teachers have used GitHub Copilot at no cost"*; 100% YoY increase in that program.

## E. Invisible labor — academic

**Meluso, J., Casari, A., McLaughlin, K., & Trujillo, M. Z. (2024/2025). "Invisible Labor in Open Source Software Ecosystems."** John Meluso (Cornell / Univ. of Vermont), **Amanda Casari (Google LLC / UVM)**, **Katie McLaughlin (Google LLC)**, Milo Z. Trujillo (Northeastern / UVM). arXiv:2401.06889v2, 10 Jan 2025, 31 pages. https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.06889 · https://research.google/pubs/invisible-labor-in-open-source-software-ecosystems-2/
(Note: this is Google OSPO research — Casari/McLaughlin, not Sophia Vargas. Vargas is a Google OSPO analyst and CHAOSS contributor — she is a listed contributor on the CHAOSS Data Use Statement and the Starter Project Health model — but is not an author of this paper.)

Verbatim abstract lines:
> "Invisible labor is work that is either not fully visible or not appropriately compensated. In open source software (OSS) ecosystems, essential tasks that do not involve code (like content moderation) often become invisible to the detriment of individuals and organizations."
> "Our study addresses this challenge, **demonstrating that roughly half of OSS work is invisible.** ... Survey respondents (**n = 142**) reported that their work is more likely to be invisible (**2 in 3 tasks**) than visible, and that **half (50.1%) is uncompensated**."
> "Priming participants with the idea of visibility caused participants to think their work was more visible, and that visibility was less important, than those primed with invisibility."
> "This suggests that **advertising OSS activities as 'open' may lead contributors to overestimate how visible their labor actually is.**"

Numbers from Fig. 1b and the results section: visibility — fully visible **33.3%**, partially visible **36.5%**, non-visible **30.3%** (so 66.7% not fully visible). Compensation — receive credit from All projects 10.9% / Most 29.2% / Some 24.8% / A Few 25.5% / None 9.5%. *"nearly 9 in 10 (89.1%) participants reported that some of their work is not fully visible (and therefore invisible)"* and *"OSS labor is only partially visible (51.9%) and roughly half receives credit (50.1%)."*

Framing quotes:
> "much of the labor performed in support of software development is undocumented, unattributed to individuals, and 'practically invisible' to outsiders and newcomers"
> "Consequently, individuals frequently burn out and stop performing crucial activities on which a growing number of scientists, organizations, and governments rely."
> "Many automated measurement techniques (like GitHub's contribution activity visualizations) only measure code as 'contributions,' thereby conferring lower status to non-coding activities."

**Gerosa, M., Wiese, I., Trinkenreich, B., Link, G., Robles, G., Treude, C., Steinmacher, I., & Sarma, A. (2021). "The Shifting Sands of Motivation: Revisiting What Drives Contributors in Open Source."** ICSE 2021, Madrid. arXiv:2101.10291. https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.10291
Survey of **242 OSS contributors**. Findings: *"Motivations related to social aspects and reputation increased in frequency"*; *"Intrinsic and internalized motivations, such as learning and intellectual stimulation, are still highly relevant"*; contributors shift *"from extrinsic motivations to intrinsic"* over time; experienced developers move toward altruism, newcomers toward *"career, fun, kinship, and learning."* (Note: Georg Link is a CHAOSS co-founder — this is the same research community that authored the metrics.)

**Also cited by CHAOSS's own guides** as the evidentiary base for maintainer-load claims:
- Avelino, G., Constantinou, E., Valente, M. T., & Serebrenik, A. (2019). "On the abandonment and survival of open source projects: An empirical investigation." ESEM 2019. https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.08058 — even popular projects can be permanently abandoned after losing key contributors.
- Eghbal, N. (2016). *Roads and Bridges: The Unseen Labor Behind Our Digital Infrastructure*, Ford Foundation. https://www.fordfoundation.org/work/learning/research-reports/roads-and-bridges-the-unseen-labor-behind-our-digital-infrastructure/
- Eghbal, N. (2020). *Working in Public*, Stripe Press. https://nadia.xyz/oss/
- Raman, N., Cao, M., Tsvetkov, Y., Kästner, C., & Vasilescu, B. (2020). "Stress and Burnout in Open Source: Toward Finding, Understanding, and Mitigating Unhealthy Interactions." ICSE-NIER. https://cmustrudel.github.io/papers/raman20toxicity.pdf
- Casari, A., Ferraioli, J., & Lovato, J. (2023). "Beyond the Repository." *ACM Queue* 21(2), 14–34. https://cacm.acm.org/practice/beyond-the-repository/ — CHAOSS's intro guide instructs readers to *"pause and read this 6-page article now."*

## F. AI-generated PRs and maintainer review burden — curl / Daniel Stenberg

Three posts, in sequence. All quotes verbatim.

**1. "The I in LLM stands for intelligence," Jan 2, 2024** — https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2024/01/02/the-i-in-llm-stands-for-intelligence/
> "Our bug bounty has resulted in over 70,000 USD paid in rewards so far. We have received **415 vulnerability reports**. Out of those, **64** were ultimately confirmed security problems. **77** of the report were informative, meaning they typically were bugs or similar. **Making 66% of the reports neither a security issue nor a normal bug.**"
> "**When reports are made to look better and to appear to have a point, it takes a longer time for us to research and eventually discard it.** Every security report has to have a human spend time to look at it and assess what it means."
> "**The better the crap, the longer time and the more energy we have to spend on the report until we close it.** A crap report does not help the project at all. It instead takes away developer time and energy from something productive."
> "A security report can take away a developer from fixing a really annoying bug. because a security issue is always more important than other bugs. If the report turned out to be crap, we did not improve security and we missed out time on fixing bugs or developing a new feature. Not to mention how it drains you on energy having to deal with rubbish."
> "the mere existence of a few give-away signs that parts of the text were generated by an AI or a similar tool is not an immediate red flag. It can still contain truths and be a valid issue. This is part of the reason why a well-formed crap report is harder and takes longer to discard."

**2. "Death by a thousand slops," July 14, 2025** — https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2025/07/14/death-by-a-thousand-slops/
> "This trend does not seem to slow down. On the contrary, it seems that we have recently not only received more AI slop but also **more human slop**. The latter differs only in the way that we cannot immediately tell that an AI made it, even though we many times still suspect it. The net effect is the same."
> "**The general trend so far in 2025 has been way more AI slop than ever before (about 20% of all submissions)** as we have averaged in about two security report submissions per week. **In early July, about 5% of the submissions in 2025 had turned out to be genuine vulnerabilities.** The valid-rate has decreased significantly compared to previous years."
> "We have run the curl Bug Bounty since 2019 ... 81 of them to be exact, with over 90,000 USD paid in awards."
> "**We need to reduce the amount of sand in the machine.**"
> "The curl security team consists of seven team members. I encourage the others to also chime in to back me up (so that we act right in each case). **Every report thus engages 3-4 persons. Perhaps for 30 minutes, sometimes up to an hour or three. Each.**"
> "My fellows however are not full time on curl. They might only have three hours per week for curl. **Not to mention the emotional toll it takes to deal with these mind-numbing stupidities.** Times eight the last week alone."
> "On HackerOne the users get their reputation lowered when we close reports as not applicable. That is only really a mild 'threat' to experienced HackerOne participants. For new users on the platform that is mostly a pointless exercise as they can just create a new account next week."
The post also publishes a running list of ~21 named slop reports with HackerOne IDs.

**3. "The end of the curl bug-bounty," January 26, 2026** — https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2026/01/26/the-end-of-the-curl-bug-bounty/
> "**There is no longer a curl bug-bounty program. It officially stops on January 31, 2026.**"
> "**87 confirmed vulnerabilities and over 100,000 USD paid** as rewards to researchers."
> "Looking back, I think we can say that the downfall of the bug-bounty program started slowly in the second half of 2024 but accelerated badly in 2025."
> "**Previous years we have had a rate of somewhere north of 15% of the submissions ending up confirmed vulnerabilities. Starting 2025, the confirmed-rate plummeted to below 5%. Not even one in twenty was real.**"
> "**The never-ending slop submissions take a serious mental toll to manage and sometimes also a long time to debunk. Time and energy that is completely wasted while also hampering our will to live.**"
> "I have also started to get the feeling that a lot of the security reporters submit reports with a bad faith attitude. These 'helpers' try too hard to twist whatever they find into something horribly bad and a critical vulnerability, but they rarely actively contribute to actually improve curl."
> "**There are these three bad trends combined that makes us take this step: the mind-numbing AI slop, humans doing worse than ever and the apparent will to poke holes rather than to help.**"
Actions taken, verbatim: *"We no longer offer any monetary rewards for security reports – no matter which severity."* · *"We stop using Hackerone as the recommended channel."* · *"We refer everyone to submit suspected curl security problems on GitHub using their Private vulnerability reporting feature."* · *"**We continue to immediately ban and publicly ridicule everyone who submits AI slop to the project.**"*
Comparative data from HackerOne, verbatim:
> "**Over the past four quarters, curl's inbound report volume has risen sharply, while other bounty-paying open source programs in the cohort, such as Ruby, Node, and Rails, have not seen a meaningful increase and have remained mostly flat or declined slightly.**"
> "We hear about projects having problems with low-quality AI slop submissions on GitHub as well, in the form of issues and pull-requests, but for curl we have not (yet) seen this."

Secondary coverage: BleepingComputer, https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/curl-ending-bug-bounty-program-after-flood-of-ai-slop-reports/ · The New Stack, "cURL's Daniel Stenberg: AI slop is DDoSing open source," https://thenewstack.io/curls-daniel-stenberg-ai-is-ddosing-open-source-and-fixing-its-bugs/

6. **Tidelift is now Sonar-owned** — the report PDFs redirect to sonarsource.com; the 2024 "Maintainer Impact Report" (a separate, marketing-forward document) is at https://www.sonarsource.com/the-2024-tidelift-maintainer-impact-report.pdf and reports paid maintainers are *"8–26 percentage points (or, on average 55%) more"* likely to implement security practices.</result>

## A. How AI-authored PRs are attributed — `contents/handbook/engineering/development-process.md` §"Creating PRs" (https://posthog.com/handbook/engineering/development-process#creating-prs)

> "All PRs should be attributable to a human author as far as possible, even if they were assisted by an agent.
>
> Fully automatically generated PRs might come from an agent like PostHog Desktop or from systems like Dependabot. These PRs are fine, but they should be clearly labelled as such and include a clear description of the changes being made and any relevant context about the generation process. These PRs should in turn never be attributed to a human author, as the changes were not directly or indirectly made by a human.
>

## B. How agent code is reviewed — `contents/handbook/engineering/how-we-review.md` (https://posthog.com/handbook/engineering/how-we-review)

> "PRs can be written by humans or by agents (like PostHog Desktop). See [Creating PRs](/handbook/engineering/development-process#creating-prs) for how we distinguish AI-assisted human-authored PRs from fully automatically generated agent-authored PRs. Either way, the normal rule is that every PR needs a review before merging, and a human always merges. If you need an urgent review, ask in the `#dev-stamp-exchange` Slack channel. For true emergencies where no one else is available, an admin can bypass review requirements.
>
> Who should review depends on who wrote the code:
>
> - **Human-authored PRs** can be reviewed by a team member or by [Stamphog, our AI approval agent](/newsletter/code-review-tips#3-add-a-pr-auto-stamper). Stamphog runs deterministic checks first (size, file ownership, tier) and then does an LLM review for approval eligibility and suggestions. Stamphog is the only AI approval agent whose approval can satisfy the review requirement, and only for eligible human-authored PRs, so a team member can merge.
> - **Agent-authored PRs** always require a human review since we want at least one human in the loop. A team member must review the PR and approve it before merging.
>
> We encourage the use of AI review agents (Codex, Copilot, Greptile, etc.) on PRs. Run them when they're useful, whether before opening a PR, while iterating, or before requesting a human review, and respond to or resolve meaningful comments. Other AI review agent comments and suggestions do not count as approval, but they catch things humans miss and speed up the review process. Avoid adding more agent reviews when the PR already has automated feedback. Three agents arguing with each other is noisy, unless the extra agent has a niche focus like security."

> "## What reviews are for
>
> Automated reviewers are useful for cheap, repetitive checks: obvious bugs, missing tests, typo-level mistakes, suspicious edge cases, and things that look like lint or static analysis. They reduce noise for humans, but they don't replace human judgment.
>
> Human reviewers should focus on things agents are bad at:
>
> - Does this solve the right problem for customers?
> - Is this the right thing to build at all?
> - Does it fit the team's direction and the surrounding product context?
> - Is the UX clear?
> - Is the approach simple, maintainable, secure, and scalable?
>
> Reviews also build shared context and collective ownership. […] The author still owns correctness: reviewers help reduce risk, but approval does not move responsibility away from the person responsible for the PR."

Also verbatim from the same file:
> "**Use AI reviewers** (e.g. Copilot) or your own agent review where useful, and resolve meaningful comments. Iterate until they're only leaving nit-level feedback."

> "If tests were AI-written, do the assertions prove the behavior is correct rather than only passing?"

## C. External AI contributions policy — https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/blob/master/AI_POLICY.md (fetched verbatim, near-complete)

> "# AI contributions policy
>
> PostHog is built with plenty of AI assistance. This policy exists because of a growing volume of low-quality, AI-generated contributions that waste maintainer time.
>
> ## The standard
>
> **You own what you submit.** Understand your code, test it, and be ready to explain why it's correct and how it interacts with the rest of the system (without re-prompting an LLM). This is no different from what we'd expect of any contribution; AI makes it easier to skip the work – please don't skip the work.
>
> **Prove it works.** Before submitting, please verify the change actually works end-to-end — don't rely on 'it compiles' or 'tests pass' alone.
> - **Frontend changes:** include a short demo (screenshot, screen recording, or GIF) of the feature working in the PR description. Ideally you demo more than just the happy path.
> - **Backend changes:** add tests for new behavior, and describe your test strategy in the PR description: what you tested, how you tested it, and what edge cases you considered.
>
> PRs that clearly weren't run or tested will be closed under this policy.
>
> **Disclose AI usage.** Our [PR template](.github/pull_request_template.md) includes an Agent context section — please use it (most agents will pick it up automatically). If an agent co-authored or authored your PR, say so and leave context about the tools and session. This helps reviewers calibrate.
>
> **Prefer PRs over AI-generated issues.** If AI helped you find a bug, fix it and open a pull request — don't paste the AI's output into an issue. Unreviewed, AI-generated bug reports and security disclosures will be closed without response.
>
> **Don't submit unsolicited AI-generated PR reviews.** If you didn't write the code and aren't a maintainer, don't point an LLM at someone else's PR and leave its output as a review comment. This is generally never helpful.
>
> ## What happens when contributions don't meet this bar
> - **First time:** We'll close the PR/issue with a link to this policy and a brief explanation.
> - **Two or more closures:** We'll block the account.
>
> ## Why we're not anti-AI
> We think the best contributions in 2026 often involve AI. A contributor who uses an LLM to help them understand unfamiliar code, draft a first pass, or catch edge cases they'd miss is probably _more_ productive than someone doing everything by hand. The key difference is that they're driving the AI, not the other way around."

## D. Engineering impact / metrics in an AI world — `contents/handbook/company/management.md` §"Weave" (https://posthog.com/handbook/company/management)

> "### Weave
>
> We use a tool called [Weave](https://workweave.dev/) to collect stats for engineers. Engineers can log in to see their numbers and those of other engineers.
>
> We understand that all the work an engineer does can't be properly represented in a tool that just looks at PR output. Data in Weave is _not_ the decision-maker for whether someone is succeeding in their role at PostHog. It can be, however, a part of the conversation.
>
> We use Weave to:
> - Look for outliers in the company in terms of output (both high and low - sometimes unexpected people are rising to the top!)
> - Watch for issues with overall team productivity to identify possible blockers
> - Start conversations with team leads
>
> We don't use Weave to:
> - Make a decision to let someone go - if and when this happens, it only follows detailed discussion with and recommendation from the team lead
> - Monitor your PRs - our management layer is stretched way too thin to micromanage this
> - **Creep on your use of AI - we don't care how or if you use AI to get a job done, as long as it gets done**
> - Make a call on how valuable someone is - some people with low PR output are very valuable to the company, and we're 100% aware that things like heavy support load can impact output
>
> We have compared statistics in Weave against other (imperfect!) metrics that can be used to gauge productivity, such as number of commits, number of PRs, total github activity, etc, and see similar patterns amongst them."

## I. The "self-driving product" vision — `contents/handbook/engineering/ai/ai-platform.md`

> "## Vision: Self driving product
>
> The overarching goal of PostHog's AI direction is **self driving product**. A self-driving product can prompt itself. It understands your codebase, your data, and your users. It proposes and ships work on its own, inside of guardrails you set.
>
> The self in self-driving isn't autonomy from the engineer. It's autonomy from user instruction as the starting point.
>
> Here's how the loop works:
> 1. **Signals**: PostHog collects signals from all products and external sources — error patterns, frustration in session recordings, experiment results, survey responses, insight thresholds, support tickets, Slack threads, and more. […]
> 2. **Enrichment**: PostHog processes and enriches these signals, deduplicating across data sources and adding context. A vague signal like 'users seem frustrated during checkout' becomes a concrete, contextualized finding.
> 3. **Plans**: The enriched signals are transformed into structured plans — similar to how Claude Code works, but driven by data rather than human prompts. […]
> 4. **Execution**: A sandboxed coding agent takes these plans and acts on them. Today, we're focused on automatically creating pull requests. The agent also handles instrumentation automatically — adding tracking events, feature flags, and experiments as part of the code it ships. Better instrumentation produces better signals, making the entire loop smarter over time. […]
> 5. **Review**: Product engineers review, iterate on, and merge (or decline) the proposed changes.
> 6. **Feedback**: Once a change ships, a new signal is created so the system can evaluate what happened after the PR was merged. Did the metric improve? Did new errors appear? This feeds back into step 1.
> 7. **Loop**: The cycle continues until the agent finds an exit condition — low actionability, non-important signals, noisy signals, de-prioritized work, etc."

<result># Research Synthesis: Criticism of "Engineering Intelligence" Vendors That Score Individual Developers

**Method note:** WebSearch budget hit its cap mid-research, so later gaps were filled by direct fetches and the Hacker News Algolia API (which lets me verify quotes against the actual comment records rather than trusting SEO aggregators). Every HN quote below is **verified against the Algolia API** with its permalink. I flag secondary/unverified material explicitly at the end — several highly-ranked pages on this topic (codepulsehq.com, pandev-metrics.com, agileanalytics.cloud) are competitor-authored SEO content that paraphrases or fabricates quotes.

---

## 1. GitPrime → Pluralsight Flow: the canonical cautionary tale

### Corporate timeline (verified)
| Date | Event | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 2015 | GitPrime founded (YC W16); co-founder/CEO Travis Kimmel. First public blog posts Sept 2015 ("Using GitPrime: What Is Churn?") | https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=10226733 |
| **May 1, 2019** | Pluralsight announces acquisition of GitPrime for **$170M all cash** | https://techcrunch.com/2019/05/01/pluralsight-will-acquire-gitprime-for-170m/ · HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19802067 (134 pts) |
| May 2019 | Pluralsight Q1 earnings call: "$170 million to be paid in cash. This amount represents a multiple of approximately **5 times to 6 times expected 2020 billings**." CEO added GitPrime "only have a **few hundred customers**." → implies ~$28–34M projected 2020 revenue | HN comment quoting the call: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19814484 |
| ~2020 | Rebranded **Pluralsight Flow** | — |
| Dec 14, 2020 | Vista Equity Partners agrees to take Pluralsight private for **$3.5B** | https://techcrunch.com/2020/12/14/vista-acquires-it-education-platform-pluralsight-for-3-5b/ |
| **May 31, 2024** | Vista **writes Pluralsight's equity to zero**; hands company to creditors | https://www.axios.com/2024/05/31/vista-equity-pluralsight · HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40536960 (189 pts) |
| **February 2025** | **Appfire acquires Flow** from Pluralsight | secondary: https://agileanalytics.cloud/blog/pluralsight-flow-end-of-life-and-alternatives |
| **June 30, 2026** | **Renewals closed.** Appfire stopped offering renewals extending past this date (60-day grace for July–Aug 2026 renewals) | secondary, same |
| **December 31, 2027** | **End of life.** Per Appfire: "On December 31, 2027, Appfire will retire Flow… the app will no longer be available for purchase or use." | appfire.com/flow (behind a Vercel bot wall — I could not fetch it directly; quoted via https://codepulsehq.com/alternative/pluralsight-flow and corroborated by https://agileanalytics.cloud/blog/pluralsight-flow-end-of-life-and-alternatives) |

So: **~$170M acquisition → three owners in six years → equity written to zero → retirement announced.** Note the product is *not* dead yet — it limps to Dec 2027 — so "sunset/deprecated" is accurate but "already shut down" is not.

Migration detail worth using: **historical data does not migrate**, and Flow's proprietary metrics — "Coding Days" and "Impact" — have no equivalent anywhere else, so switching creates "a visible break in the trend line." (agileanalytics.cloud, secondary.)

### What it actually measured
From GitClear's side-by-side comparison of GitClear / Pluralsight Flow / Code Climate Velocity / Pinpoint (updated Feb 8, 2021, https://www.gitclear.com/pluralsight_gitclear_pinpoint_code_climate_code_development_kpi_metric_alternatives), all four drew on the same three sources:

1. **Lines of code** → "Impact/Diff Delta," "Code Churn," "Efficiency"
2. **Issues & PRs** → "Cycle time," "Issue Throughput," "Lead Time"
3. **Commits** → "Active Days," "Time to Open," "Big/Risky" work

GitClear's own verdict on the third: commits are "**a dicey data source**" with "**no intrinsic signal**," and "**commits are the most trivially 'gameable' of the three data sources**," creating team friction when used for individual measurement. It also calls "Issues resolved" "**one of the four worst developer metrics**."

Verified user description of the metric design, from a 2018 trial (HN, nwhatt, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19817441):
> "There were some simple metrics like **'does a developer commit code every business day'** and 'how long do your PRs sit waiting for review'. Other more complex things they produced from the git log were statistics about **churn (how often you touch the same code), and new code vs. refactoring vs. bug fixing**."

And on churn's definition (HN, kerbs, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19929459):
> "They defined churn as '**modifying a line that had been previously modified in the last month**'… It would chart if an engineer made a large number of 'churn' diffs vs new code vs 'legacy/refactoring'."

Flow still ships **individual contributor views via "Developer360" profiles** — a fact Jellyfish's own competitive page cites as a Flow differentiator (https://jellyfish.co/blog/waydev-alternatives/). This is the load-bearing point: the individual dashboard was never removed; it was a selling feature to the end.

### The criticism — verified primary quotes

**The stack-ranking use case.** This is the single most-cited harm, and it recurs across independent commenters over five years.

> "Good ole Gitprime! The source of so many bad memories. I used to be on a 4 person team and **Gitprime was used to stack rank us for every quarterly 'performance' review. Woe to the one who ended up ranked at the bottom**…"
> — BruiseLee, HN, 2020-11-24, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=25200638

> "I used to work for a company that started using Gitprime to measure developer productivity. **Gitprime would show a nice dashboard with stack ranked employees based on their git commits.** Besides the obvious effect that it had on cooperation (**you don't want to help another developer lest they go before you in the stack rank**) it had also funny effect on the code we wrote. For example, **replacing old code with new code was penalized as 'code churn', so we had to write something like `if (false) { // old code } // new code`**. In Golang projects we avoided pushing the vendors directory in one commit. Instead we had to **strategically commit it piece by piece to satisfy 'frequent small commits'** metric that apparently is a signature of good developers."
> — InfamousRece, HN, 2024-11-04, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42040887

That `if (false) { }` anecdote is the best single artifact in this entire body of discourse: a metric that literally caused engineers to leave dead code in the repository.

> "In my case it was gitprime. This is a software to **stack rank based on git commits**. Since good developers supposedly make lots of small commits, if someone makes too few, they are bad. **Also bug fixes are penalized as 'code churn'.**"
> — benttoothpaste, HN, 2021-10-01 (on a thread titled *"Senior developers are leading the great resignation movement"*), https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=28717211

**The perverse-incentive mechanism, stated cleanly:**

> "I used to work at a company which used GitPrime, a product which tries to use git statistics to create graphs and productivity rankings for management, but of course **it lacks any context**. **The easiest way to shoot up the ranking was to avoid any work where you'd not be instantly coding. Never fix a bug where you need to spend time tracking down the issue, never take on the more complicated pieces of work, never use your time to help out junior team members.** Instead focus on simple work and trivial refactoring… the old quote applies: '**when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure**.'"
> — bjohnson225, HN, 2020-11-24, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=25199703
> *(This is the verbatim source that competitor SEO sites paraphrase and mis-quote. Use this original.)*

**The most-quoted line, and the "top coder" story:**

> "**Not a fan of git prime. It's built for micro managers, measures mostly meaningless metrics.** Encourages frequent small commits with low 'churn'. **Trivial to game if you write a script to split your commits and artificially remove 'churn'** by making sure you don't touch your changes more than once. Also penalizes you for high 'impact' commits. Adding a bunch of docs, renaming packages, or even running auto format penalizes you in metrics. It's completely blind to the language. **Doesn't understand the code one bit.** Doesn't tell you anything about code quality or if your 'rockstar' only writes so much code because he copy pasted everything. **Not kidding, almost all the code our 'top coder', per git prime, wrote had to be redone after he got canned. He was copy pasting trash everywhere.**"
> — nullwasamistake, HN, 2019-05-04, on the acquisition thread, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19824747

**Three companies, two immediate misuses — the "it depends how you use it" defense empirically fails:**

> "I've had **three jobs where Pluralsight Flow was introduced. At two of them, the managers immediately started using the metrics for feedback, performance reviews, employment decisions.** At the third, the developers saw this coming a mile away and refused to engage with or evaluate the tool. Unfortunately, **the absurd pricing of these tools means that people who approve them have to get some sort of ROI**. Since they don't have a good way to measure productivity/output/knowledge silos, they instead turn to '**Well Jose had less PRs this week…**'"
> — healsdata, HN, 2024-11-12, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42117191

That last point is an underrated structural argument: Flow started "around $10k/year" (kerbs, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19814900), which forces the buyer to justify spend, which drives them toward the most legible output — per-person counts.

**The honest-defender position** (worth including for balance — a former EM):
> "**Git stats have been used against me on performance reviews** / That sounds awful… I've been an engineering manager, for a time, and I used Gitprime to track stats. **It was never used for performance reviews or in making promotion decisions.** What it was used for was to manage upwards and demonstrate to the upper management how decisions affect the team… I don't see metrics as 'surveillance,' **unless they're used that way**."
> — agentultra, HN, 2020-11-24, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=25202901

**On measured uselessness:**
> "A previous company was using it and I think it was **largely useless**. The manager knew it and was quite vocal about it, **but we still went through the tool in our 1-2-1s**."
> — rocgf, HN, 2019-05-03, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19816851

**On the churn metric penalizing longevity:**
> "I noticed this on gitprime btw. **My code churn rate was waaaay below my peers.** So basically if I merged a line of code to main, it tended to not need updating for years."
> — maerF0x0, HN, 2023-01-28, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=34561130

**On post-acquisition neglect:**
> "PS acquired git prime and rebranded it as Flow, and then **basically just kinda ignored it** tbh… The problem imo is that while that kind of info is certainly interesting, in most cases **it's not really that useful or actionable in practice**."
> — rawdeg, HN, 2024-06-03, on the Vista write-off thread, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40559362

**Practitioner critique with a named author.** DX's article on activity metrics cites **Bryan Finster** (founder of Walmart's DevOps Dojo) on a GitPrime deployment. Documented harms: teams cherry-picked the easiest tasks; code-review participation *declined* because peer feedback didn't move individual numbers; staff engineers abandoned technical direction and mentoring to close issues; and **one team inflated code-review comment counts to hit "GitPrime's recommended minimums,"** adding noise with zero customer value. Finster's verdict: "**Under no circumstances should this be used.**" And: "'What gets measured gets managed' isn't a recommendation, it's a warning."
https://getdx.com/blog/pitfalls-of-developer-activity-metrics/

**GitPrime's own marketing.** GitPrime published a help-center page titled roughly "Can't you just game the metrics?" (cited by HN user jeanlaf, 2018-11-27, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=18539572, on a thread literally titled *"Don't measure developers, measure projects"*). The original URL `help.gitprime.com/general/cant-you-just-game-the-met…` is **now dead** (the intercom.help/gitprime help center returns 404), and archive.org was fully offline during this research, so I could not retrieve the original text. Worth a retry when the Wayback Machine is back — it's the strongest single piece of evidence that the vendor knew about and pre-rebutted the gaming objection.

### On Kent Beck and GitPrime specifically
**I could not find any Kent Beck writing about GitPrime by name.** The "Kent Beck on developer metrics" corpus that exists is his **August 2023 response to McKinsey**, co-published with Gergely Orosz — that's the real citable artifact, and it is devastating but not vendor-specific:

- "**The report is so absurd and naive that it makes no sense to critique it in detail.**" — Kent Beck
- "The thinking that's evident in the article is **absurdly naive and ignores the dynamics of high-performing software engineering teams**."
- "We believe that introducing such a framework is **wrong-headed and certain to backfire**."
- On effort/output metrics: "**the only folks who care about these metrics are the people collecting them. Customers don't care. Executives don't care. Investors don't care.**"
- "**The act of measurement changes how developers work**, as they try to 'game' the system."
- On why he bothered: "**What they published damages people I care about**" — and this kind of surveillance "makes geeks feel less safe."
- On his Facebook experience with a metrics/survey regime: "Things started getting unhinged. Directors put pressure on managers for better scores." … "Give me a 5 & I'll make sure you get an 'exceeds expectations'." … "**we know even less about how things are going. But they are definitely going worse because people are now gaming the system.**"
- The general law: "**The earlier in the cycle you measure, the easier it is to measure. And also the more likely that you introduce unintended consequences.**"

Sources: https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity (Aug 29, 2023) · https://newsletter.kentbeck.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity · Beck's LinkedIn thread drew 309 comments: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kentbeck_mckinsey-claims-its-possible-to-measure-activity-7099764438496407552-v8P2 · Dan North joined the reaction panel: https://mozaicworks.com/blog/reactions-to-mckinseys-dev-productivity-metrics-kent-beck-gergely-orosz-and-dan-north

**I also found no Jason Cohen or Dan North writing on GitPrime specifically.** Dan North appears only in the McKinsey reaction panel above. If you need a named-authority attack on GitPrime itself, the strongest available are Bryan Finster (via DX) and GitClear's Bill Harding (via the comparison page) — not Beck.

## 2. Code Climate Velocity

- **CEO Bryan Helmkamp posted a public defense of the category on HN** (2020-05-06, on the GitHub Insights thread), which is a useful primary source for how vendors framed this: "CEO of Code Climate here. We have a product Velocity… which offers what we call **Engineering Intelligence**… engineers inherently want to be productive, and are happiest when they can work friction-free. Unfortunately, it can be quite difficult to get visibility into roadblocks that slow down developers (e.g. overly nitpicky code review, late changing product requirements, slow/flaky CI), **especially for managers who are one or two levels removed from programming**."
  https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23095725
- **Metrics:** same three data sources as Flow — LOC-derived Impact/Churn/Efficiency, issue/PR cycle time and throughput, commit-derived Active Days (GitClear comparison, Feb 2021).
- **Sunset — be careful here, the popular claim is half wrong.** What was actually shut down was the **free tier, "Velocity for Teams"**: announced week of **12/18/2023**, access retained until **March 18, 2024**, when "accounts were deactivated, integrations disconnected, and data deleted." Paid subscriptions were unaffected. Doc: `https://docs.velocity.codeclimate.com/en/articles/8719212-ending-support-for-velocity-for-teams` (that hostname no longer resolves — itself a signal).
- Separately, **Code Climate Quality was spun out as a new company, Qlty Software**, with Code Climate refocusing entirely on enterprise Velocity as an "SEI" product.
- Gartner still lists it: https://www.gartner.com/reviews/product/code-climate-velocity

**Net:** Code Climate Velocity's *free/SMB* product was killed in March 2024 and its sibling product was spun out; the enterprise SEI product continued. Don't say "Code Climate Velocity shut down" without that qualifier.

---

## 3. Vendor-by-vendor: who scores individuals

### Swarmia — the loudest anti-individual-metrics stance in the category
Their Git-analytics positioning page (https://www.swarmia.com/git-analytics/) is a direct broadside:

> "**Just because something is easy to measure doesn't mean it should be tracked.** We've **intentionally left out** traditional Git analytics metrics like the following: **Lines of code (LOC), Code churn and rework, Developer stack ranking.**"
> "**These metrics don't help teams improve—they can lead to developers gaming the system and misguided managerial decisions.**"
> "**In Swarmia, you won't see leaderboards ranking developers or teams from best to worst.**"
> "We know that **the best teams focus on optimizing for the whole, not the individual**."

Their developer-overview post (Hugo Kiiski, Software Engineer, **Mar 15, 2023**, https://www.swarmia.com/blog/bringing-visibility-into-a-developers-work/) states the three product constraints explicitly — Swarmia will **not** "allow comparing individuals side by side," **not** "expose the code metrics of an individual, like lines of code written or their PR throughput," and **not** "limit the access to managers only" (i.e. the developer sees their own view). Rationale: "**These metrics are too situational to draw conclusions from, and do more harm than good when evaluating an individual.**"

Founder/CEO **Otto Hilska**, "Don't stack rank your developers," **Sep 26, 2025** (https://www.swarmia.com/blog/dont-stack-rank-your-developers/):
> "**Stack ranking doesn't deliver what it promises. Instead of objectivity, you get gaming.**"
> "**Knowledge becomes currency. Developers stop documenting their work, and they avoid doing things like pair programming.**"
> "**The developers you most want to keep are the first to leave.**"
> "**Some vendors in this space will still try to sell you a single number or normalized 'productivity score' — which is often just lines of code with a few extra steps.**"

**Rebecca Murphey** (then Field CTO, Swarmia), **Jul 23, 2025** (https://www.swarmia.com/blog/developer-productivity-metrics-missing-the-point/):
> "counting lines of code, tracking commits per day, measuring story points per sprint. **These metrics don't only fail to capture what matters, but actively make things worse.**"
> Developers hear "developer productivity" and "**imagine being reduced to a number**."

Also useful: **Ari-Pekka Koponen**, "Busting the 10x software engineer myth," Sep 21, 2021 (https://www.swarmia.com/blog/busting-the-10x-software-engineer-myth/): "**while programmers are better and/or faster than others, the importance and scale has been greatly exaggerated**," and "**The real key to success is to improve the average performance of everyone in the company.**"

Swarmia's docs even extend the rule to their AI features: "**Swarmia AI doesn't measure individual productivity, performance, or competence.**" (https://help.swarmia.com/features/swarmia-ai)

### Waydev — historically the individual-dashboard vendor, now publicly repositioning
This is the most interesting finding of the vendor section. Waydev was named alongside GitPrime as the archetype of roll-up individual scoring (see GitSense founder quote in §4, and the 2020 Ask HN which named exactly two tools: "**Gitprime (now owned by Pluralsight?) and waydev.co**" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23208139).

Its product still has a **"For Contributors"** section — "**Keep track of your own performance**" — and a **"Contributor Insights"** capability (https://waydev.co/measure-developer-productivity/), i.e. individual-level analytics remain in the product.

But its recent content marketing now argues *against* individual reporting, almost in Swarmia's language (https://waydev.co/key-metrics-to-include-on-a-board-level-engineering-dashboard/):
> "**Board dashboards should track teams, products, and value streams rather than individual developers. Individual activity counts can distort behavior and miss work such as planning, review, incident response, or mentoring.**"
> "**Use team or product trends, not individual rankings.** … **Individual activity counts invite the wrong behavior and rarely explain business performance.**"
> "**Don't use metrics to micromanage. They're tools for support, not surveillance.**" (https://waydev.co/measure-developer-productivity/)

**The gap between "we ship Contributor Insights" and "don't rank individuals" is the story here** — the guardrail is documentation, not product architecture. Swarmia's is product architecture.

### Jellyfish
Positions as team/business-alignment ("allocation model," "scenario planning," "capacity forecasting"). Secondary summary of its stance: "**Jellyfish is built to elevate team performance, not micromanage individuals**," providing "visibility into individual trends for better 1:1 coaching" — i.e. individual data exists but is framed as coaching input. I could not retrieve a first-party Jellyfish page stating this verbatim (their `/blog/developer-productivity-metrics/`, `/library/…`, and sitemap.xml all 404'd). **Treat the Jellyfish stance as not first-party-verified.** Its competitive page does confirm the Flow feature name: https://jellyfish.co/blog/waydev-alternatives/

### LinearB
First-party, explicit, and it names names (https://linearb.io/blog/developer-productivity-metrics):
> "Some companies and leaders focus on **output metrics like lines of code to stack rank devs**, rather than gaining visibility into the process–*cough cough* **Elon Musk**. This approach is great…**for killing productivity, diminishing motivation, and creating a bad habit of gaming outputs** (often at the cost of code quality)."

LinearB advocates team-level efficiency/effectiveness/experience metrics and "coaching dashboards" that provide context for 1:1s — so, like Jellyfish, individual data exists but is positioned as coaching, not ranking.

### Faros AI
No individual-scoring product stance found; its writing consistently frames the failure mode as *system-level*. CEO **Vitaly Gordon**, "McKinsey is talking about developer productivity and that's a good thing" (Aug 24, 2023; updated Aug 14, 2024, https://www.faros.ai/blog/mckinsey-is-talking-about-developer-productivity-and-thats-a-good-thing): advocates "crossing productivity metrics with HR information about role and tenure" to avoid misreading, and warns "**certain outer-loop activities can be vital to ensuring high-quality, secure, and compliant code**."

**Thierry Donneau-Golencer**, Faros AI, **Jan 5, 2026** — the single best 2026-dated framing of the AI-era version of this problem (https://www.faros.ai/blog/lines-of-code-metric-ai-vanity-outcome):
> "**Lines of code was already a discredited productivity metric.**"
> "**The best developers often ship features by removing code, not adding it.**"
> Their finding: "developers on teams with high AI adoption were completing **21% more tasks and merging 98% more pull requests**, but organizations were seeing **no measurable improvement in delivery outcomes**."
> "**Individual velocity was real. System-level impact was not.**"

That last pair of sentences is the sharpest 2026 formulation of the whole critique: individual metrics can rise while the system delivers nothing more.

### Uplevel
Uplevel's public writing is team/system-framed ("engineering effectiveness," WAVE framework), and its blog does **not** state an explicit individual-vs-team position (https://uplevelteam.com/blog). Historically Uplevel has drawn surveillance criticism for "Always On"/deep-work-hours style metrics — its own Copilot study used "**'Always On' working hours**" as a measured variable (below), which is a working-hours metric, not an output metric.

## 4. General critiques of individual developer metrics (academic + practitioner)

### Goodhart's Law / Campbell's Law — the recurring frame
The HN discourse converges on it independently and repeatedly:
- "**when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure**" — bjohnson225, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=25199703
- "'**What gets measured gets managed**' … These numbers are handy but they absolutely do not tell the whole story and it's dangerous to think they do. You can often find yourself optimizing the wrong area and in large organizations even **marginalizing your best performers because they don't fit the mold**." — robalfonso, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19817514
- Bryan Finster's inversion: "'**What gets measured gets managed' isn't a recommendation, it's a warning.**" (https://getdx.com/blog/pitfalls-of-developer-activity-metrics/)
- The **Cobra effect** was cited directly on the 2020 Ask HN: "If you have tools that use git to pull metrics to see who your 'best' developers are, **don't be surprised if developers create or use tools to optimize their changes for the metrics rather than add value to the codebase**." — thesuperbigfrog, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23208817

### The Bill Gates line
> "**Measuring programming progress by lines of code is like measuring aircraft building progress by weight.**"

Widely attributed to Bill Gates; note that even Faros AI hedges it as "**reportedly**" from Gates (https://www.faros.ai/blog/lines-of-code-metric-ai-vanity-outcome). Treat the attribution as apocryphal-but-canonical. The empirical companion piece HN reaches for is Bill Atkinson's **"-2000 lines of code"** Apple anecdote (https://www.folklore.org/Negative_2000_Lines_Of_Code.html), invoked here:
> "They aren't top of the leaderboard in git commits, because they actually read the RFCs or dependency source code while working. They sure as hell don't always write the most LOC in a week — **I want the '-2000 lines of code' guy, not the one who's best at gaming whatever metrics you use.**" — bigiain, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42039141

### The research base — DX's literature review (best single academic-adjacent citation)
Abi Noda, DX, "Measuring developer activity: what the research says," last updated **Nov 26, 2025** (https://getdx.com/blog/measuring-developer-activity/) collects:
- **Collin Green & Ciera Jaspan (Google):** "**lines of code per minute will not tell you which software developers are the best**."
- **Ciera Jaspan:** developers also do "**code review, system design, releases, mentoring**" — invisible to activity metrics.
- **Dr. Margaret-Anne Storey** (SPACE co-author): warns against focusing on "**pull requests, which we do not recommend**."
- **Dr. Nicole Forsgren:** "**Rewarding developers for lines of code leads to bloated software.**" And metrics "**should never be used in isolation**."
- **Jaspan & Sadowski (Google):** metrics create gaming behavior; developers fear "**misinterpretation by non-technical managers**." Google's research finds individual tracking "**can create a morale issue**" and "**bring down overall productivity**."
- On the stated business case: managers "**frequently already know who low performers are**" — i.e. the tool solves a problem that wasn't the bottleneck.

### SPACE (Forsgren, Storey, Maddila, Zimmermann, Butler, Houck — ACM Queue, 2021)
The framework's own guidance is that it exists to **understand and improve the system, not to score individual developers**; it explicitly warns against activity as a standalone proxy for productivity and against any single metric or dimension. (Paper: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/the-space-of-developer-productivity-theres-more-to-it-than-you-think/ — note queue.acm.org returned 403 to automated fetch.) Swarmia's SPACE guide: https://www.swarmia.com/blog/space-framework/

### The AI-era study you asked about — Uplevel on GitHub Copilot (Sept 2024)
Report: *"Can Generative AI Improve Developer Productivity?"* — https://resources.uplevelteam.com/gen-ai-for-coding
- **Sample: ~800 developers** (351 in the Copilot test group), comparing a ~3-month baseline in early 2023 to a ~3-month follow-up in 2024.
- Metrics: **cycle time, PR throughput, bug rate, "Always On" working hours**.
- **Headline finding: "The group using Copilot introduced 41% more bugs, suggesting Copilot might affect code quality, given it didn't affect PR throughput."** No significant change in efficiency metrics.
- Burnout: non-Copilot developers cut extended working hours **28%**; Copilot users only **17%**.
- Coverage: https://visualstudiomagazine.com/articles/2024/09/17/another-report-weighs-in-on-github-copilot-dev-productivity.aspx · https://www.cio.com/article/3540579/devs-gaining-little-if-anything-from-ai-coding-assistants.html
- **Methodological caveat you should carry:** the study measured whether developers had **access** to Copilot, not actual usage. Critic Jason St-Cyr (https://jasonstcyr.com/2024/10/09/does-github-copilot-actually-raise-bugs-in-code-by-41/) notes the published report contains minimal underlying data and questions whether it is "a genuine issue or merely marketing for Uplevel's competing products." GitHub's own counter-research (Nov 2024) claims quality *gains*: https://visualstudiomagazine.com/articles/2024/11/22/article_0github-copilot-research-claims-code-quality-gains-in-addition-to-productivity.aspx
- The irony worth naming: **an engineering-intelligence vendor used aggregate engineering metrics to debunk a productivity claim** — which is the defensible use of the exact same data that becomes toxic at the individual level.

### The category's own honest critic (a competing founder, so read with bias, but substantively right)
**sdesol** (founder, GitSense), HN 2021-04-29 (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=26982204):
> "**GitPrime (now Pluralsight Flow), GitHub Insights (formerly Gitalytics), Waydev and others have been very effective at giving the impression that you can easily roll-up metrics to quantify developer productivity.** You will be surprised by how many times **people want a simple score or a simple graph to summarize how productive a developer is**."

Earlier, same author, 2020-07-10 (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23793532):
> "Unfortunately **what we have now, in my opinion, borders on snake oil**."

### The marketing/incentive critique — who the product is sold to

### What it actually measured
From GitClear's side-by-side comparison of GitClear / Pluralsight Flow / Code Climate Velocity / Pinpoint (updated Feb 8, 2021, https://www.gitclear.com/pluralsight_gitclear_pinpoint_code_climate_code_development_kpi_metric_alternatives), all four drew on the same three sources:

1. **Lines of code** → "Impact/Diff Delta," "Code Churn," "Efficiency"
2. **Issues & PRs** → "Cycle time," "Issue Throughput," "Lead Time"
3. **Commits** → "Active Days," "Time to Open," "Big/Risky" work

GitClear's own verdict on the third: commits are "**a dicey data source**" with "**no intrinsic signal**," and "**commits are the most trivially 'gameable' of the three data sources**," creating team friction when used for individual measurement. It also calls "Issues resolved" "**one of the four worst developer metrics**."

Verified user description of the metric design, from a 2018 trial (HN, nwhatt, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19817441):
> "There were some simple metrics like **'does a developer commit code every business day'** and 'how long do your PRs sit waiting for review'. Other more complex things they produced from the git log were statistics about **churn (how often you touch the same code), and new code vs. refactoring vs. bug fixing**."

And on churn's definition (HN, kerbs, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19929459):
> "They defined churn as '**modifying a line that had been previously modified in the last month**'… It would chart if an engineer made a large number of 'churn' diffs vs new code vs 'legacy/refactoring'."

Flow still ships **individual contributor views via "Developer360" profiles** — a fact Jellyfish's own competitive page cites as a Flow differentiator (https://jellyfish.co/blog/waydev-alternatives/). This is the load-bearing point: the individual dashboard was never removed; it was a selling feature to the end.

> "I used to work for a company that started using Gitprime to measure developer productivity. **Gitprime would show a nice dashboard with stack ranked employees based on their git commits.** Besides the obvious effect that it had on cooperation (**you don't want to help another developer lest they go before you in the stack rank**) it had also funny effect on the code we wrote. For example, **replacing old code with new code was penalized as 'code churn', so we had to write something like `if (false) { // old code } // new code`**. # Impact Model — full specification

## 0. Attribution (applied before anything else)

```
DRI(pr) = pr.assignees[0]  ??  pr.author
```

PostHog's own PR template: *"If a human directed this work, assign them as the PR assignee (the DRI)."* Bot-authored PRs carry the real engineer as assignee.

- Drop the PR from person-scoring if `DRI` resolves to a bot (fully autonomous, unassigned) → these are counted in an org-level stat instead, never credited to a person.
- **Eligibility floor:** ≥5 merged PRs as DRI **or** ≥10 human reviews given. Prevents tiny-denominator noise.

## 1. Per-PR weight — every dimension uses this, so nothing is ever a raw count

```
W(pr) = C(scope) × A(autonomy) × G(substance)
```

| Factor | Definition | Range |
|---|---|---|
| **C — centrality** (blast radius) | `scope` parsed from `type(scope):` title. `centrality(s)` = # distinct human DRIs who shipped into `s` in 90d. Percentile-mapped: `C = 0.6 + 1.4 × pct(centrality(s))` | 0.6 – 2.0 |
| **A — autonomy** | `assisted` / `none` = 1.0 · `autonomous` (agent-driven, human triaged) = 0.5 | 0.5 – 1.0 |
| **G — substance gate** | 0.4 if `(additions+deletions) < 10 AND changedFiles ≤ 1`, else 1.0 | 0.4 – 1.0 |

**Blast radius is a multiplier, not a slider** — that's deliberate. It means "Feature Delivery" can never degrade into a PR count: a `feat` in a directory 40 engineers depend on outweighs three in a corner nobody touches. One less slider, and it makes the other sliders honest.

## 2. The six dimensions (one slider stack, in this order)

**① Feature Delivery** — *new capability shipped, weighted by how central the code is*
```
FD(e) = Σ W(pr)   for merged PRs where DRI=e and type = feat
```

**② Reliability** — *fixes delivered × whether their own work stays fixed*
```
FX(e)    = Σ W(pr)   for type ∈ {fix, perf}
churn(e) = (# of e's feat PRs followed by any fix in the SAME scope within 14d) / (# of e's feat PRs)
Q(e)     = clamp(1 + (median_churn − churn(e)), 0.5, 1.5)
reverts(e) = PRs titled `Revert "<title>"` matching one of e's merged PRs   → −0.15 each on Q

Reliability(e) = FX(e) × Q(e)
```
*Honest caveat, stated in the UI:* a fix landing after a feature in the same scope is a **proxy** for rework, not proof of a regression. Reverts are the hard signal; churn is the soft one.

**③ Review Leverage** — *how many different people you unblock, how fast* (human reviews only; bots filtered entirely; self-reviews excluded)
```
Lat(e) = clamp(median_latency_all / median_latency(e), 0.5, 1.5)     # latency = PR opened → e's first review
Leverage(e) = √( distinct_authors(e) × reviews(e) ) × Lat(e)
```
Geometric mean is the point: 100 reviews for 2 people (squad lead) and 3 reviews for 3 people (tourist) both lose to broad, sustained review.

**④ Review Depth** — *did your review actually change the code*
```
effective(r) = 1 if pr.lastCommitDate > r.submittedAt else 0      # author pushed commits after your review
Depth(e) = Σ over e's human reviews r of  [ (1 + r.inlineComments)^0.6 − 1 ] × (1 + effective(r))
```
Reviews that provably caused follow-up commits count **double**. The `^0.6` gives diminishing returns so one nitpick storm can't dominate. Reported alongside as a plain rate: *"71% of their reviews were followed by new commits."*

**⑤ Ownership & Bus Factor** — *are they the person who holds a critical area*
```
share(e,s) = e's weighted PRs in scope s / all weighted PRs in s
Ownership(e) = Σ over scopes where share(e,s) ≥ 0.25  of  [ share(e,s) × centrality(s) ]

⚠ key-person flag: share(e,s) ≥ 0.5 AND distinct contributors to s ≤ 3
```
Doubles as a risk readout — the leader learns who they can't afford to lose.

**⑥ Agent Leverage** — *ships through agents and it sticks*
```
Agent(e) = Σ W(pr) × Q(e)   for e's merged PRs where autonomy ∈ {assisted, autonomous, agent_unspecified}
```
This encodes `AI_POLICY.md` directly — *"the key difference is that they're driving the AI, not the other way around."* Volume through agents only counts when the churn factor `Q(e)` says the work held up.

## 3. Normalization & final score

Each raw dimension → **percentile rank within the eligible cohort** → 0–100. Percentile, not z-score, because the distribution is heavily skewed. Raw values shown next to every percentile.

```
Score(e) = Σ_d ( w_d × Norm_d(e) ) / Σ_d w_d          w_d ∈ [0..5]
```

## 4. Presets (the sliders animate to these)

| Preset | ① Feat | ② Rel | ③ Lev | ④ Depth | ⑤ Own | ⑥ Agent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Balanced** (default) | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| **Ship features** | 5 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| **Stability first** | 1 | 5 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
| **Force multipliers** | 1 | 2 | 5 | 5 | 2 | 2 |
| **Key-person risk** | 3 | 3 | 1 | 1 | 5 | 1 |

**Advanced (collapsed):** per-work-type multipliers for `feat / fix / perf / refactor / chore`, defaulting to 1.0 — for when a leader wants to say "chores count for nothing this quarter."

---

**Two things I want your call on before I build:**

1. **Churn window = 14 days.** Shorter (7d) is a tighter causal claim but catches less; longer (30d) picks up unrelated fixes. I lean 14.
2. **Blast radius as multiplier vs. its own 7th slider.** I've made it a multiplier for legibility, but it's the one dimension a leader might genuinely want to dial. Happy to promote it if you'd rather have the control.
