# Scope of Influence as the Real Axis of Seniority: Evidence from Published Engineering Ladders

## 1. The aggregator: progression.fyi

**Source:** https://progression.fyi/

Self-described: *"Progression.fyi is a collection of public and open source career frameworks and templates brought to you by Progression."*

It indexes **75 public frameworks**. Companies/orgs listed: Circle CI, Intercom, Medium, Amazon, Monzo, Walmart, Buffer, Buzzfeed, Dropbox, Figma, Kickstarter, Rent The Runway, Wise, 8th Light, Apptension, Artsy, Attest, Basecamp, Blendle, Blinkist, Brad Fults, Brandwatch, Carta, Charlie HR, Chuck Groom, Clearleft, Cleo, Construx, Coryndon Luxmoore, David Spinks, Devexperts, Envato, Envoy, Etsy, Farewill, Financeit, Financial Times, FirstPort, Fog Creek, GOV.UK, Gitlab, Gorgias, Gusto, Healx, Intent Media, Inviqa, Jorge Fioranelli, Khan Academy, Leapsome, Liefery, Loblaw Digital, Lyst, Marshmallow, Meetup, Money Supermarket Group, Ockam, Ope, Patreon, Peter Merholz, Planet Argon, Pleo, Progression, Proton AI, Red Hat, Redgate Software, Sarah Drasner, Songkick, Spotify, Square, Superside, Urban Airship, WeTransfer, Zendesk, accuRx, dxw.

---

## 2. THE COMMON PATTERN — verbatim scope ladders from 7 companies

### Dropbox — the most explicit. "Scope" is a literal named field on every level page.

**Source:** https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/

The framework declares the axis up front (https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/overview.html):

> "**Level Expectations** define the scope, collaborative reach, and levers for impact at every level; these expectations are the *what* that determines the difference between an IC3 and IC4, for example"

And on the impact page (https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/what_is_impact.html):

> "Our career growth framework is anchored on results, aka **business impact**, which is a function of our **scope of impact** and how we **execute** against that scope."

The **Scope** field ("Area of ownership and level of autonomy / ambiguity"), verbatim, level by level:

| Level | Scope (verbatim) |
|---|---|
| IC1 | "I execute on defined tasks and contribute to solving problems with defined solutions." |
| IC2 | "I execute on defined projects to achieve team-level goals." |
| IC3 | "I own and deliver projects in service of quarterly goals on the team" |
| IC4 | "I own and deliver semi-annual/annual goals for my team." |
| IC5 (Staff) | "I deliver multi-year, multi-team product or platform goals" |
| IC6 (Principal) | "I own and deliver org/company-wide multi-year, multi-team goals" |
| IC7 (Sr. Principal) | "I own and deliver company-wide product or platform goals with multi-year, multi-team effect" |

Dropbox runs a **second, parallel axis** called **Collaborative Reach** — subtitled verbatim *"Organizational reach and extent of influence"*:

| Level | Collaborative Reach (verbatim) |
|---|---|
| IC1 | "I work within the scope of my team with specific guidance from my manager/TL" |
| IC2 | "I work primarily within the scope of my team with high level guidance from my manager/TL" |
| IC3 | "I work primarily with my direct team and cross-functional partners while driving cross-team collaboration for my project" |
| IC4 | "I am a strong leader for my team with my impact beginning to extend outside my team" |
| IC5 | "I am increasingly influencing the roadmaps of other Dropbox teams to achieve business impacting goals" |
| IC6 | "I typically influence the technical strategy of a group. I am often partnering closely with Directors/senior EPD leadership… I transcend organizational boundaries and proactively identify the best ways to leverage myself" |
| IC7 | "I typically influence EPD and company-wide strategy to achieve business-impacting goals." |

IC5's scope statement contains the clearest anti-local-optimum line in any public ladder:

> "I exercise judgement that favors the priorities of the wider engineering org rather than favoring locally optimal outcomes" — IC5 Staff Software Engineer, https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/ic5_staff_software_engineer.html

And the one-line level summaries alone trace the ladder:
- IC1: "I deliver lots of high quality production-ready code with direction from the team"
- IC3: "I independently identify and deliver software solutions through a set of milestones spanning a specific product focus or a multi-component system"
- IC4: "I autonomously deliver ongoing business impact across a team, product capability, or technical system"
- IC5: "I set the multi-year, multi-team technical strategy and deliver it through direct implementation or broad technical leadership"
- IC6: "I deliver results against a strategic company-level business objective or key component of the EPD mission"
- IC7: "I deliver results against either a portfolio of strategic company level business objectives… or a single strategic objective with significant complexity"

**Archetypes page** (https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/archetypes_behaviors.html) — Dropbox explicitly credits Larson:

> "As engineers gain more seniority, how they achieve impact and leverage themselves can vary broadly. There is more than one path to senior IC levels and we want to make it clear that it does not necessarily require one to become a Tech Lead to get there. To extend this idea, we wanted to introduce the notion of archetypes, which is heavily inspired from Will Larson's book *Staff Engineer*."

Its three archetypes — **Technical Lead**, **Architect**, **Solver** — are transcribed near-verbatim from Larson (compare §5 below).

---

### Monzo — scope is a literal labelled field with an emoji per level

**Source:** https://monzo.com/documents/engineering-progression-framework-v2-0.pdf (Engineering Progression Framework v2)

Guiding pillars, verbatim:

> "We will focus on the impact an individual engineer can have on driving Monzo forwards, rather than specific behaviours"
>
> "**Scope is an additional measure for different levels of seniority. As Monzo grows, so should the size or reach of the problems we encounter as engineers.**"

> "Impact is the main driver for progression at Monzo. Put simply, **impact measures your sphere of influence** and individual input on our success as a business, through contributing to Monzo's mission and goals."

The ladder, verbatim (the `Scope:` line is printed at the top of every level):

| Level | Scope (verbatim) | Summary (verbatim) |
|---|---|---|
| L1 Engineer | "✅ Task" | "A new engineer, with high potential, picking up the fundamentals they need to be successful in their squad." |
| L2 Engineer | "✅ Task" | "A productive and reliable engineer working effectively within a squad" |
| L3 Engineer | "🎨 Project or feature" | "A strong individual contributor. Responsible for the entire lifecycle of a project or feature" |
| L4 Senior | "👥 Team or Domain" | "An experienced individual contributor, leading in a team or domain area" |
| L5 Staff & Senior Staff | "🍱 Collective or Discipline" | "A highly experienced individual leader, leading in a large domain or collective." |
| L6 Principal | "🏦 Company" | "An engineering leader having impact across a broad area of the company, wider than a single collective or discipline." |

L4's prose is the cleanest statement of the transition anywhere:

> "**The scope and impact of a Level 4 engineer is typically felt at the team or domain level, with their influence beginning to spread wider across the business.**"

L5:

> "As an engineer they're a technical authority at Monzo, with influence and respect across multiple squads, disciplines and projects. They proactively drive cross-team initiatives…"

L6:

> "They're respected by both the wider Monzo engineering community, and the industry at large, because their past impact speaks for itself"

---

### Square / Block — "Scope & Impact contain the defining criteria of a level"

**Sources:** https://developer.squareup.com/blog/squares-growth-framework-for-engineers-and-engineering-managers/ and the ladder PDF at https://assets.ctfassets.net/1wryd5vd9xez/6bDnTwb4H7bfiFvg55ldRR/b1cb8514f0afd0a4050991d35ccbac03/Square_Software_Engineering_Career_Ladder.pdf

Blog, verbatim — this is the single most direct statement of the thesis in any public ladder:

> "Our level criteria are organized into two major sections: Scope & Impact and Behaviors. **Scope & Impact contain the defining criteria of a level. To be meeting the expectations of that level, an engineer or manager must be meeting every Scope & Impact criterion.** We also enumerate a set of behaviors that exemplify that level of scope and impact… While we don't expect everyone to demonstrate every single behavior listed for their level, we do need to see criteria from every category."

> "Every employee has a level, which describes the **scope, complexity, and impact** of their role and factors into compensation."

> "…we provide a path to take on larger scope and demonstrate leadership as an individual contributor… **Engineers and managers at the same level will have comparable scope and impact on the business.**"

> "Promotions are descriptive not prescriptive: We promote engineers and managers when they have demonstrated that they are consistently performing at the next level. **Promotions don't unlock new responsibilities; the new responsibilities and increased scope come first and then we recognize it with a promotion.**"

The PDF's IC level **titles alone** are a scope ladder (and it defines its terms: *"In this document, team refers to an engineer's immediate team; organization refers to the group under a GM or Core Lead"*):

| Level | Title (verbatim) |
|---|---|
| L3 | "A new engineer with potential" |
| L4 | "A solid contributor" |
| L5 | "A strong independent contributor" |
| L6 | "A team leader" |
| L7 | "An organizational leader" |
| L8 | "A company leader" |
| L9 | "An industry leader" |

Scope & Impact bullets, verbatim:
- **L3:** "Writes, tests, and documents code according to Square Engineering standards and practices."
- **L4:** "Designs, develops, ships, and maintains features with guidance from more experienced engineers."
- **L5:** "Independently responsible for the entire lifecycle of projects or features including eng design, development, and deployment."
- **L6:** "Leads or significantly contributes to medium-to-large feature releases; usually **multi-person projects that cross engineering team boundaries**."
- **L7:** "Sets architectural direction for **the broader organization** and helps evolve systems toward it." / "Has a track record of influencing and delivering projects with **organizational impact** and priority"
- **L8:** "Develops architecture, libraries and systems with **company-wide impact**." / "Has and continues to build a track record of strategic work with **company-wide, sometimes industry-wide, impact**." / "[Shared] Impact affects many teams, many customers, and/or a percentage of revenue."
- **L9:** "Ownership includes a broad strategic asset at Square." / "**Impact and decisions affect the entire company.**"

Square's L7 note is a direct statement that the job stops being about output:

> "The work of L7+ individual contributors **differs qualitatively** from that of earlier levels. **Significantly more time is spent on non-coding activities** and it will require a conscious shift in career goals and way of working. Many, if not most, engineers will prefer to stay at L6."

---

### Etsy — every level's expectation block names the reach explicitly

**Source:** https://etsy.github.io/Etsy-Engineering-Career-Ladder/ (raw: https://github.com/etsy/Etsy-Engineering-Career-Ladder/blob/master/index.md)

Verbatim expectations:

- **Engineer I:** "You complete **narrowly-defined tasks with clear instructions**."
- **Engineer II:** "You work within guidelines set by your teammates to independently tackle **well-scoped problems**." / "You work on features and projects **within a broader product or system**."
- **Senior Engineer:** "You take the lead on directing and implementing solutions to **moderately complex, loosely scoped problems** that are aligned with your team's goals." / "**Your work extends to many parts of a product or system.**" / "You enable other engineers on your team to be successful."
- **Staff Engineer:** "You take the lead on directing and implementing solutions to **significantly complex, unscoped problems**." / "**Your work extends to many parts of a domain, and may begin to influence your entire department or domain.**" / "You set technical direction for your teammates."
- **Senior Staff Engineer:** "You define the architecture and technical strategy that **guide many engineers in your domain or department**." / "Your work has significant and lasting impact on Etsy's business and Engineering goals."
- **Principal Engineer:** "You define the technical vision and strategy that **guide engineers across departments** to solve Etsy's thorniest, most intractable technical problems." / "Your work creates significant and lasting impact on Etsy's business and Engineering goals, **while enabling many other teams to reach their goals as well**."

Note the clean progression of *problem scoping* as a separate dial: "narrowly-defined tasks with clear instructions" → "well-scoped problems" → "loosely scoped problems" → "**unscoped** problems" → "complex, unbounded technical problems" (Senior Staff).

---

### GitLab — "operates at a team level scope" vs. "at an organizational … level scope"

**Source:** https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/careers/matrix/

Verbatim, the defining sentence of each level:

- **Staff** (https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/careers/matrix/staff/): "A staff engineer generally **operates at a team level scope**, serving as the technical leader for one or more of their team's domains of responsibility." / "Represents their team as a domain expert when interfacing with other teams." / "Able to take on complex requirements and decompose them into a proposal of small deliverables."
- **Principal** (https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/careers/matrix/principal/): "A principal engineer generally **operates at an organizational (sub-department or stage, for example) level scope**, serving as their organization's technical lead and connecting their organization to other parts of GitLab." / "Unblocks and enables team members and counterparts **across multiple teams**." / "Addresses **cross-team** challenges related to customers, quality and security." / "Able to take on **cross-team** complex requirements…"

The two paragraphs are otherwise word-for-word identical with "team" swapped for "organization" — which is about as literal a demonstration as you can get that scope *is* the variable.

Lower rungs for contrast: **Intermediate** — "Independently plans, estimates and, delivers small and moderate solutions." / "Performs thorough reviews **within their domain**." **Senior** — "Able to deliver work, even when given unclear requirements, **within the context of their team**."

---

### CircleCI — the single best one-sentence summary of the whole pattern

**Source:** https://circleci.com/blog/why-we-re-designed-our-engineering-career-paths-at-circleci/ (Lena Reinhard). Companion: https://circleci.com/blog/7-steps-to-building-an-engineering-competency-matrix/

Verbatim, in full:

> "**Engineers grow over time** by expanding their areas of impact, **from task to epic, team level, and onwards by working with their team and the team's business stakeholders, to across several teams and, ultimately, across the organization.** The second important aspect of growth is the ability to demonstrate skills more frequently – from frequently to usually to generally."

That is the axis stated as a five-stop progression: task → epic → team → several teams → organization. Levels run E1 (Associate) to E6 (Principal).

Their design criteria also name scope as the thing that must be legible:

> "Even without knowing all details of one level, it should be easy to develop an idea of **the area of work and impact** that engineers would be focusing on."
>
> "Descriptors should be unambiguous and clearly denote **shifts in frequency or scope** of skills demonstrated."

---

### Rent the Runway (Camille Fournier) — output is an "adder," impact/influence are "multipliers"

**Sources:** original — https://dresscode.renttherunway.com/blog/ladder (live, HTTP 200); markdown transcription — https://github.com/nelz9999/rtr2md (`IndividualContributorTrack.md`, `README.md`), which states it is a transcription of *"Copies of their public docs as of 2019-05-05"* and credits *"The Manager's Path by Camille Fournier (who wrote this ladder)."*

RTR uses four D&D-style attribute columns: **Dex** (Technical Skills), **Str** (Get Stuff Done), **Wis** (Impact), **Cha** (Communication & Leadership).

The README's "Pro tips" are the thesis in miniature:

> "**Dex and Str (the 'adder' attributes) are the primary drivers of promotions at lower levels. At higher levels, the importance gradually shifts to Wis and Cha (the 'multiplier' attributes).**"
>
> "The expectations at each level are cumulative."
>
> "Not everyone will progress in each column in lockstep. If you are Dex:6/Cha:3, you will not be stuck at L3, but you will likely not be promoted all the way L6."

I.e. "Get Stuff Done" — the throughput column — explicitly *stops being the driver* above mid-level. The **Wis – Impact** column, verbatim:

| Level | Wis – Impact (verbatim) |
|---|---|
| Engineer I | "Developing knowledge of **a single component** of our architecture" |
| Engineer II (Rear) | "Self-sufficient in **at least one large area of the codebase** (multiple services in a pillar, all frontend code related to a main funnel flow) with a high-level understanding of other components" |
| Senior Engineer I | "**End-to-end responsibility on projects** of increasing complexity; contributes to common code." / "Understands the business supported by their Pillar or the Pillars they support" |
| Senior Engineer II (Rear) | "Takes initiative to identify and solve important problems, **coordinating with others on cross-cutting technical issues**" |
| Senior Engineer II (Vice) | "**Sets direction at the project/service level and consistently influences decision-making at the Pillar level**" |
| Staff (Rear) | "**Shapes broad architecture**; ships multiple large services, complex libraries or major pieces of infrastructure" |
| Staff (Vice) | "Has made an obvious positive impact on **the entire company's technical trajectory**" |
| Senior Staff (Rear) | "Plays a key role in developing **multi-year technology strategy** for complete and critical areas of the business that **encompass multiple systems and teams**" |
| Senior Staff (Vice) | "**Decisions have a direct impact on the long-term success or failure of Rent the Runway.**" |

Supporting **Cha – Communication & Leadership** at Staff: "**Multiplies the effectiveness of others** by facilitating cross-team work"; Senior Staff: "Primarily acts as a **multiplier** by building systems, authoring tools, or introducing policies or patterns that raise the level of productivity of **the entire org**."

---

## 3. Explicit statements that output / volume / checkbox counting is NOT the measure

**Monzo** (https://monzo.com/documents/engineering-progression-framework-v2-0.pdf) — the strongest, and it appears three separate times:

> "**We wish to do away with levelling exercises or calculations. Attempting to boil performance and progression down to numbers and equations is lazy, and leaves little room for the different ways engineers can add value.** Instead we rely on managers to clearly articulate how an engineer is meeting the scope and impact of each level…"

> "**This framework should not be used to mathematically calculate level.** Different behaviours are important in different ways, and attempting to create algorithms or formulae to support conversations naively assumes that each behaviour is important to different parts of the business in the same way. In the past 'levelling exercises' have been used to quantify progression, but going forwards this should not be the approach."

> "This framework does not intend to be an exhaustive list of everything an engineer does or can do… **We do not wish to create an exercise that can be 'checkboxed' to completion.**"

> "…we should not list specific tasks such as '**writes complex RPC handlers**' but instead articulate the standards of technical contribution we should expect from engineers of different levels."

> "**Focusing on impact enables us to reward engineers who 'get stuff done' without them needing to perform specific routines.**"

**Dropbox** — the Clarifications and Myths page (https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/cr_clarifications_and_myths.html) answers a stated myth head-on:

> Myth: "The career framework favors deeper and more complex projects rather than a breadth of projects that deliver customer value."
>
> Answer: "The focus in the career framework has shifted towards **driving impact** in order to align with company goals in delivering value, and **less around complex projects**. Impact takes many forms ranging from product and domain expertise to project and technical leadership. Read more in the career framework's 'What is Impact' page, **where you'll also notice it has no mention of complexity.**"

> "**This framework is not a checklist.** This is a guide to help you figure out what your impact could look like at the next level."

And from Overview / Promotion Principles (https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/promotion_principles.html):

> "**This framework is not a promotion checklist** for your role; rather, it's designed to help you figure out what your impact could look like at the next level."

> "**No checkbox game**: There is no set of checkboxes that you can check off to guarantee a promotion. Promotions are a recognition of the talent development that has enabled you to consistently deliver results at the next level over a sustained period of time."

> "**Evidence, not faith**: Promotions are a recognition of demonstrated, sustained impact at the next level. We don't promote someone because we hope they can handle it."

Dropbox also distinguishes *rate* from *volume*:

> "**Velocity:** We consider **the rate at which you deliver impact, not just the cumulative impact that you have achieved.**" — https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/what_is_impact.html

**CircleCI** (https://circleci.com/blog/why-we-re-designed-our-engineering-career-paths-at-circleci/):

> "**What makes a good engineer goes far beyond their coding skills.** Our experience and our conversations with our engineers at different experience levels confirm this, and **often the more experienced engineers are, the less time they spend coding. This is why technical skills currently make up 20% of all competencies** we ask engineers to develop, and the same proportion of skills is dedicated to feedback, communication, and collaboration."

> "**Our competency matrix is not a checklist, it's a guideline**, and smaller deviations are to be expected."

**Square** (https://developer.squareup.com/blog/squares-growth-framework-for-engineers-and-engineering-managers/):

> "**We do not have strict minimum requirements for years of experience at any given level. We evaluate scope of responsibility and impact**, and we never want to fail to recognize high performance because of a litmus test like years of experience."

---

## 4. Scope as the differentiator between Senior / Staff / Principal

**Will Larson** — https://staffeng.com/guides/staff-archetypes/ (companion to *Staff Engineer*):

> "Everyone benefits from clear role expectations, but **career ladders are a tool that applies better against populations than people.** This is particularly true for Staff-plus engineers, whose career ladders often paper over several distinct roles hidden behind a single moniker."

The four archetypes, verbatim, each defined purely by scope:

> "**Tech Lead** guides the approach and execution of a particular team. They partner closely with a single manager, but sometimes they partner with two or three managers within a focused area."
>
> "**Architect** is responsible for the direction, quality, and approach within a critical area. They combine in-depth knowledge of technical constraints, user needs, and organization level leadership."
>
> "**Solver** digs deep into arbitrarily complex problems and finds an appropriate path forward. Some focus on a given area for long periods. Others bounce from hotspot to hotspot as guided by organizational leadership."
>
> "**Right Hand** extends an executive's attention, **borrowing their scope and authority** to operate particularly complex organizations. They provide additional leadership bandwidth to leaders of large-scale organizations."

On what changes at Staff (https://staffeng.com/guides/what-do-staff-engineers-actually-do/):

> "The most straightforward answer is that Staff engineers keep doing much of what made them successful as Senior engineers: building relationships, writing software, coordinating projects. However, that's a misleading answer. **Staff engineers do those same tasks, but whereas previously they were the core of their work, now they're auxiliary tasks.**"

> "There's a popular vision of heroic leadership that centers on extraordinarily productive individuals whose decisions change their company's future. Most of those narratives are intentionally designed by public relations teams to create a good story. **You're far more likely to change your company's long-term trajectory by growing the engineers around you than through personal heroics.**"

> "Sometimes folks see a requirement for mentorship in their career ladder and **try to mechanically check that box**, which is a shame…"

On Tech Lead delegating rather than out-producing:

> "Earlier in their career, they will have implemented their team's most complex technical projects, but at this point, **they default to delegating such projects across the team.** They do this both to grow their teammates and in acknowledgment that **the team's impact grows as the [team grows]**"

**Larson on visibility-as-proxy-for-impact** — https://lethain.com/work-on-what-matters/:

> "Where 'snacking' is the broad category of doing easy and low-impact work, there's a particularly seductive subset of snacking that I call '**preening**.' **Preening is doing low-impact, high-visibility work. Many companies conflate high-visibility and high-impact so strongly that they can't distinguish between preening and impact**, which is why it's not uncommon to see some companies' senior-most engineers spend the majority of their time doing work of dubious value but that is frequently recognized in company meetings."

**Tanya Reilly, "Being Glue"** — https://noidea.dog/glue (Reilly identifies herself in the piece: *"Hello, my name's Tanya and I'm a principal software engineer at Squarespace."*). This is the canonical counter-case: an engineer whose scope grew but whose output shrank, and a ladder that couldn't see it.

> "You know that thing where everyone on a software engineering team turns up and just writes code for eight hours a day and then later the project is successful? No you don't. **Projects don't work like that!**"

> "Of course coding is an important skill in a software engineering team. But there are a ton of [other skills] that we need to bring to work every day. **Skills that can mean the difference between a project that succeeds and one that fails.**"

The promotion committee's verdict, verbatim:

> "**Your project isn't finished. You're not producing much code. You didn't have enough impact yet.**"

And Reilly's diagnosis:

> "**At every point, this engineer did the highest impact work that was available. The project wouldn't have shipped without her. She was the glue that held the whole thing together.**"

> "But this company doesn't consider that to be sufficient promotable work, at least not at this level. **Although they didn't explicitly say so, they want code or other quantifiable technical work.**"

> "Every senior person in an organisation should be aware of the less glamorous - and often less-promotable - work that needs to happen to make a team successful. **Managed deliberately, glue work demonstrates and builds strong technical leadership skills. Left unconscious, it can be career limiting.**"

## 5. The synthesized cross-company pattern

Laid side by side, seven independently-authored ladders converge on the same five or six rungs:

| Rung | Dropbox | Monzo | Square | Etsy | GitLab | CircleCI | RTR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Own tasks** | "defined tasks… defined solutions" | "✅ Task" | "A new engineer with potential" | "narrowly-defined tasks with clear instructions" | "small and moderate solutions" | "task" | "a single component" |
| **Own a project/feature** | "own and deliver projects in service of quarterly goals" | "🎨 Project or feature" | "A strong independent contributor" | "well-scoped problems… within a broader product or system" | "within the context of their team" | "epic" | "End-to-end responsibility on projects" |
| **Team impact** | "own and deliver semi-annual/annual goals for my team" | "👥 Team or Domain" | "A team leader" | "extends to many parts of a product or system" | "operates at a team level scope" | "team level" | "influences decision-making at the Pillar level" |
| **Multi-team / group** | "multi-year, multi-team product or platform goals" | "🍱 Collective or Discipline" | "An organizational leader" | "many parts of a domain… may begin to influence your entire department" | "operates at an organizational … level scope" | "across several teams" | "encompass multiple systems and teams" |
| **Org / company** | "org/company-wide multi-year, multi-team goals" | "🏦 Company" | "A company leader" | "guide engineers across departments" | — | "across the organization" | "the entire company's technical trajectory" |
| **Industry** | "a multi-year, industry-leading perspective" (IC6/IC7) | "the industry at large" (L6) | "An industry leader" (L9) | — | — | — | — |

Two structural facts recur in nearly every framework and reinforce the thesis:

1. **Levels are cumulative, so the only thing that can differentiate them is reach.** Dropbox: "Each level implicitly includes all criteria and responsibilities of prior levels" (Square's phrasing); Monzo: "Levels are broadly cumulative, each one building on what comes before"; Etsy: "Mastery of a competency is cumulative. At each successive level, engineers are expected to retain the skills and characteristics required at earlier levels"; RTR: "The expectations at each level are cumulative."

2. **IC and manager tracks are pegged to each other by scope, not by output.** Square: "Engineers and managers at the same level will have comparable scope and impact on the business" and "**Becoming a manager is not a promotion**… When an engineer first becomes a manager, they remain in the same level and move laterally." Its PDF prints IC and EM criteria for L5–L9 side by side under the *same* "Scope & Impact" heading, with `[Shared]` markers on criteria identical across both — e.g. at L8: "[Shared] Impact affects many teams, many customers, and/or a percentage of revenue." Dropbox says the same: "A manager's impact comes from **organizational leverage**… Engineers, as a part of mastering their craft, develop **technical leverage** to increase their business impact."

# Scope of Influence as the Real Axis of Seniority: Evidence from Published Engineering Ladders

## 1. The aggregator: progression.fyi

**Source:** https://progression.fyi/

Self-described: *"Progression.fyi is a collection of public and open source career frameworks and templates brought to you by Progression."*

## 2. THE COMMON PATTERN — verbatim scope ladders from 7 companies

### Dropbox — the most explicit. "Scope" is a literal named field on every level page.

**Source:** https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/

The framework declares the axis up front (https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/overview.html):

> "**Level Expectations** define the scope, collaborative reach, and levers for impact at every level; these expectations are the *what* that determines the difference between an IC3 and IC4, for example"

And on the impact page (https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/what_is_impact.html):

> "Our career growth framework is anchored on results, aka **business impact**, which is a function of our **scope of impact** and how we **execute** against that scope."

The **Scope** field ("Area of ownership and level of autonomy / ambiguity"), verbatim, level by level:

| Level | Scope (verbatim) |
|---|---|
| IC1 | "I execute on defined tasks and contribute to solving problems with defined solutions." |
| IC2 | "I execute on defined projects to achieve team-level goals." |
| IC3 | "I own and deliver projects in service of quarterly goals on the team" |
| IC4 | "I own and deliver semi-annual/annual goals for my team." |
| IC5 (Staff) | "I deliver multi-year, multi-team product or platform goals" |
| IC6 (Principal) | "I own and deliver org/company-wide multi-year, multi-team goals" |
| IC7 (Sr. Principal) | "I own and deliver company-wide product or platform goals with multi-year, multi-team effect" |

Dropbox runs a **second, parallel axis** called **Collaborative Reach** — subtitled verbatim *"Organizational reach and extent of influence"*:

| Level | Collaborative Reach (verbatim) |
|---|---|
| IC1 | "I work within the scope of my team with specific guidance from my manager/TL" |
| IC2 | "I work primarily within the scope of my team with high level guidance from my manager/TL" |
| IC3 | "I work primarily with my direct team and cross-functional partners while driving cross-team collaboration for my project" |
| IC4 | "I am a strong leader for my team with my impact beginning to extend outside my team" |
| IC5 | "I am increasingly influencing the roadmaps of other Dropbox teams to achieve business impacting goals" |
| IC6 | "I typically influence the technical strategy of a group. I am often partnering closely with Directors/senior EPD leadership… I transcend organizational boundaries and proactively identify the best ways to leverage myself" |
| IC7 | "I typically influence EPD and company-wide strategy to achieve business-impacting goals." |

IC5's scope statement contains the clearest anti-local-optimum line in any public ladder:

> "I exercise judgement that favors the priorities of the wider engineering org rather than favoring locally optimal outcomes" — IC5 Staff Software Engineer, https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/ic5_staff_software_engineer.html

And the one-line level summaries alone trace the ladder:
- IC1: "I deliver lots of high quality production-ready code with direction from the team"
- IC3: "I independently identify and deliver software solutions through a set of milestones spanning a specific product focus or a multi-component system"
- IC4: "I autonomously deliver ongoing business impact across a team, product capability, or technical system"
- IC5: "I set the multi-year, multi-team technical strategy and deliver it through direct implementation or broad technical leadership"
- IC6: "I deliver results against a strategic company-level business objective or key component of the EPD mission"
- IC7: "I deliver results against either a portfolio of strategic company level business objectives… or a single strategic objective with significant complexity"

**Archetypes page** (https://dropbox.github.io/dbx-career-framework/archetypes_behaviors.html) — Dropbox explicitly credits Larson:

> "As engineers gain more seniority, how they achieve impact and leverage themselves can vary broadly. There is more than one path to senior IC levels and we want to make it clear that it does not necessarily require one to become a Tech Lead to get there. To extend this idea, we wanted to introduce the notion of archetypes, which is heavily inspired from Will Larson's book *Staff Engineer*."

Its three archetypes — **Technical Lead**, **Architect**, **Solver** — are transcribed near-verbatim from Larson (compare §5 below).

### Monzo — scope is a literal labelled field with an emoji per level

**Source:** https://monzo.com/documents/engineering-progression-framework-v2-0.pdf (Engineering Progression Framework v2)

Guiding pillars, verbatim:

> "We will focus on the impact an individual engineer can have on driving Monzo forwards, rather than specific behaviours"
>
> "**Scope is an additional measure for different levels of seniority. As Monzo grows, so should the size or reach of the problems we encounter as engineers.**"

> "Impact is the main driver for progression at Monzo. Put simply, **impact measures your sphere of influence** and individual input on our success as a business, through contributing to Monzo's mission and goals."

The ladder, verbatim (the `Scope:` line is printed at the top of every level):

| Level | Scope (verbatim) | Summary (verbatim) |
|---|---|---|
| L1 Engineer | "✅ Task" | "A new engineer, with high potential, picking up the fundamentals they need to be successful in their squad." |
| L2 Engineer | "✅ Task" | "A productive and reliable engineer working effectively within a squad" |
| L3 Engineer | "🎨 Project or feature" | "A strong individual contributor. Responsible for the entire lifecycle of a project or feature" |
| L4 Senior | "👥 Team or Domain" | "An experienced individual contributor, leading in a team or domain area" |
| L5 Staff & Senior Staff | "🍱 Collective or Discipline" | "A highly experienced individual leader, leading in a large domain or collective." |
| L6 Principal | "🏦 Company" | "An engineering leader having impact across a broad area of the company, wider than a single collective or discipline." |

L4's prose is the cleanest statement of the transition anywhere:

> "**The scope and impact of a Level 4 engineer is typically felt at the team or domain level, with their influence beginning to spread wider across the business.**"

L5:

> "As an engineer they're a technical authority at Monzo, with influence and respect across multiple squads, disciplines and projects. They proactively drive cross-team initiatives…"

L6:

> "They're respected by both the wider Monzo engineering community, and the industry at large, because their past impact speaks for itself"

### Square / Block — "Scope & Impact contain the defining criteria of a level"

**Sources:** https://developer.squareup.com/blog/squares-growth-framework-for-engineers-and-engineering-managers/ and the ladder PDF at https://assets.ctfassets.net/1wryd5vd9xez/6bDnTwb4H7bfiFvg55ldRR/b1cb8514f0afd0a4050991d35ccbac03/Square_Software_Engineering_Career_Ladder.pdf

Blog, verbatim — this is the single most direct statement of the thesis in any public ladder:

> "Our level criteria are organized into two major sections: Scope & Impact and Behaviors. **Scope & Impact contain the defining criteria of a level. To be meeting the expectations of that level, an engineer or manager must be meeting every Scope & Impact criterion.** We also enumerate a set of behaviors that exemplify that level of scope and impact… While we don't expect everyone to demonstrate every single behavior listed for their level, we do need to see criteria from every category."

> "Every employee has a level, which describes the **scope, complexity, and impact** of their role and factors into compensation."

> "…we provide a path to take on larger scope and demonstrate leadership as an individual contributor… **Engineers and managers at the same level will have comparable scope and impact on the business.**"

> "Promotions are descriptive not prescriptive: We promote engineers and managers when they have demonstrated that they are consistently performing at the next level. **Promotions don't unlock new responsibilities; the new responsibilities and increased scope come first and then we recognize it with a promotion.**"

The PDF's IC level **titles alone** are a scope ladder (and it defines its terms: *"In this document, team refers to an engineer's immediate team; organization refers to the group under a GM or Core Lead"*):

| Level | Title (verbatim) |
|---|---|
| L3 | "A new engineer with potential" |
| L4 | "A solid contributor" |
| L5 | "A strong independent contributor" |
| L6 | "A team leader" |
| L7 | "An organizational leader" |
| L8 | "A company leader" |
| L9 | "An industry leader" |

Scope & Impact bullets, verbatim:
- **L3:** "Writes, tests, and documents code according to Square Engineering standards and practices."
- **L4:** "Designs, develops, ships, and maintains features with guidance from more experienced engineers."
- **L5:** "Independently responsible for the entire lifecycle of projects or features including eng design, development, and deployment."
- **L6:** "Leads or significantly contributes to medium-to-large feature releases; usually **multi-person projects that cross engineering team boundaries**."
- **L7:** "Sets architectural direction for **the broader organization** and helps evolve systems toward it." / "Has a track record of influencing and delivering projects with **organizational impact** and priority"
- **L8:** "Develops architecture, libraries and systems with **company-wide impact**." / "Has and continues to build a track record of strategic work with **company-wide, sometimes industry-wide, impact**." / "[Shared] Impact affects many teams, many customers, and/or a percentage of revenue."
- **L9:** "Ownership includes a broad strategic asset at Square." / "**Impact and decisions affect the entire company.**"

Square's L7 note is a direct statement that the job stops being about output:

> "The work of L7+ individual contributors **differs qualitatively** from that of earlier levels. **Significantly more time is spent on non-coding activities** and it will require a conscious shift in career goals and way of working. Many, if not most, engineers will prefer to stay at L6."

### Etsy — every level's expectation block names the reach explicitly

**Source:** https://etsy.github.io/Etsy-Engineering-Career-Ladder/ (raw: https://github.com/etsy/Etsy-Engineering-Career-Ladder/blob/master/index.md)

Verbatim expectations:

- **Engineer I:** "You complete **narrowly-defined tasks with clear instructions**."
- **Engineer II:** "You work within guidelines set by your teammates to independently tackle **well-scoped problems**." / "You work on features and projects **within a broader product or system**."
- **Senior Engineer:** "You take the lead on directing and implementing solutions to **moderately complex, loosely scoped problems** that are aligned with your team's goals." / "**Your work extends to many parts of a product or system.**" / "You enable other engineers on your team to be successful."
- **Staff Engineer:** "You take the lead on directing and implementing solutions to **significantly complex, unscoped problems**." / "**Your work extends to many parts of a domain, and may begin to influence your entire department or domain.**" / "You set technical direction for your teammates."
- **Senior Staff Engineer:** "You define the architecture and technical strategy that **guide many engineers in your domain or department**." / "Your work has significant and lasting impact on Etsy's business and Engineering goals."
- **Principal Engineer:** "You define the technical vision and strategy that **guide engineers across departments** to solve Etsy's thorniest, most intractable technical problems." / "Your work creates significant and lasting impact on Etsy's business and Engineering goals, **while enabling many other teams to reach their goals as well**."

Note the clean progression of *problem scoping* as a separate dial: "narrowly-defined tasks with clear instructions" → "well-scoped problems" → "loosely scoped problems" → "**unscoped** problems" → "complex, unbounded technical problems" (Senior Staff).

### GitLab — "operates at a team level scope" vs. "at an organizational … level scope"

**Source:** https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/careers/matrix/

Verbatim, the defining sentence of each level:

- **Staff** (https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/careers/matrix/staff/): "A staff engineer generally **operates at a team level scope**, serving as the technical leader for one or more of their team's domains of responsibility." / "Represents their team as a domain expert when interfacing with other teams." / "Able to take on complex requirements and decompose them into a proposal of small deliverables."
- **Principal** (https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/careers/matrix/principal/): "A principal engineer generally **operates at an organizational (sub-department or stage, for example) level scope**, serving as their organization's technical lead and connecting their organization to other parts of GitLab." / "Unblocks and enables team members and counterparts **across multiple teams**." / "Addresses **cross-team** challenges related to customers, quality and security." / "Able to take on **cross-team** complex requirements…"

The two paragraphs are otherwise word-for-word identical with "team" swapped for "organization" — which is about as literal a demonstration as you can get that scope *is* the variable.

Lower rungs for contrast: **Intermediate** — "Independently plans, estimates and, delivers small and moderate solutions." / "Performs thorough reviews **within their domain**." **Senior** — "Able to deliver work, even when given unclear requirements, **within the context of their team**."

### CircleCI — the single best one-sentence summary of the whole pattern

**Source:** https://circleci.com/blog/why-we-re-designed-our-engineering-career-paths-at-circleci/ (Lena Reinhard). Companion: https://circleci.com/blog/7-steps-to-building-an-engineering-competency-matrix/

Verbatim, in full:

> "**Engineers grow over time** by expanding their areas of impact, **from task to epic, team level, and onwards by working with their team and the team's business stakeholders, to across several teams and, ultimately, across the organization.** The second important aspect of growth is the ability to demonstrate skills more frequently – from frequently to usually to generally."

That is the axis stated as a five-stop progression: task → epic → team → several teams → organization. Levels run E1 (Associate) to E6 (Principal).

Their design criteria also name scope as the thing that must be legible:

> "Even without knowing all details of one level, it should be easy to develop an idea of **the area of work and impact** that engineers would be focusing on."
>
> "Descriptors should be unambiguous and clearly denote **shifts in frequency or scope** of skills demonstrated."

**Sources:** original — https://dresscode.renttherunway.com/blog/ladder (live, HTTP 200); markdown transcription — https://github.com/nelz9999/rtr2md (`IndividualContributorTrack.md`, `README.md`), which states it is a transcription of *"Copies of their public docs as of 2019-05-05"* and credits *"The Manager's Path by Camille Fournier (who wrote this ladder)."*

## 3. Explicit statements that output / volume / checkbox counting is NOT the measure

**Monzo** (https://monzo.com/documents/engineering-progression-framework-v2-0.pdf) — the strongest, and it appears three separate times:

> "**We wish to do away with levelling exercises or calculations. Attempting to boil performance and progression down to numbers and equations is lazy, and leaves little room for the different ways engineers can add value.** Instead we rely on managers to clearly articulate how an engineer is meeting the scope and impact of each level…"

## 4. Scope as the differentiator between Senior / Staff / Principal

**Will Larson** — https://staffeng.com/guides/staff-archetypes/ (companion to *Staff Engineer*):

> "Everyone benefits from clear role expectations, but **career ladders are a tool that applies better against populations than people.** This is particularly true for Staff-plus engineers, whose career ladders often paper over several distinct roles hidden behind a single moniker."

The four archetypes, verbatim, each defined purely by scope:

> "**Tech Lead** guides the approach and execution of a particular team. They partner closely with a single manager, but sometimes they partner with two or three managers within a focused area."
>
> "**Architect** is responsible for the direction, quality, and approach within a critical area. They combine in-depth knowledge of technical constraints, user needs, and organization level leadership."
>
> "**Solver** digs deep into arbitrarily complex problems and finds an appropriate path forward. Some focus on a given area for long periods. Others bounce from hotspot to hotspot as guided by organizational leadership."
>
> "**Right Hand** extends an executive's attention, **borrowing their scope and authority** to operate particularly complex organizations. They provide additional leadership bandwidth to leaders of large-scale organizations."

On what changes at Staff (https://staffeng.com/guides/what-do-staff-engineers-actually-do/):

> "The most straightforward answer is that Staff engineers keep doing much of what made them successful as Senior engineers: building relationships, writing software, coordinating projects. However, that's a misleading answer. **Staff engineers do those same tasks, but whereas previously they were the core of their work, now they're auxiliary tasks.**"

> "There's a popular vision of heroic leadership that centers on extraordinarily productive individuals whose decisions change their company's future. Most of those narratives are intentionally designed by public relations teams to create a good story. **You're far more likely to change your company's long-term trajectory by growing the engineers around you than through personal heroics.**"

> "Sometimes folks see a requirement for mentorship in their career ladder and **try to mechanically check that box**, which is a shame…"

On Tech Lead delegating rather than out-producing:

> "Earlier in their career, they will have implemented their team's most complex technical projects, but at this point, **they default to delegating such projects across the team.** They do this both to grow their teammates and in acknowledgment that **the team's impact grows as the [team grows]**"

**Larson on visibility-as-proxy-for-impact** — https://lethain.com/work-on-what-matters/:

> "Where 'snacking' is the broad category of doing easy and low-impact work, there's a particularly seductive subset of snacking that I call '**preening**.' **Preening is doing low-impact, high-visibility work. Many companies conflate high-visibility and high-impact so strongly that they can't distinguish between preening and impact**, which is why it's not uncommon to see some companies' senior-most engineers spend the majority of their time doing work of dubious value but that is frequently recognized in company meetings."

**Tanya Reilly, "Being Glue"** — https://noidea.dog/glue (Reilly identifies herself in the piece: *"Hello, my name's Tanya and I'm a principal software engineer at Squarespace."*). This is the canonical counter-case: an engineer whose scope grew but whose output shrank, and a ladder that couldn't see it.

> "You know that thing where everyone on a software engineering team turns up and just writes code for eight hours a day and then later the project is successful? No you don't. **Projects don't work like that!**"

> "Of course coding is an important skill in a software engineering team. But there are a ton of [other skills] that we need to bring to work every day. **Skills that can mean the difference between a project that succeeds and one that fails.**"

The promotion committee's verdict, verbatim:

> "**Your project isn't finished. You're not producing much code. You didn't have enough impact yet.**"

And Reilly's diagnosis:

> "**At every point, this engineer did the highest impact work that was available. The project wouldn't have shipped without her. She was the glue that held the whole thing together.**"

> "But this company doesn't consider that to be sufficient promotable work, at least not at this level. **Although they didn't explicitly say so, they want code or other quantifiable technical work.**"

> "Every senior person in an organisation should be aware of the less glamorous - and often less-promotable - work that needs to happen to make a team successful. **Managed deliberately, glue work demonstrates and builds strong technical leadership skills. Left unconscious, it can be career limiting.**"

## 5. The synthesized cross-company pattern

Laid side by side, seven independently-authored ladders converge on the same five or six rungs:

| Rung | Dropbox | Monzo | Square | Etsy | GitLab | CircleCI | RTR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Own tasks** | "defined tasks… defined solutions" | "✅ Task" | "A new engineer with potential" | "narrowly-defined tasks with clear instructions" | "small and moderate solutions" | "task" | "a single component" |
| **Own a project/feature** | "own and deliver projects in service of quarterly goals" | "🎨 Project or feature" | "A strong independent contributor" | "well-scoped problems… within a broader product or system" | "within the context of their team" | "epic" | "End-to-end responsibility on projects" |
| **Team impact** | "own and deliver semi-annual/annual goals for my team" | "👥 Team or Domain" | "A team leader" | "extends to many parts of a product or system" | "operates at a team level scope" | "team level" | "influences decision-making at the Pillar level" |
| **Multi-team / group** | "multi-year, multi-team product or platform goals" | "🍱 Collective or Discipline" | "An organizational leader" | "many parts of a domain… may begin to influence your entire department" | "operates at an organizational … level scope" | "across several teams" | "encompass multiple systems and teams" |
| **Org / company** | "org/company-wide multi-year, multi-team goals" | "🏦 Company" | "A company leader" | "guide engineers across departments" | — | "across the organization" | "the entire company's technical trajectory" |
| **Industry** | "a multi-year, industry-leading perspective" (IC6/IC7) | "the industry at large" (L6) | "An industry leader" (L9) | — | — | — | — |

Two structural facts recur in nearly every framework and reinforce the thesis:

1. **Levels are cumulative, so the only thing that can differentiate them is reach.** Dropbox: "Each level implicitly includes all criteria and responsibilities of prior levels" (Square's phrasing); Monzo: "Levels are broadly cumulative, each one building on what comes before"; Etsy: "Mastery of a competency is cumulative. At each successive level, engineers are expected to retain the skills and characteristics required at earlier levels"; RTR: "The expectations at each level are cumulative."

2. **IC and manager tracks are pegged to each other by scope, not by output.** Square: "Engineers and managers at the same level will have comparable scope and impact on the business" and "**Becoming a manager is not a promotion**… When an engineer first becomes a manager, they remain in the same level and move laterally." Its PDF prints IC and EM criteria for L5–L9 side by side under the *same* "Scope & Impact" heading, with `[Shared]` markers on criteria identical across both — e.g. at L8: "[Shared] Impact affects many teams, many customers, and/or a percentage of revenue." Dropbox says the same: "A manager's impact comes from **organizational leverage**… Engineers, as a part of mastering their craft, develop **technical leverage** to increase their business impact."

## A1. The canonical academic paper: Avelino, Passos, Hora, Valente (ICPC 2016)

**"A Novel Approach for Estimating Truck Factors"**, Guilherme Avelino, Leonardo Passos, Andre Hora, Marco Tulio Valente, *24th IEEE International Conference on Program Comprehension (ICPC 2016)*, pp. 1–10. Preprint: arXiv:1604.06766 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.06766 (PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1604.06766). Tool: https://github.com/aserg-ufmg/Truck-Factor

**Definition (verbatim):**
> "A system's truck factor (TF) is defined as 'the number of people on your team that have to be hit by a truck (or quit) before the project is in serious trouble'."

> "Truck Factor (TF) is a metric proposed by the agile community as a tool to identify concentration of knowledge in software development environments. It states the minimal number of developers that have to be hit by a truck (or quit) before a project is incapacitated. In other words, TF helps to measure how prepared is a project to deal with developer turnover."

> "Systems with a low truck factor spot strong dependencies towards specific personnel, forming knowledge silos among developer teams."

**Their definition of authorship (important nuance — it's not "who created the file"):**
> "Authorship, in this case, is not a strict notion. Stated otherwise, authorship is not a matter of who creates a file. Rather, authorship is a statement of who will be able to maintain a file from the latest system snapshot onward."

**The DOA formula, verbatim from the paper:**
> "DOA(md, fp) = 3.293 + 1.098 × FA(md, fp) + 0.164 × DL(md, fp) − 0.321 × ln(1 + AC(md, fp))"

> "From the equation, DOA depends on three factors: (i) first authorship (FA): if md originally created f, FA is 1; otherwise it is 0; (ii) number of deliveries (DL): number of changes in f made by md; and (iii) number of acceptances (AC): number of changes in f made by any developer, except md."

> "DOA weights contributions differently, accounting for both changes of a developer in a file (increases DOA), as well as the changes performed by others (decreases DOA)."

**The "main developer" thresholds, verbatim:**
> "A normalized DOA-value ranges from 0 to 1. We grant 1 to the developer with the highest absolute DOA among all developers that worked on f; altogether, we consider a developer as an author of a file if its resulting normalized DOA is greater than a threshold k and its absolute DOA is not lower than a value m. Currently, k and m stands as configurable parameters in our approach. As we show in Section IV-B, k = 0.75 and m = 3.293 seem to provide good results."

So: **normalized DOA ≥ 0.75 × max DOA for that file, AND absolute DOA ≥ 3.293** — 3.293 being exactly the intercept of Fritz's regression, i.e. the DOA of someone who has done nothing.

**The 50% coverage threshold, verbatim:**
> "Our estimation relies on a coverage assumption: a system will face serious delays or will be likely discontinued if its current set of authors covers less than 50% of the current set of files in the system."

The algorithm (Algorithm 1 in the paper) is a greedy heuristic: `while A ≠ ∅ { coverage ← getCoverage(F, A); if coverage < 0.5 break; A ← removeTopAuthor(A); tf ← tf + 1 }`.

**Headline empirical findings (exact numbers, verbatim):**
> "we propose a novel (and automated) approach for estimating TF-values, which we execute against a corpus of 133 popular project in GitHub… Among others, we find that the majority of our target systems (65%) have TF ≤ 2."

> "Figure 5 presents the distribution of the truck factor amongst our subjects. The first, second, and third quartiles are 1, 2, and 4, respectively. Most systems have a small truck factor: 45 systems (34%) have TF = 1 (e.g., mbostock/d3 and less/less.js); in 42 systems (31%), TF = 2 including well-known systems such as clojure/clojure, cucumber/cucumber, ashkenas/backbone and elasticsearch/elasticsearch."

> "torvalds/linux has TF = 57, followed by fzaninotto/Faker (TF = 23) and android/platform frameworks base (TF = 19). Other well-known systems include php/php-src (TF = 18), git/git (TF = 12), v8/v8 (TF = 11), and rails/rails (TF = 9)."

Corpus scale: *"133 systems in GitHub. In total, such systems have over 373K files and 41 MLOC; their combined evolution history sums to over 2 million commits."*

**Validation:** *"in 84% of valid answers developers agree or partially agree that the TF's authors are the main authors of their systems; in 53% we receive a positive or partially positive answer regarding our estimated truck factors."* (106 respondents, 84 of them top-10 contributors, 62 systems.)

**Author-ratio findings (relevant to "concentration is normal"):**
> "the first, second, and third quartiles are 16%, 23%, and 36%" (proportion of developers who qualify as authors). And: *"Backbone is also an example, with only six authors amongst its 248 developers. These six authors monopolize 67% of commits."*

**On mitigation, verbatim:** *"According to the surveyed developers, documentation is the most effective development practice to overcome a truck factor event, followed by the existence of an active community…"*

## A2. The DOA formula's origin: Fritz et al. (ICSE 2010)

**"A Degree-of-Knowledge Model to Capture Source Code Familiarity"**, Thomas Fritz, Jingwen Ou, Gail C. Murphy, Emerson Murphy-Hill, *ICSE 2010*, pp. 385–394. PDF: https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~fritz/papers/icse10_dok_web.pdf

I verified the coefficients directly against Table 1 of the paper. **They are exactly right, and they come from a multiple linear regression on developer self-ratings:**

| | Weighting | Std. Error | p-value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intercept | 3.293 | 0.133 | <0.001 |
| FA | 1.098 | 0.179 | <0.001 |
| DL | 0.164 | 0.053 | 0.002 |
| ln(1 + AC) | −0.321 | 0.105 | 0.002 |
| ln(1 + DOI) | 0.190 | 0.100 | 0.059 |

The **full DOK** equation, verbatim:
> "DOK = 3.293 + 1.098 ∗ FA + 0.164 ∗ DL − 0.321 ∗ ln(1 + AC) + 0.19 ∗ ln(1 + DOI)"

The truck-factor literature uses only the first four terms (DOA) — the DOI term needs IDE interaction logs, which VCS mining doesn't have.

**Crucial caveat that almost nobody quoting this formula mentions, verbatim from Fritz et al.:**
> "The overall model has an estimated 'goodness of fit', R Square, of 0.25 (adjusted R Square is 0.23)… The correlation coefficient R that represents a measure of the overall fit between our predictor variables and the user rating is 0.50. The standard error of the estimate is 1.17. The 0.25 R Square value shows that our model does not predict the user rating completely."

Also: the model was fit on **246 ratings from seven developers** at one site, validated on 80 elements from two developers at a second site (Spearman rs = 0.3847, p = 0.0004). And: *"Determining weightings that might apply across a broader range of development situations would require gathering data from many more projects, which was not warranted at this early stage of investigation."* Those magic constants are far more contingent than their four-decimal precision suggests.

## A3. Cosentino, Cánovas Izquierdo, Cabot (SANER 2015)

**"Assessing the bus factor of Git repositories"**, Valerio Cosentino, Javier Luis Cánovas Izquierdo, Jordi Cabot, *2015 IEEE 22nd International Conference on Software Analysis, Evolution, and Reengineering (SANER)*, pp. 499–503. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1109/SANER.2015.7081864 · https://dblp.org/pers/hd/c/Cosentino:Valerio

The published PDF is paywalled (IEEE) and the HAL/ResearchGate/Academia mirrors all returned 403 to me, so I could not verify quotes against the original. **The canonical definition, quoted verbatim from a secondary source that quotes it in quotation marks** — Aliza Lisan and Boyana Norris, "Guiding Effort Allocation in Open-Source Software Projects Using Bus Factor Analysis," arXiv:2401.03303 (2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03303:
> "Formally known as the Bus Factor (BF) of a project and defined as 'the number of key developers who would need to be incapacitated to make a project unable to proceed'."

**The Cosentino algorithm described verbatim** in Jabrayilzade et al. (ICSE-SEIP 2022, §2.2, see A4):
> "Cosentino et al. [10] suggest a set of algorithms to compute the bus factor. The authors define the notion of primary and secondary developers. The file is abandoned when none of the primary or secondary developers who worked on it are present in the project. The bus factor problem happens when a certain amount of files is abandoned. The analysis can be carried out at either file-level or line-level of granularity. The authors suggest four different metrics (M1 to M4) for measuring contribution."
> "• M1 assigns all knowledge to the last contributor.
> • M2 considers every change with equal weight (e.g., if A committed to a file twice and B committed once, A has 2/3 knowledge and B has 1/3).
> • M3 is the same as M2, but consecutive changes are considered to be one change…
> • M4 adds weights to the changes; for a file with N commits, the oldest commit has weight 1, the second-oldest has weight 2, and so on."
> "For a file that has been edited by N contributors, primary developers are those who have done at least 100/N % of edits and secondary developers have done 100/N % > x > 50/N % of edits."

Same source, on the earlier **Zazworka/Ricca** approach and why it's weak:
> "The algorithm finds the minimal set of the developers such that these developers belong to more than X% of the project files… The threshold was varied from 50% to 70%." Findings: *"The threshold value affects the computed bus factor. • The idea that every person who did at least one commit to a file has knowledge about a file may be too strong. • There are 'update' commits that cover many files but probably do not signify that the committer has knowledge about them. • The algorithm performs well for the small projects, but seems to be problematic for projects with > 30 committers."*

## A7. The normative question: is concentration bad and spreading good?

**Arguments that concentration is bad:**

*Software Engineering at Google* (Titus Winters, Tom Manshreck, Hyrum Wright, O'Reilly 2020), Ch. 3 "Knowledge Sharing" — https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch03.html
> Single Point of Failure: "A bottleneck that occurs when critical information is available from only a single person."
> On how it happens: "it can be easy to fall into a habit of 'Let me take care of that for you.'"
> On the resulting shape of expertise: a split "between people who know 'everything' and novices, with little middle ground."
> On information islands: "knowledge fragmentation that occurs in different parts of an organization that don't communicate with one another."

Martin Fowler, "CodeOwnership," martinfowler.com — https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CodeOwnership.html
> "Of the three the one I really don't like is strong code ownership."
> Strong: "Developers are only allowed to make changes to modules they own. If they need a change made to someone else's module they need to talk to the module owner and get them to make the change."
> Collective: "The code base is owned by the entire team and anyone may make changes anywhere."
> "Personally I prefer the dynamics of a collective code ownership team—particularly in the context of Extreme Programming."

Avelino et al. (ICPC 2016): *"If such knowledgeable personnel abandon the project, the system's lifecycle is seriously compromised, leading to delays in launching new releases, and ultimately to the discontinuation of the project as whole."* And the Python 1994 anecdote quoted in the paper: *"I just returned from a meeting in which the major objection to using Python was its dependence on Guido. They wanted to know if Python would survive if Guido disappeared."*

**The strongest evidence-backed argument that deep ownership is GOOD:**

**"Don't Touch My Code! Examining the Effects of Ownership on Software Quality"**, Christian Bird, Nachiappan Nagappan, Brendan Murphy, Harald Gall, Premkumar Devanbu, *ESEC/FSE 2011*, Szeged. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/dont-touch-my-code-examining-the-effects-of-ownership-on-software-quality/ · PDF: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/bird2011dtm.pdf

Definitions, verbatim:
> "Minor Contributor – A developer who has made changes to a component, but whose ownership is below 5% is considered a minor contributor to that component."
> "Major Contributor – A developer who has made changes to a component and whose ownership is at or above 5% is a major contributor to the component."
> "Ownership – proportion of ownership for the contributor with the highest proportion of ownership"

Their theory, verbatim — **note this is precisely the pro-concentration argument:**
> "If Ownership is high, that indicates that there is one developer who 'owns' the component and has a high level of expertise. This person can also act as a single point of contact for others who need to use the component, need changes to it, or just have questions about it. We theorize that when such a person exists, the software quality is higher resulting in fewer failures."
> "Hypothesis 2 - Software components with a high level of ownership will have fewer failures than components with lower top ownership levels."
> "Hypothesis 1 - Software components with many minor contributors will have more failures than software components that have fewer."

Findings, verbatim:
> "1. The number of minor contributors has a strong positive relationship with both pre- and post-release failures even when controlling for metrics such as size, churn, and complexity."
> "2. Higher levels of ownership for the top contributor to a component results in fewer failures when controlling for the same metrics, but the effect is smaller than the number of minor contributors."
> "We found that high levels of ownership, specifically operationalized as high values of Ownership and Major, and low values of Minor, are associated with less defects."

Their recommendations, verbatim — **these are anti-spreading:**
> "1. Changes made by minor contributors should be reviewed with more scrutiny… When possible, major contributors should perform these code inspections."
> "2. Potential minor contributors should communicate desired changes to developers experienced with the respective binary… Rather than making a desired change directly, these developers should contact a major contributor and communicate the desired change so that it can be made by someone who has higher levels of expertise."
> "3. Components with low ownership should be given priority by QA resources."

And their own scope caveat, verbatim:
> "Microsoft employs strong ownership practices and our results are much more likely to hold in other industrial settings where similar policies are in place. Examining the effect of ownership in contexts where ownership is not stressed as highly, such as in many open source software (OSS) projects, is an area of continued study."

Also from Bird et al.'s framing of *why* the question matters — the cleanest statement of the trade-off in the literature:
> "If ownership has a big effect, then policies to enforce strong code ownership can be put into place… If ownership has little effect, then the normal bottlenecks associated with having one person in charge of each component can be removed, and available talent reassigned at will."

**Google's practice is closer to strong ownership than to collective ownership** — *Software Engineering at Google*, Ch. 9 — https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch09.html
> "Specially named OWNERS files list usernames of people who have ownership responsibilities for a directory and its children."
> "A change might be proposed by any engineer and LGTM'ed by any other engineer, but an owner of the directory in question must also approve this addition to their part of the codebase."
> Ownership "implies a set of responsibilities, such as understanding the code that is owned or knowing how to find somebody who does."

**Practitioner harms of publishing the metric itself** — Jabrayilzade et al., §4.2.5 "Pitfalls of using bus factor," verbatim:
> "The bus factor metric and especially the key engineers part of it may not be received well by the team. Some of the concerns mentioned by the respondents include:
> • Too much attention may be paid to the implicated modules.
> • A key engineer may feel irreplaceable, which may negatively impact their relationship with their employer and teammates (IP1)…
> • Those not listed as key engineers may feel underestimated and uncomfortable about their role in the project.
> • If the bus factor metric is taken at a face value, overestimation of the bus factor may result in false feeling of security.
> • Engineers who work at the projects with low bus factor may be discouraged by the risk or even leave the project."

And their governance recommendation, verbatim:
> "The tool should never be perceived as an ultimate arbiter on the bus factor (or any other health metric) of a project. It should be used as an additional source of information on the project that allows condensing scattered information about the code ownership into a small description with an inevitable loss of context."
> "we believe that the tool should be used on an opt-in basis per team, and the opt-in decision should involve the development team."

Note also from that paper's own framing that the *sign* of the signal is not settled: *"even though a significant share of the open-source projects have experienced bus factor problem, it is unclear whether this result was undesirable or it was simply end of life for a project no longer needed."*

**The 2025–2026 threat to the whole method (AI authorship):**
- Otávio Cury, Guilherme Avelino (the original TF author), "The Impact of Generative AI on Code Expertise Models: An Exploratory Study," arXiv:2507.08160 (2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08160: *"we present an exploratory analysis of how a knowledge model and a Truck Factor algorithm built upon it can be affected by GenAI usage… Our findings reveal that most scenarios led to measurable impacts, indicating the sensitivity of current expertise metrics. This suggests that as GenAI becomes more integrated into development workflows, the reliability of such metrics may decrease."*
- Brett Wheeler, "The Substrate Collapse: AI Code Generation Invalidates Authorship-Based Knowledge Metrics," arXiv:2606.20882 (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20882 — **flagging as a single-author argumentative preprint, not peer-reviewed empirical work**: *"The truck factor, the Degree-of-Authorship metric, and the degree-of-knowledge model all rest on one inference — that authoring a region of code is evidence of understanding it… When an agent generates a module and a human merges it, the version-control record still attributes authorship, but the attribution no longer licenses any conclusion about comprehension: the same footprint is now compatible with full, partial, or no understanding."*
